Duration matching (immunization)
Most cost-efficient
Mechanism: Match asset BPV to liability BPV. Uses corporate bonds + derivatives overlay. When rates rise, capital losses are offset by reinvestment gains — the two effects cancel. Why cheapest: Corporate credit spread means less capital needed up front to fund the same liability. Lower funding cost than Treasuries. Liability: Stays on balance sheet. No defeasance.
Rebalancing
Continuous
Parallel shift
Hedged ✓
Twist risk
Exposed ✗
Cost rank
1st (cheapest)
Cash flow matching
Moderate cost
Mechanism: Buy bonds whose coupons and principal arrive exactly when liability payments are due. No rate assumption — the match is structural. Asset choice: Treasuries chosen for timing, not yield. Cash flow schedule drives selection. Liability: Qualifies for accounting defeasance if Treasuries used — removed from balance sheet.
Rebalancing
None needed
Twist risk
Immune ✓
Defeasance
Yes (Treasuries)
Cost rank
2nd
Tender offer
Most expensive
Mechanism: Repurchase own debt in the open market. Eliminates liability immediately — no portfolio construction. Cost trap: Repurchasing at a tighter spread than actual rating = paying above market price.
BBB issuer at A-rated spread → A spread < BBB spread → A price > BBB price → premium paid, most expensive route.
Execution risk
High
Liability removed
Immediately
Cost rank
3rd (highest)
Exam trap: "accounting defeasance" ≠ "cost efficient." Cash flow matching (Treasuries) qualifies for defeasance but costs more capital. When the question asks for cost efficiency → always duration matching with corporates.

Seven properties of a valid benchmark
PropertyWhat it meansClassic violation
Specified in advanceRules known before period startsBenchmark changed mid-period
AppropriateConsistent with manager's styleEquity benchmark for bond manager
MeasurableValued at same frequency as portfolioWeekly valuation ✗
UnambiguousClearly identified securities + weightsVague inclusion rules
Reflective of opinionsManager has views on constituentsSecurities manager knows nothing about
AccountableManager accepts responsibilityBenchmark imposed without agreement
InvestableCan be replicated passivelyIlliquid or untradeable securities
Weekly valuation violates measurability. Fixed income portfolios must be valued daily. Weekly = cannot track performance on any given day, cannot rebalance against stale prices.
Characteristic 1 (investment-grade + $250M minimum) → valid: unambiguous, investable rules.
Characteristic 3 (historical prices available) → valid: supports accountability and auditability.
1. Classical single-period immunization
Single liability
Match asset duration to a single liability at a fixed future date. Continuous rebalancing required. Assumes parallel shifts only.
Conditions: Asset PV ≥ Liability PV Asset duration = Liability duration Asset convexity ≥ Liability convexity
2. Multiple liability immunization (Fong & Vasicek)
Multiple liabilities
Same three conditions PLUS the asset duration distribution must bracket the liability duration distribution — some assets shorter AND some longer than the liability range. Matching portfolio duration alone is insufficient.
3. Cash flow matching
Twist-immune
Directly pair asset cash flows to each liability date. No rate assumption. No rebalancing. Immune to all shifts — parallel and non-parallel. Eligible for defeasance if Treasuries used.
4. Contingent immunization
Active + safety net
Pursue active management while portfolio value exceeds the trigger. Switch to full immunization immediately when value hits the trigger.
Trigger = PV(liability) at current rates Cushion = Portfolio value − Trigger Active management stops when Cushion = 0
Risk: a sudden large rate move can erode the cushion faster than the manager can react, forcing immunization at an unfavorable level.

Why twists break duration matching — and the one thing that reduces the damage.

The root cause
Duration assumes one uniform rate change across all maturities. Under a twist, short-end and long-end rates move differently. Asset cash flows (spread across maturities) and liability cash flows (concentrated at one date) experience different effective rate changes — creating a funding gap even with a perfect duration match.
Bullet vs barbell — why it matters for twist risk
Bullet portfolioBarbell portfolio
Cash flow distributionConcentrated near liability dateSpread at short and long ends
ConvexityLower (closer to liability)Higher (more dispersed)
Twist exposureLower — all CFs experience similar rate changeHigher — short/long CFs diverge under twist
Parallel shift protectionSame — both duration-matched
Exam rule: to reduce non-parallel shift risk → minimize convexity (bullet structure). NOT maximize cash flow yield. NOT minimize duration gap.
Statement 1 (measurement errors on known liability) → Correct: duration/convexity parameter errors still apply even when the liability amount and date are certain.

Statement 2 (cash flow matching mitigates non-parallel shift risk) → Correct: structural match = immune to all yield curve shapes.
Step 1 — Screen on convexity (hard rule, no exceptions)
Any portfolio with convexity below the liability convexity is immediately eliminated. Non-negotiable — no BPV proximity can save it.
Asset convexity < Liability convexity → ELIMINATED
Step 2 — Smallest BPV gap among survivors
Smallest gap = fewest futures contracts needed = least basis risk and transaction cost.
Nf = (BPV_liability − BPV_portfolio) / BPV_futures BPV_futures = BPV_CTD / conversion factor Negative Nf = short futures · BPV gap = |portfolio BPV − liability BPV|
Step 3 — Don't maximize convexity
Excess convexity = more dispersed cash flows = more twist exposure. Prefer convexity just above the liability level, not maximized.

Yield gap = 0.000% and MV difference tiny (±$4–18). Assets and liabilities move in lockstep. Duration matching succeeds exactly as designed.

Yield curve twists — immunization breaks
MV differences blow out to ±$2,300+. Yield gap opens to ±0.088%. Different maturities move differently → structural mismatch between assets and liabilities.

Critical insight: twist MV differences (~$2,300) dwarf parallel-shift differences (~$4–18). Twist risk is far larger in practice — yet duration matching only addresses parallel shifts.
AM constructed response structure
1. State overall verdict: effective for parallel shifts, fails for twists 2. Cite the specific numbers from the table — yield gap AND MV difference for each scenario type 3. Explain the mechanism: parallel → both sides respond equally; twist → assets and liabilities sit at different maturities and experience different rate changes 4. Conclude: residual structural exposure to non-parallel shifts that duration matching cannot eliminate
Yield Curve Strategies · Interactive Study Map
Receive-fixed swap — two return components
Duration extension tool
What it does: Synthetically increases portfolio duration. You receive the fixed rate and pay MRR (floating). No bond purchase needed — pure rate exposure. Component 1 — Carry: Fixed rate − MRR = daily accrual. Accrues daily, settled periodically (quarterly/semi-annually). Can be positive or negative. Component 2 — Mark-to-market: As rates move, the swap's present value changes. Not a cash flow — only realized if you exit. Rates fall → swap gains value. Rates rise → swap loses value.
Carry settlement
Periodic (quarterly)
MTM settlement
On exit only
Duration effect
Increases ✓
Carry: can be positive OR negative
ConditionCarryWhen it happens
Fixed rate > MRRPositive ✓Normal upward-sloping curve — you earn the spread daily
MRR > Fixed rateNegative ✗Inverted curve or aggressive hike cycle — you pay out the difference
Worst case for receive-fixed: rates rise sharply → carry turns negative AND MTM loses value simultaneously. You lose on both legs.
Pay-fixed swap — the mirror image
You pay the fixed rate and receive MRR. Synthetically reduces or negatives portfolio duration. Profits when rates rise (MTM gain) and when MRR > fixed rate (positive carry in inverted curve). A bearish manager uses pay-fixed swaps (or shorts futures) to push total portfolio duration negative.
Negative portfolio duration — how to achieve it
Bonds always have positive duration — you cannot get negative duration from physical bonds alone. You need derivatives sized large enough to more than offset the positive duration of the bond holdings.
Tools: pay-fixed swaps · short bond futures · buy bond puts Size the notional so: |Derivative duration| > Portfolio bond duration Net duration = Bond duration − Derivative duration offset → negative
If duration = −2: rates rise 100bps → portfolio gains ~2%. Behaves like a short bond position.

Identification is on the government curve. Implementation uses swaps and futures.

How to identify: watch 2s10s spread on the government curve
2s10s = 10-year yield − 2-year yield. Spread widening = steepening. Spread narrowing = flattening. Identify bull vs bear: decompose what each end actually did. If 2yr fell 30bps and 10yr unchanged → bull steepening. If 10yr rose 30bps and 2yr unchanged → bear steepening.
Implementation tools — steepening trade
ViewShort end positionLong end positionNet duration
Bull steepeningReceive-fixed 2yr swap OR long 2yr futuresPay-fixed 10yr OR short 10yr futuresRoughly neutral
Bear steepeningNeutral or long short endPay-fixed 10yr OR short 10yr futures OR buy 30yr payer swaptionRoughly neutral
Key rate duration positioning for bear steepening (Boyd example)
Bear steepening = long rates rise → you want low KRD at the long end relative to the index. Portfolio B had 10yr KRD of 2.85 vs index 7.25 — significantly underweight the long end. Correct position. Portfolio C was overweight the long end (KRD 8.35 vs 7.25) — would underperform badly.
Duration-neutral discipline: a steepening trade is a view on curve shape, not overall rate level. Keep total duration close to benchmark. Only the distribution across maturities changes.
Options-based steepening trade
TradeLong endShort endView
SteepeningBuy payer swaption (right to pay fixed at 30yr)Buy bond call (right to buy 2yr bond)Long rates ↑ · Short rates ↓
FlatteningBuy receiver swaption (right to receive fixed at 30yr)Buy bond put (right to sell 2yr bond)Long rates ↓ · Short rates ↑
Exam trap: receiver swaption profits when rates FALL (you lock in receiving a high fixed rate). Payer swaption profits when rates RISE. Never mix these up.
2s10s is a concept, not one instrument — always specify the curve
VersionWhat it isUsed for
Government bond curve10yr Treasury − 2yr Treasury (US) · 10yr Bund − 2yr Bund (EU)Identification of steepening/flattening · pure policy signal · default meaning of "2s10s"
Swap curve10yr swap rate − 2yr swap rateImplementation · what managers actually trade · includes small credit component
Swap spreadSwap rate − govt bond yield at same maturityCompletely different signal — banking system credit and liquidity conditions
What drives the 2-year yield
Almost entirely monetary policy expectations over the next 24 months. Central bank hikes / hawkish signals → 2yr rises immediately Central bank cuts / dovish pivot → 2yr falls immediately Hot CPI or strong payrolls → more hikes priced in → 2yr rises The 2yr barely cares about 2030 — it's anchored to what the CB does right now
What drives the 10-year yield — two components
1. Expected future short rates: what do investors think policy rates will average over 10 years? Connects to monetary policy at a much longer horizon. 2. Term premium: extra compensation for locking up money for 10 years. Captures inflation uncertainty, fiscal risk, government bond supply, global demand for safe assets.
Spread = gap between now and the future
Spread signalWhat it meansSteepening type likely
CB hiking aggressively2yr rises fast → spread narrows/invertsFlattening / inversion
CB cuts or signals cuts2yr falls → spread widensBull steepening
LT inflation expectations rise10yr rises via term premiumBear steepening
Heavy LT government bond supply10yr rises → spread widensBear steepening
Strong foreign CB demand for USTTerm premium suppressed → 10yr lowFlattening
Identification workflow: (1) observe 2s10s widening on govt curve → steepening confirmed. (2) Check which end moved → identifies bull vs bear. (3) Check macro drivers (CB language, inflation breakevens, term premium, fiscal) → anticipates which type is coming next.
What key rate duration (KRD) actually measures
Sensitivity of portfolio value to a rate change at one specific maturity point on the yield curve, holding all other maturities constant. Unlike overall duration which assumes parallel shifts.
KRD at 10yr = +6 means: 10yr rate falls 1% → portfolio gains ~6% 10yr rate rises 1% → portfolio loses ~6% (other maturities unchanged)
Positive vs negative KRD — what each means
KRD at maturity XManager's viewPositionExample instrument
High positiveRate at X will fallOverweight that maturityBuy bonds at X tenor · receive-fixed swap at X
High negativeRate at X will riseUnderweight / short that maturityShort futures at X · pay-fixed swap at X
Neutral (= index)No view on that maturityMatch index weight—
The surgical power of KRD — expressing curve shape views
A manager can simultaneously hold: Positive KRD at 2yr → expects short rates to fall Negative KRD at 10yr → expects long rates to rise = Bear steepening bet, total duration roughly neutral
You cannot see this nuance by looking at total portfolio duration alone. Two portfolios with identical total duration can have completely different curve exposures.

Swaption fundamentals — what you own
A swaption gives you the right but not obligation to enter into a swap at a pre-agreed fixed rate on a future date.
TypeRight to…Exercise when…Rate viewDuration effect
Receiver swaptionReceive fixed, pay floatingRates fall (fixed rate you receive > market)Bullish (rates fall)Long duration when exercised
Payer swaptionPay fixed, receive floatingRates rise (fixed rate you pay < market)Bearish (rates rise)Short duration when exercised
Long vs short swaption positions
PositionYou…Max lossMax gain
Long receiver swaptionPay premium upfrontPremium paidUnlimited (if rates fall far)
Short receiver swaptionCollect premiumUnlimitedPremium collected
Long payer swaptionPay premium upfrontPremium paidUnlimited (if rates rise far)
Short payer swaptionCollect premiumUnlimitedPremium collected
Cook example — downward parallel shift 50bps
Cook expects rates to fall. She wants to benefit. Long receiver swaption = right to receive fixed. If rates fall, she exercises and receives an above-market fixed rate. The swaption gains value as rates fall. Correct position ✓ Short receiver swaption = she sold the right to someone else. If rates fall, the counterparty exercises against her — she loses. Wrong direction.
The most common exam trap: confusing which swaption benefits from which rate direction. Anchor it to the underlying swap logic — receiver swaption = you want to receive fixed = you want rates to fall so your fixed rate looks attractive. Payer swaption = you want to pay fixed = you want rates to rise so paying the lower locked-in fixed rate is valuable.
Steepening trade with swaptions — summary
Steepening = long rates rise, short rates fall Long payer swaption at 30yr → right to pay fixed at 30yr → profits when 30yr rates rise ✓ Long call on 2yr bond → right to buy 2yr bond → profits when 2yr bond price rises = 2yr rates fall ✓ Combined = pure steepening bet with limited downside (premium paid)
The full expected return formula
E(R) = Rolldown return + (−Duration × Δyield) + (0.5 × Convexity × Δyield²) + ΔFX (if unhedged foreign bond)
Never drop the convexity term — even if the yield move seems small. The exam tests whether you include it. With 50bps move it's tiny (0.02%) but it's the difference between answer choices.
Component 1 — Rolldown return
The price appreciation from a bond "rolling down" an upward-sloping stable yield curve as time passes. A 2-year bond becomes a 1-year bond after one year — and since 1-year yields are lower, its price rises.
Rolldown = (Expected price in 1yr − Price today) / Price today Example: (98.75 − 97.00) / 97.00 = 1.804%
The expected price in 1yr assumes an unchanged yield curve — it is the price the bond would have if it simply aged one year with no rate moves. It is given in the exhibit, not calculated from scratch.
Component 2 — Duration + Convexity price effect
Price effect = (−Duration × Δyield) + (0.5 × Convexity × Δyield²) Example (bullet, −50bps shift): = (−4.50 × −0.0050) + (0.5 × 17.0 × 0.0050²) = +2.250% + 0.021% = 2.271%
Use the expected duration and convexity in 1 year (from exhibit), not today's values. Δyield is negative for rate falls. Always convert bps to decimals: 50bps = 0.0050.
Component 3 — Currency effect
If the foreign currency appreciates vs your home currency → add positive FX return If the foreign currency depreciates vs your home currency → subtract FX loss Cook example: USD depreciates against EUR by 0.75% → USD-denominated returns lose 0.75% when converted to EUR → −0.75%
Watch the direction carefully. "USD depreciates against EUR" = your USD bonds are worth less in EUR terms = negative FX contribution. Don't flip the sign.
Cook worked example — full calculation
ComponentBulletBarbell
Rolldown(98.75−97.00)/97.00 = 1.804%(99.75−97.75)/97.75 = 2.046%
Duration effect (−D × −0.005)−4.50 × −0.005 = +2.250%−4.45 × −0.005 = +2.225%
Convexity effect (0.5×Cx×0.005²)0.5×17.0×0.000025 = +0.021%0.5×40.0×0.000025 = +0.050%
FX (USD depreciates vs EUR)−0.750%−0.750%
Total3.325% ≈ 3.32%3.571% ≈ 3.58%
Barbell wins because of higher convexity (40 vs 17) and higher rolldown (2.046% vs 1.804%). In a falling rate environment, convexity advantage is amplified.
Rolldown strategy — why it works
Buy further out on an upward-sloping curve. As time passes the bond rolls toward a lower-yield, higher-price point. You earn rolldown return on top of yield — as long as the curve stays stable and upward-sloping. This is why the 2-year zero-coupon (bought at 96.1169, expected to be worth 99.0090 in a year) earns more than the 1-year zero-coupon in the Thai bond example.
BPV / DV01 — same thing, different names
Dollar change in portfolio value for a 1bp (0.01%) move in rates.
BPV = Modified duration × Market value × 0.0001 Example: Duration 5 · MV $10M → BPV = 5 × $10M × 0.0001 = $5,000 per bp
Why it matters: Duration is a percentage — you can't subtract durations across portfolios of different sizes. BPV puts everything in the same unit (dollars per bp) so arithmetic works. Hedging: Nf = (BPV_target − BPV_portfolio) / BPV_futures Immunization: match asset BPV to liability BPV so a 1bp move hits both equally
Negative convexity — callable bonds
At high yields: call is out of the money, callable bond behaves like option-free bond — normal positive convexity. At low yields: call is deep in the money. Issuer's right to call becomes very valuable. Market knows bond may be called → price stops rising at normal pace → price-yield curve bends the wrong way → negative convexity. The asymmetry: less upside when rates fall (call caps price) but full downside when rates rise (call not exercised). You keep all the risk, lose some of the reward.
Why callable bonds must offer a higher yield: compensation for this asymmetric payoff. You are short the call option → you must be paid for it.
Forward rate bias
What theory says (UIP): high-yield currency should depreciate by exactly the yield differential — no free lunch. What actually happens: high-yield currencies depreciate by less than predicted, or not at all. The yield advantage is not fully offset. Implication: go unhedged into high-yielding currencies to earn excess returns. Amplify by borrowing in low-yield currencies (carry trade).
Carry trade = borrow in low-yield currency (JPY at 0.5%) · invest in high-yield currency (BRL at 10%) · pocket the spread. Works because forward rate bias means the low-yield currency doesn't appreciate enough to wipe out the carry.
Stable yield curve — what generates excess return
When rates don't move, you cannot earn excess return from predicting rate direction. The only way to beat the benchmark is to earn more carry.
StrategyWorks under stable curve?Why
Increase duration above benchmarkYesLonger bonds earn more yield + rolldown without rate rise penalty
Add leverageYesBorrow at short rates, invest in longer bonds, pocket the spread
Reduce duration below benchmarkNo — least likelyShorter bonds earn less yield, no rate protection needed, guaranteed underperformance vs benchmark
Reducing duration only makes sense if you expect rates to RISE — then shorter portfolio loses less than benchmark. Under a stable curve it just sacrifices yield for nothing.

Two approaches to credit risk modelling
Both estimate probability of default (POD) and derive fair credit spreads — from different angles.
StructuralReduced form
Core ideaAsset value falls below default thresholdMacro + financials → default intensity
Also calledDistance to default modelsIntensity models
Data sourceEquity market data (price, vol, mkt cap)Financial ratios, macro variables
OutputDaily POD + implied fair spreadDefault intensity → fair spread
ExamplesMoody's EDF, Bloomberg DRSKAltman z-score
Core intuition
A firm defaults when asset value falls below liabilities. Structural models track the asset value process and estimate the probability it crosses below the default threshold.
Why "distance to default"?
The model measures how far asset value is from the default threshold, in units of asset volatility.
Distance to default = (Asset value − Default threshold) / Asset volatility Higher distance → lower POD → tighter credit spread Lower distance → higher POD → wider credit spread
Inputs — inferred from equity markets
Asset value and volatility are unobservable. Equity = call option on firm assets → infer from equity data.
Market capitalization → proxy for asset value Equity price volatility → proxy for asset volatility
Examples
Moody's EDF — Expected Default Frequency, daily POD estimates Bloomberg DRSK — daily POD + implied fair credit spreads
Core intuition
Rather than modelling asset value, reduced form models look at statistical relationships between macro conditions, issuer financials, and observed defaults. Default is a surprise event whose intensity varies with observable inputs.
What they estimate
A default intensity — probability of default per unit time — as a function of observable variables.
Fair credit spread ≈ Default intensity × LGD
Inputs used
Macroeconomic conditions (GDP growth, credit conditions) Issuer financial ratios (leverage, coverage, profitability) Industry and sector characteristics
Key difference: reduced form models don't need equity market data — works for private firms, sovereigns, any issuer without listed equity.
Altman z-score formula
z = (1.2×A) + (1.4×B) + (3.3×C) + (0.6×D) + (0.999×E) A = Working capital / Total assets B = Retained earnings / Total assets C = EBIT / Total assets D = Market value of equity / Total liabilities E = Sales / Total assets
Interactive z-score calculator
A (WC/TA)0.20
B (RE/TA)0.20
C (EBIT/TA)0.10
D (MVE/TL)1.00
E (Sales/TA)1.00
Exam note: the formula is always given in the question. Focus on plugging in the inputs correctly and interpreting the z-score against the three bands.
Standardized fixed coupon
CDS contracts pay a standardized fixed coupon — makes settlement operationally straightforward. This is NOT the fair spread.
IG issuers → fixed coupon = 1% (100bps) per year HY issuers → fixed coupon = 5% (500bps) per year
The fixed coupon ≠ fair CDS spread. The difference is settled via an up-front payment at initiation.
Who pays whom at initiation?
Fair spread > fixed coupon → buyer pays up-front to seller (buyer pays below-market coupon, compensates upfront) Fair spread < fixed coupon → seller pays up-front to buyer (seller receives above-market coupon, compensates upfront) Fair spread = fixed coupon → no up-front payment
Inverse price / spread relationship
Spreads rise → protection more expensive → old contract (low fixed coupon) worth less → CDS price falls Spreads fall → old contract worth more → CDS price rises
Same logic as bonds: price and yield move in opposite directions.
Up-front premium formula
CDS spread > fixed coupon: Up-front = (CDS spread − fixed coupon) × EffSpreadDur → paid by protection BUYER to seller CDS spread < fixed coupon: Up-front = (fixed coupon − CDS spread) × EffSpreadDur → paid by protection SELLER to buyer
Intuition: up-front payment = PV of the difference between what you pay (fixed coupon) and what is fair (CDS spread), scaled by duration.

CDS price formula
CDS price ≈ 1 + [(fixed coupon − CDS spread) × EffSpreadDur]
Expressed as % of notional. Same inverse spread/price relationship as bonds.
Spread rises → (coupon − spread) more negative → price falls below 1 Spread falls → (coupon − spread) more positive → price rises above 1

Credit cycle drives strategy
The shape of the credit spread curve changes predictably across the economic cycle. An active manager exploits these changes using both cash bonds and CDS.
Economic stageHY curve shapeHY spreads vs IG
RecoverySteepensHY narrows more than IG
SlowdownFlattens / invertsHY widens more than IG
Economic recovery
HY spreads narrow more than IG spreads. HY credit curve steepens.
Cash strategy
BuyShort-term HY bonds
BuyLong-term HY bonds
SellIG bonds
CDS strategy
SellHY protection
BuyIG protection
HY spreads compress faster in recovery — you want to be long HY (cash) or short HY protection (CDS). Hedge via IG: sell IG bonds or buy IG protection.
Economic slowdown
HY spreads widen more than IG spreads. HY credit curve flattens/inverts.
Cash strategy
BuyIG bonds
BuyLong-term HY bonds
SellShort-term HY bonds
CDS strategy
SellIG protection
BuyLong-term HY protection
BuyShort-term HY protection
HY spreads blow out fastest in a slowdown — especially short-term HY (inverted curve). Buy HY protection (CDS) or sell HY bonds. Shift to IG or buy IG bonds.
Why the HY curve inverts in a slowdown
Near-term default risk spikes faster than long-term risk. Short-dated HY spreads must compensate investors for immediate default risk — they blow out more than long-dated spreads. The short end rises sharply relative to the long end → curve inverts.
Cash vs CDS — same view, different instrument
Bullish credit (recovery) → Cash: buy bonds / CDS: sell protection Bearish credit (slowdown) → Cash: sell bonds / CDS: buy protection
CDS allows more surgical positioning: you can be bearish on short-term HY and bullish on long-term HY simultaneously — a pure curve trade that is harder to implement efficiently in cash bonds.
IG vs HY — the relative value dimension
Recovery: HY benefits more than IG → overweight HY, underweight IG Slowdown: HY suffers more than IG → underweight HY, overweight IG
Steepening — long end rises more than short end
View: fiscal stress, inflation risk, or heavy long-end supply pushes long-term spreads higher. Short end stays anchored. The gap between 10yr and 1yr widens.
Current
Expected
Buy protection
Sell protection
Sellprotection at 1yr — short-end spreads stable → collect premium
Buyprotection at 10yr — long-end spreads rise → position gains in value
Both legs profit as the curve steepens. The trade is a pure shape bet — not a directional view on whether spreads go up or down overall.
Flattening — short end rises, long end falls
View: near-term credit stress pushes short-end spreads higher while the long end falls (recovery priced in further out). The gap between 10yr and 1yr narrows.
Buyprotection at 1yr — short-end spreads rise → position gains in value
Sellprotection at 10yr — long-end spreads fall → position gains in value
Both legs profit as the curve flattens. The two ends converge — the gap narrows.
Buy protection = bearish on credit at that maturity
You pay a fixed premium. If spreads widen, your contract is below market — your CDS gains in mark-to-market value.
Spread rises 100 → 150bps: your contract (paying only 100bps) is worth more than a new contract → MTM gain
Sell protection = bullish on credit at that maturity
You receive a fixed premium. If spreads narrow, your contract (receiving above-market premium) gains in value.
Spread falls 100 → 50bps: your contract (receiving 100bps) is worth more than a new contract → MTM gain
Duration weighting — isolating curve shape
Long-dated CDS has more spread duration than short-dated. An equal-notional trade is not curve-neutral — it has directional exposure.
Ratio = EffSpreadDur(long) / EffSpreadDur(short) e.g. 8.9 / 4.9 = 1.82× → for every $1 of 10yr notional, use $1.82 of 5yr notional
Without duration weighting, the trade accidentally becomes a bet on overall spread level instead of pure curve shape.
What an FRN pays
An FRN pays a coupon that resets every period to the current benchmark rate (MRR) plus a fixed quoted margin (QM). The QM is set at issuance and never changes.
Coupon = MRR + QM Example: MRR 3.00% + QM 0.50% → coupon = 3.50% this period Next reset: MRR becomes whatever the market rate is → new coupon
Two separate risks
Because the coupon resets automatically, the FRN has very low rate risk. But it still carries credit / spread risk — if the issuer deteriorates, the market demands a higher spread than QM, and the price falls.
Risk typeDriverFRN exposure
Rate riskMRR benchmark movesNear zero — coupon resets
Spread / credit riskIssuer credit quality (DM)Meaningful — DM can widen
An FRN doesn't eliminate risk — it swaps rate risk for credit risk.
Why rate duration is near zero
When MRR rises 100bps, the next coupon also rises 100bps — you are automatically compensated. The bond's price barely needs to move.
Fixed-rate bond: coupon is fixed → price must fall when rates rise to make yield competitive FRN: coupon rises with rates → price stays near par → rate duration ≈ 0
Not exactly zero — time to next reset
Rate duration ≈ time until the next coupon reset. Quarterly reset → rate duration ≈ 0.25 years. Right after a reset it is at its minimum; right before the next reset it is slightly higher.
This is why EffRateDur is still calculated — to measure this small but non-zero residual rate sensitivity.
FRN vs fixed-rate bond
Fixed-rate bondFRN
CouponFixed foreverResets to MRR + QM
Rate durationHigh (full maturity)Near zero (time to reset)
Spread durationHighHigh (full maturity)
Price when rates riseFalls significantlyBarely changes
Price when DM widensFallsFalls
Spread duration — the real risk of an FRN
Even though MRR resets automatically, the discount margin (DM) — the spread investors actually require — can change any time credit conditions change.
Credit deteriorates → DM widens → bond price falls Credit improves → DM narrows → bond price rises MRR stays constant throughout → pure spread risk, no rate risk
Spread duration magnitude
Spread duration ≈ full maturity of the FRN. The coupon reset protects against rate moves but provides zero protection against credit spread moves.
Common mistake: assuming FRNs have low duration full stop. They have low rate duration but normal spread duration. In 2008, FRN prices fell sharply — not because rates moved, but because credit spreads exploded.
DM is yield, QM is coupon
Exactly like a fixed-rate bond: yield > coupon → discount; yield < coupon → premium.
DM = QM → par (coupon matches what market demands) DM > QM → below par (market demands more than bond pays) DM < QM → above par (bond pays more than market demands)
Interactive: move DM vs QM
QM (bond pays)50 bps
DM (mkt requires)50 bps
EffRateDur — sensitivity to MRR moves
EffRateDurFRN = PV− − PV+2 × ΔMRR × PV0
PV0 = current price · PV− = price when MRR shifted down · PV+ = price when MRR shifted up · ΔMRR = shock size
EffSpreadDur — sensitivity to DM (spread) moves
EffSpreadDurFRN = PV− − PV+2 × ΔDM × PV0
Same structure — PV− = price when DM shifted down · PV+ = price when DM shifted up · ΔDM = shock size
Why the two formulas are identical in structure
Both are the general effective duration formula. The only difference is what you shock in the denominator:
Shock MRR → measures price sensitivity to benchmark rate moves → EffRateDur Shock DM → measures price sensitivity to credit spread moves → EffSpreadDur
The numerator (PV− − PV+) is always the same. The denominator answers: sensitive to what?
Calculator
PV₀ (current)100.00
PV− (down)101.00
PV+ (up)99.00
Shock (bps)25 bps
Analytical duration — the textbook assumption
Measures price sensitivity to a change in the risk-free benchmark rate, assuming the credit spread stays frozen. It's a pure mathematical calculation from the bond's cash flows.
Price change ≈ −Duration × Δbenchmark rate (spread held constant)
The real-world problem: spreads don't stay frozen
When benchmark rates rise (e.g. central bank tightening), the economy is usually still growing. For risky bonds, this tends to narrow credit spreads because default risk falls in a healthy economy.
These two forces work in opposite directions on the bond price:
Benchmark rate rises → price falls (standard duration effect) Spread narrows → price rises (partially offsets the fall)
The net price move is smaller than analytical duration predicts.
Empirical duration — measured from reality
Run a regression of actual bond price returns against actual benchmark rate changes. The slope of that regression is the empirical duration — it captures the true net price sensitivity including the spread offset.
Because spreads move opposite to rates for risky bonds, empirical duration is always lower than analytical duration for low-quality bonds. The lower the credit quality, the bigger the gap.
The two opposing forces — visual decomposition
A 100bps rate rise hits the bond from two directions simultaneously. The chart below tracks the price path through both effects for three credit qualities.
Reading the chart
All three bonds start at 0%. The rate shock pushes every bond down the same amount (−2% at duration 5). What happens next depends on credit quality:
IG (blue) — spreads barely move, bond stays at −1.95%. Empirical ≈ Analytical. HY (orange) — spreads tighten meaningfully, bond recovers to −0.8%. Empirical is ~60% lower than analytical. Distressed (red) — spread move dominates, bond returns almost to 0%. Empirical ≈ 0.
Same mathematical duration, three completely different empirical durations. The difference is entirely driven by how much the credit spread co-moves with the rate shock.
Interactive example
Adjust the inputs to see the gap between what analytical duration predicts and the net empirical price move.
Analytical dur 5.0
Rate change (bps) +100
Spread offset (bps) −40

Spread offset = how much spreads narrow when rates rise (0 = IG · 40+ = HY typical · 80+ = distressed)

Why credit quality determines the gap
The lower the credit quality, the more the bond price is driven by default probability rather than benchmark rates. Default probability is mostly driven by the economy — which is also what drives spread changes.
Credit qualitySpread sizeRate-spread correlationEmpirical vs Analytical
IG Small, stable Weak Nearly equal
HY Large Moderate negative Empirical noticeably lower
Distressed Very large Strong negative Empirical near zero
The distressed bond extreme
A distressed bond trades almost entirely on its recovery value and default probability. A 100bps move in Treasury yields barely affects its price — the price is set by whether the company survives, not by the risk-free rate. Empirical duration approaches zero.
Why this matters for portfolio management
Using analytical duration overstates rate risk for HY portfolios — you would over-hedge Empirical duration gives the true hedge ratio needed to neutralize actual price sensitivity Duration matching using analytical duration will leave residual rate risk for low-quality portfolios
One-line anchor
Analytical duration assumes spreads are frozen. Empirical duration captures the real world — for risky bonds, spreads move opposite to rates, so the net price sensitivity is lower than the formula suggests.
The mechanism in 3 steps
1. Benchmark rate rises → bond price should fall (duration effect) 2. Rising rates = healthy economy → credit spreads narrow → bond price rises back up 3. Net price change < analytical prediction → empirical duration < analytical duration
How empirical duration is estimated
Regress actual historical bond price returns on actual benchmark rate changes. The regression slope = empirical duration. It picks up the true net sensitivity including all real-world correlations — spread movements, liquidity, and risk appetite shifts — that the analytical formula ignores.
Exam trap: empirical duration is not always lower than analytical. For some bonds (e.g. high-quality munis with tax effects) it can differ in unexpected ways. The curriculum focuses on the low-quality case where spread offsets dominate.
1CDS MTM — protection buyer direction
Manager buys CDS protection at 1.75% spread. Spread immediately falls to 1.60%.
Wrong reasoning: calculated +€131,250 gain but forgot direction. A spread fall is BAD for the protection buyer.
Correct: the protection buyer profits when spreads WIDEN (credit deteriorates). When spreads NARROW the buyer loses — the contract locked in at 1.75% is now above market. → Loss of €131,250.
MTM = −EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread × Notional = −8.75 × (1.60% − 1.75%) × €10,000,000 = −8.75 × (−0.0015) × €10,000,000 = +€131,250 in absolute terms → but LOSS for buyer Direction rule: Buy protection → profit when spreads WIDEN Sell protection → profit when spreads NARROW
2Stone's three suggestions for Palma
Which suggestion is most likely correct when buying foreign bonds?
Wrong: said Statement 3 (credit cycles must coincide) was correct.
Correct: Statement 1 (spread advantage vs hedge cost) is correct. The other two have inverted logic.
✓ Spread advantage: hedging cost can negate the yield pickup — covered interest parity means hedge cost ≈ rate differential. Always evaluate net of hedge cost. ✗ Pegged currencies: Stone said avoid local currency in pegged countries — WRONG. A peg REDUCES currency risk → pegged currencies are MORE attractive, not less. ✗ Credit cycles coincide: Stone said ensure cycles coincide — WRONG. Coinciding cycles = no diversification benefit. You WANT different cycle stages.
3Larent's CDO statements — which is correct?
Three statements: relative value, diversification, senior vs mezzanine with increasing correlations.
Wrong: confused the direction of senior vs mezzanine when correlations increase.
Correct: relative value statement is correct. The other two are wrong.
✓ Relative value: AA CDO priced at BB default rate expectation = spread overcompensates for actual risk → genuine relative value. ✗ Diversification: CDO + its own underlying bonds = same exposure. No diversification — just concentration. ✗ Senior vs mezzanine: Larent said senior gains more as correlations increase — WRONG. Higher correlation → bimodal distribution → senior loses relative value, mezzanine gains.
4Nucor/Smith — which liquidity statement is least likely correct?
Three statements about market liquidity. Which is least likely correct?
Wrong: said Statement 2 (embedded options → lower liquidity) was incorrect. Statement 3 is actually the wrong one.
Correct: Statement 3 is least likely correct. Liquidity is HIGHEST immediately after issuance — new issues attract maximum activity.
✓ Statement 1: Gov bonds and higher-quality corporates more liquid in stress → correct, flight to quality. ✓ Statement 2: Bonds with embedded options trade with lower liquidity → correct. Option complexity widens bid-ask. ✗ Statement 3: "Liquidity reduced when new supply issued" → WRONG. Liquidity is highest immediately after issuance.
5Benchmark spread vs G-spread
Dealers quote a spread to Treasuries whose maturity does not match the bond's maturity. Which spread measure is this?
Wrong: said G-spread. The G-spread actually corrects for maturity mismatch through interpolation.
Correct: Benchmark spread. Dealers quote against the nearest on-the-run Treasury regardless of maturity match.
Benchmark spread: spread over nearest on-the-run Treasury → maturity DOES NOT match (what dealers quote on Bloomberg) G-spread: spread over INTERPOLATED government yield → maturity-matched by construction (requires calculation) I-spread: spread over swap rate of matching maturity Key phrase: "maturity does not match" = benchmark spread Key phrase: "interpolated" = G-spread
6BBB bond excess return — yield decline vs spread
50bp decline in yield over one year. BBB bond: OAS 2.75%, EffSpreadDur 6, POD 0.75%, LGD 40%.
Wrong: reinterpreted "yield decline" as a benchmark rate move (not a spread move) and got 2.45% instead of 5.45%.
Correct: use the decline directly as ΔSpread = −0.50% in the excess return formula. Answer = 5.45%.
Excess return = Spread₀ − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD) = 2.75% − (6 × −0.50%) − (0.75% × 40%) = 2.75% + 3.00% − 0.30% = 5.45% Rule: when the formula gives a clean answer matching an option, trust the first calculation. Don't reinterpret the question.
7CDO tranches — increasing default correlations
Choate: long subordinated (Class B), short senior (Class A). What does this signal about expected default correlations?
Wrong: initially said decreasing correlations benefit subordinated relative to senior.
Correct: INCREASING correlations → mezzanine/subordinated gains relative to senior. Long sub / short senior = bet on increasing correlations.
Low correlation: defaults predictable and moderate → reliably hit lower tranches → senior very safe → senior is valuable High correlation: loss distribution bimodal (near-zero OR catastrophic) → catastrophic tail now threatens senior too → senior loses relative value → mezzanine gains
Long sub + short senior → profits when sub outperforms senior Sub outperforms senior when correlations INCREASE → Choate expects INCREASING default correlations Memory anchor: high correlation = bimodal = senior no longer safely remote
8Goodwin Q29 — alternative to individual bonds
Goodwin wants credit exposure while limiting liquidity risk in a rapidly changing market. What should XBK traders suggest?
Wrong: answered "Bond 2" — misread the question. Asked for an ALTERNATIVE to individual bonds.
Correct: CDS or bond ETFs. Both provide credit exposure with better liquidity than individual bonds.
CDS: highly liquid even in volatile markets, surgical credit exposure, easy to unwind Bond ETFs: trade on exchange with continuous pricing, instant diversified exposure
Read the question carefully. "Gain credit exposure while limiting liquidity risk" asks for a liquid instrument TYPE, not which of the three bonds is best.

Q1 · Stone/Palma ✗ got wrong
Stone outlines three suggestions for Palma investing outside EU markets:
1. Evaluate whether spread advantage is negated by cost of currency hedge.
2. Avoid local currency investments in countries where exchange rate is pegged.
3. Ensure timing of credit cycles across markets coincides.

Which suggestion is most likely correct?
B — Spread advantage is most likely correct
A — Credit cycles coinciding = no diversification benefit
C — Pegged currency = less risk, not more; logic is inverted
Spread advantage: correct — you must net FX hedge cost against spread pickup. If hedge cost ≥ spread, no real advantage.

Pegged currency: wrong direction — a peg reduces FX risk, making local currency more attractive.

Credit cycles coinciding: wrong logic — if cycles coincide, there is no diversification.
Trap: peg = stable FX = lower risk = MORE attractive for unhedged investment.
Q2 · CDS Mark-to-Market ✗ got wrong
Manager buys CDS protection at 1.75% spread (EffSpreadDur = 8.75, notional €10M). Spread immediately falls to 1.60%. MTM?
A — Loss of €131,250
MTM = EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread × Notional = 8.75 × (1.60% − 1.75%) × €10,000,000 = 8.75 × (−0.0015) × €10,000,000 = −€131,250 → LOSS Buying protection is bearish on credit — you profit when spreads widen. Spreads fell here (credit improved), so the protection buyer loses.
Trap: Spread fell → protection buyer loses. Spread fell → protection seller gains.
Q3 · Unhedged excess return ✗ got wrong
Equal-weighted portfolio: USD IG (OAS 1.25%, EL 0.40%), USD HY (3.00%, EL 2.25%), EUR IG (1.15%, EL 0.50%), EUR HY (3.25%, EL 2.50%). EUR depreciates 2% vs USD.
A — −0.257%
Excess return per asset = OAS − Expected Loss (± FX for non-base currency) USD IG: 1.25% − 0.40% = +0.85% USD HY: 3.00% − 2.25% = +0.75% EUR IG: 1.15% − 0.50% − 2.00% = −1.35% EUR HY: 3.25% − 2.50% − 2.00% = −1.25% Average = (0.85 + 0.75 − 1.35 − 1.25) / 4 ≈ −0.25% FX drag only applies to EUR allocations.
Trap: Subtract 2% EUR depreciation only from EUR-denominated positions.
Q4 · Goodwin — alternative to individual bonds ✗ got wrong
Goodwin wants to gain credit exposure while limiting liquidity risk. Best alternative?
C — CDS contracts or bond ETFs
A/B — Individual bonds have worse liquidity, not better
The question asks for an alternative to individual bonds — not which individual bond to buy. CDS contracts trade in a highly liquid OTC market. Bond ETFs trade on exchange with continuous pricing.
Trap: Misreading the question. Asks what to use INSTEAD of individual bonds.
Q5 · Larent — structured instruments ✗ got wrong
Three statements: (A) AA-rated CDOs offer relative value because yield spread reflects BB default expectations, (B) CDOs provide diversification beyond underlying bonds, (C) increasing default correlations increase value of senior tranches. Which is correct?
A — Relative value
B — Wrong: CDO exposure = same underlying bonds, no diversification
C — Wrong: increasing correlations hurt senior, benefit mezzanine
B incorrect: CDO + underlying bonds = concentrated, not diversified exposure.
C incorrect: rising correlations → bimodal loss distribution → catastrophic tail threatens senior. Mezzanine/subordinated gains relative to senior.
Higher correlation → bimodal distribution → senior LOSES relative value.
Q6 · Smith liquidity statements ✗ got wrong
Which is least likely correct?
1: Gov bonds and high-quality corporates more liquid than lower-rated in high volatility.
2: Bonds with embedded options trade with lower liquidity than conventional bonds.
3: Liquidity is reduced when significant new supply of bonds is issued.
C — Statement 3 is least likely correct
Statement 3 is backwards. Liquidity is actually highest immediately after issuance. New bonds attract most market participants, price discovery freshest.
Trap: Statement 3 sounds intuitive. But the exam tests the seasoning effect: new issues = peak liquidity.
Q7 · Choate COF structured instruments ✗ got wrong
COF portfolio: overweight MBS, long CDO subordinated Class B, short CDO senior Class A. What is Choate expecting?
B — Lower rate volatility + increasing default correlations
MBS overweight → MBS has negative convexity from prepayment optionality. Lower rate vol = prepayment option worth less = MBS prices rise. Bet on lower rate volatility.

Long sub / short senior → profits from increasing correlations as mezzanine outperforms senior.
Long sub / short senior = bet on INCREASING correlations.
Q8 · Island spread / Stone data / West report ✗ got wrong
Part 1: Dealers quote a spread over a Treasury whose maturity does not match the bond's maturity. Which spread measure?
Part 2: Assuming no change in credit spreads, which analyst data item is most useful?
Part 3: Is West's two-section top-down report correctly structured?
Part 1: C — Benchmark spread (maturity mismatch is the key clue)
Part 2: C — Expected probability of default (forward-looking)
Part 3: B — Incorrect on macro factors (KRD is risk measure, not macro)
Benchmark spread = nearest on-the-run Treasury → maturity mismatch. G-spread = interpolated yield → matches maturity.

West's report: KRD belongs in risk measures section, not macro section.
G-spread corrects maturity mismatch via interpolation. Benchmark spread doesn't.

Q10 · Credit spread measures — Z-DM vs DM ✗ got wrong
Which is most accurate?
A. DM is yield spread over MRR established upon issuance.
B. Z-DM above DM if MRR expected constant.
C. Yield spread = G-spread if government yield curve is flat.
C — Yield spread = G-spread when government yield curve is flat
A — Wrong: describes QM, not DM (DM recalculated each period)
B — Wrong: if MRR constant, Z-DM = DM (no difference)
G-spread uses interpolated government yield at bond's maturity. When curve is flat, interpolation gives same rate as nearest Treasury → both spreads converge.
DM vs QM: DM floats each period; QM fixed at issuance.
Q11 · BB bond — instantaneous excess return ✗ got wrong
BB bond: credit spread 3.50%, EffSpreadDur 5. Spread widens 50bps instantaneously (holding period = zero).
B — −2.50%
Instantaneous excess return = −EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread = −5 × 0.50% = −2.50% Zero holding period → no carry, no expected loss. Only price impact counts. Widening → price falls.
Spread widening = loss for bond holder.
Q12 · BBB bond — 1-year excess return ✗ got wrong
BBB bond: spread 2.75%, EffSpreadDur 6, POD 0.75%, LGD 40%. Spread declines 50bps over one-year holding period.
C — 5.45%
Excess return = Spread₀ − (EffSpreadDur × ΔSpread) − (POD × LGD) = 2.75% − (6 × −0.50%) − (0.75% × 40%) = 2.75% + 3.00% − 0.30% = 5.45%
"50bp decline in yield" = spread tightens 50bps → ΔSpread = −0.50% → positive price contribution.

Q16 · VaR calculation ✗ got wrong
Bond: $75M face, price 104.0175, ModDur 9.887. Daily yield vol = 1.50bps. 99% confidence (z = 2.33), 1-month (21 trading days).
A — $1,234,105
Step 1: MV = $75M × (104.0175/100) = $78,013,125 Step 2: VaR = MV × ModDur × Daily yield vol × z × √days = $78,013,125 × 9.887 × 0.00015 × 2.33 × √21 = $78,013,125 × 9.887 × 0.00015 × 2.33 × 4.583 ≈ $1,234,105
Daily yield vol = 1.50bps = 0.00015. Scale monthly using √21. Compute MV first.

Index-Based Equity · Interactive Study Map
The 5 main weighting methods
MethodWeight driverExample
Price-weightedShare price onlyDJIA · Nikkei 225
Market-cap (full)Price × total sharesOld-school cap indexes
Float-adjusted capPrice × floating sharesS&P 500 · MSCI · FTSE
Equal-weighted1/N — same weight eachS&P 500 Equal Weight
FundamentalBook value · earnings · dividendsRAFI indexes
Price-weighted — the mental model that sticks
A price-weighted index is equivalent to a portfolio holding one share of each constituent. High-priced stocks automatically get high weights — regardless of their economic size.
Weight of stock i = Price_i / Σ(all prices) Replication: 1 share of A + 1 share of B + 1 share of C... → no need to know shares outstanding → no need to know market cap
Example: A ($100) + B ($50) + C ($25). Weights = 57.1% / 28.6% / 14.3%. Holding 1 of each replicates exactly.
Price-weighted traps — what the exam tests
Sensitive to stock splits: a 2-for-1 split halves the price → halves the weight, with no economic change. Index providers must adjust the divisor to preserve continuity. No economic justification: a $500 stock dominates a $50 stock, but the $50 stock might have 10× more shares and thus 10× more market cap. Price alone is arbitrary. Only 2 major indexes matter: DJIA (30 stocks), Nikkei 225 (225 stocks). Everything else is cap-weighted or float-adjusted.
Answer trap: "price-weighted index is unaffected by stock splits" → FALSE. It's the most split-sensitive method. Divisor adjustments are required at every split.
Equal-weighted — the natural small-cap value tilt
Each stock gets weight 1/N. Relative to market-cap weighting, this overweights smaller names and underweights megacaps.
Result: positive Size factor loading (small-cap tilt) Result: positive Value factor loading (cap-weighting biases toward growth, so equal-weight pulls in the opposite direction) Higher turnover: small stocks drift, rebalancing costs accumulate
Exam anchor: if you see an index with positive Size + positive Value + higher yield than market, it's likely equal-weighted.
Fundamental weighting — the often-misstated one
Weights based on economic fundamentals (book value, earnings, cash flow, dividends), not price. Because price doesn't enter the weight, fundamental weighting overweights stocks priced below intrinsic value and underweights overpriced stocks.
Classic exam trap: "fundamental weighting has the disadvantage of overweighting overpriced stocks and underweighting underpriced stocks." — FALSE. That's what market-cap weighting is accused of (price inflation → weight inflation). Fundamental weighting is the correction, not the problem.
Anchor: Fundamental weighting = built-in value tilt. It rewards underpriced, punishes overpriced.
HHI — how concentrated is this index?
HHI = Σ(w_i²) Effective number of stocks = 1 / HHI
HHI = 0.0286 → 1/0.0286 ≈ 35 equivalent equally-weighted stocks. If the index has 150 names but HHI implies only 35 effective stocks, it's heavily concentrated in a few megacaps.
HHI value0.0286
The big anchor: factor strategies CONCENTRATE risk
This is the single most-tested concept in Index-Based Equity. Relative to broad-market-cap weighting, any factor-based strategy (momentum, value, size, quality, low-vol, yield) concentrates risk exposure — it deliberately tilts toward one characteristic.
Exam trap (appears 3+ times across vignettes): "factor-based strategies diversify risk exposure" → FALSE. They do the opposite. Broad-market-cap weighting is diversified; factor tilts concentrate.
The 6 classic factors — what each one bets on
FactorBets onOverweights stocks with
SizeSmall-cap premiumLow market cap
ValueMean reversion in valuationsLow P/E, low P/B
MomentumTrend continuationRecent winners (price up)
QualityStable earners outperformHigh ROE, low debt, earnings stability
Low VolatilityLow-vol anomalyLow beta, low return vol
YieldDividend premiumHigh dividend yield
Two most-confused factor pairs
Value ≠ Low Volatility: value hunts cheap valuations (P/B, P/E) — a bet on mean reversion. Low-vol hunts stable low-beta stocks — a bet on the low-vol anomaly. Different factors with different risk profiles. Momentum ≠ Contrarian: momentum BUYS recent winners (price just went up). Contrarian/reversal buys recent losers. Opposite strategies.
Common exam wrong answer: "momentum overweights stocks that recently experienced large price decreases." That describes reversal, not momentum. Momentum = buy winners.
Three properties of factor strategies vs cap weighting
✗ Diversify risk — FALSE, they concentrate ✓ Transparent — TRUE, factor selection/weighting/rebalancing are rule-based and disclosed ✓ Replicable by others — TRUE, which creates overcrowding risk and can erode alpha
Memory anchor: "transparent + replicable + concentrated" — two positives, one negative. The trap statement swaps "concentrate" for "diversify".
The 3 replication methods — full decision table
MethodHoldingsSophisticationCovariances?Typical TE
Full replication≈ 100% of indexNoneN/ALowest
Stratified samplingSubset (buckets)LowNoModerate
OptimizationSubset (factor model)HighYesLow
Full replication — the "all securities" method
Keyword trigger: "all index constituents must be available for trading" Holds every security at exact index weight → tracking error near zero in theory Best when: index is small and liquid (e.g. S&P 500), AUM is large enough to afford many trades Weakness: brokerage commissions explode when index is large (Russell 3000 → 3000 trades at every rebalance)
If the question says "available for trading" or "significant commissions when index is large" → full replication.
Stratified sampling — the "simple subset" method
Keyword trigger: "technically unsophisticated" · "fewer individual securities" Divides the index into strata (sector × size × style), picks a few representative names in each cell Best when: index has many constituents, AUM is modest, simplicity is preferred Does NOT account for covariances — ignores how stocks co-move. This is the key exam differentiator.
If the question says "technically straightforward" or "unsophisticated" → stratified sampling. Optimization is explicitly sophisticated.
Optimization — the "factor-model minimization" method
Keyword trigger: "accounts for covariances" · "minimize tracking error" Uses a factor model + covariance matrix to pick the subset that minimizes TE for a given number of holdings Best when: index is very large, tracking error discipline is critical, team has quant expertise Can achieve lower TE than stratified with similar (or even fewer) holdings
Tell-tale sign of optimization: the manager explicitly "accounts for covariances". Stratified sampling never does this.
Replication manager skill — counter-intuitive but critical
For replication managers, skill is measured by LOW tracking error, not by positive excess return. The goal is to match the index — NOT to beat it.
High excess return + high TE → NOT skill. The manager deviated from the benchmark and got lucky. Low TE → genuine skill at the replication mandate. Excess return for a replication manager should be near zero (minus fees). Anything large suggests unintended bets.
For ACTIVE managers, high excess return + moderate TE = skill (measured by Information Ratio). For REPLICATION managers, the evaluation inverts: excess return is a bug, not a feature.
TE drivers under full replication — what raises TE
Number of constituents — more names = more trades, more slippage, more rebalancing cost Expense ratio — directly deducted from return, creates a constant gap Constituent liquidity — small/illiquid names at the tail of the index are harder to trade International exposure — time zones, FX, settlement delays, stale pricing add friction
Classic comparison: MSCI EAFE (933 names, international, 0.33% fee) will have HIGHER TE than S&P 500 (506 names, domestic, 0.10% fee) or S&P/TSX 60 (60 names, 0.18% fee). All three factors push EAFE to highest TE.
Brinson attribution on factors — the decomposition
When a fund uses factor-based weights (growth, value, quality, momentum), the excess return vs benchmark splits into two sources — exactly like classical sector-based BHB attribution.
SourceConditionMeaning
Factor weighting effectWeights different · returns sameActive tilt vs benchmark factor weights
Security selection effectWeights same · returns differentStock picking within factor bucket
InteractionBoth differentCross-term (usually small)
The calculation walkthrough
For each factor: Fund contribution = Weight_fund × Return_fund Bench contribution = Weight_bench × Return_bench Total effect = Fund − Bench Then classify: If weight differs but return same → factor weighting effect If weight same but return differs → security selection If both differ → interaction Sum them up → total active return % from factor weighting = (sum of factor weighting effects) / (total active return)

The three answer traps on factor attribution questions
Trap 1 — Total effect instead of split: question asks "% from factor weighting" but answer gives the absolute total effect. Wrong because it doesn't split into sources. Trap 2 — Absolute instead of percentage: answer gives the dollar/% contribution of factor weighting but forgets to divide by total effect. ✓ Correct: (factor weighting contribution) / (total effect) × 100 = percentage.
Reading factor exposures from a regression table
Exam questions give you a table of factor loadings (coefficients) for 2-3 indexes, plus a description of an investor. Match the investor to the index whose loadings align with their style.
Factor coefficientPositive = tilt towardNegative = tilt toward
SizeSmall-capLarge-cap
ValueValue (low P/B, low P/E)Growth
YieldHigh dividendLow/no dividend
MomentumTrend followersContrarian
QualityStable earnersJunk / high leverage
MarketHigh beta to broad mktLow beta / distinct
Critical: negative loadings reverse the interpretation. Size = −0.16 means the index tilts LARGE-cap, not small-cap. Same for Value → negative = growth.
Interactive investor matcher
Pick an investor profile and see which index matches best. Based on the Jones-type exam questions.
Investor profile
Equal-weighted index = natural small+value tilt
When you see a factor loading table with Size positive + Value positive + moderate Yield positive → likely an equal-weighted index. By construction, equal weighting overweights smaller names (size tilt) and resists the growth bias of cap-weighting (value tilt).
Price-weighted and volatility-weighted indexes tend to be large-cap-growth oriented (negative Size, negative Value loadings). The equal-weighted one stands out by loading positive on both.
Two rules that both improve investability
RuleWhat it doesEffect on investability
Free-float adjustmentExclude locked-up shares from weightsRaises liquidity ✓
Buffering policyNo-action zone around thresholdsReduces turnover ✓
Classic exam wrong answer: "free-float adjustment lowers liquidity." FALSE. It does the opposite — by restricting weights to tradeable shares only, index funds can actually replicate the index without chasing shares that aren't for sale.
Free-float adjustment — the mechanics
Free-float weight_i = (Price_i × Free-float shares_i) / Σ(Price × Free-float shares)
Excluded from the free float:
Founder and insider holdings Government strategic stakes Corporate cross-holdings Post-IPO lockups and restricted shares
Buffering policy — keeping stable what should be stable
A security hovering near a rank threshold (e.g. #500 in an index of 500 names) shouldn't be deleted the moment it slips to #501. Buffering sets two lines: an outer trigger and an inner reset — you only act on outer breaches, and you rebalance to the inner target.
Reduces transaction costs (fewer forced trades) Reduces turnover and tax drag Reduces tracking error caused by trading noise Trade-off: portfolio drifts slightly further from the pure target
Buffering applies to: index inclusion/exclusion rules, style/factor classifications, rebalancing corridors. All versions of the same idea.
The 7 properties of a valid benchmark
From the benchmark rules tab in LDI — but also tested here:
Specified in advance · Appropriate · Measurable · Unambiguous · Reflective of opinions · Accountable · Investable
"Investable" is the one that ties directly to the free-float and buffering policies — an index isn't investable if funds can't actually replicate it.
Equity futures for passive exposure — the step-by-step
Step 1: Cash to invest (bonus, new contribution, etc.) Step 2: Apply POLICY WEIGHT for the target asset class Step 3: Contract value = Futures price × multiplier Step 4: Number of contracts = (Cash × weight) / Contract value Step 5: Direction: BUY to pre-invest cash · SELL to hedge existing exposure
The multiplier trap — standard vs E-mini
ContractMultiplierContract size @ 2464.29
S&P 500 standard250$616,072
S&P 500 E-mini50$123,214
S&P 500 Micro5$12,321
Critical: always check which multiplier the question specifies. Using 250 instead of 50 gives 1/5 the right number of contracts — a classic wrong answer is built exactly around this mistake.
