Why futures drift from the underlying index
Dividends: index futures don't pay dividends; underlying index does. The futures price embeds this — as the ex-div date approaches, futures drop relative to index by the dividend amount. Stock splits: require contract adjustments; creates short-term tracking noise. Financing cost (cost of carry): futures price = spot × (1 + r − d) × t. Rising rates widen the basis.
For exam performance-attribution questions: if the portfolio used futures and returns differ from the cash index, it's usually corporate actions (dividends, splits) — not manager skill or lack thereof.
The 3 key differences — memorize these
FeatureMutual fundETF
Margin purchases✗ No✓ Yes
Short selling✗ No✓ Yes
LiquidityRedeemed at NAV, end-of-day onlyIntraday trading, but subject to market liquidity
PricingNAV only (one price per day)Market price, may deviate from NAV
Tax efficiencyLower (cash redemptions trigger gains)Higher (in-kind creation/redemption)
The liquidity nuance — not what most people think
"ETFs are more liquid than mutual funds" is too simplistic. They offer DIFFERENT kinds of liquidity:
Mutual funds — guaranteed NAV redemption, but once per day only. Liquidity is certain in magnitude but limited in timing. ETFs — intraday trading at market prices, but during stress can trade at significant discounts to NAV (2020 bond ETFs). Liquidity is continuous in timing but uncertain in price.
Exam trap: "mutual funds and ETFs have the same degree of liquidity" → FALSE. They have different types of liquidity, not the same degree.
Currency overlay — hedge, not leverage
A currency overlay uses FX forwards/futures to hedge the currency risk of foreign securities back to the home currency. It neutralizes FX exposure — it does NOT amplify returns.
Exam trap: "currency overlay used to lever returns of foreign securities" → FALSE. Overlay = hedge. To lever, you'd need leverage (margin, futures notional beyond the underlying exposure).
Lending portfolio securities — incremental income with hidden risks
ETFs and index funds can lend their securities to short-sellers for a small fee, generating extra income that partially offsets expenses. But this creates:
Counterparty risk — the borrower might default Collateral risk — collateral held may lose value or be illiquid
Used to reduce expense ratios but adds a non-market risk dimension.
1Jones small-cap value investor
Jones invests in small-cap + low P/B + high yield. Which of three indexes matches?
Wrong approach: picked an index with negative Size loading (Index 2 or 3). Negative Size = large-cap tilt, opposite of what Jones wants.
Correct: the index with POSITIVE Size (+0.33) + POSITIVE Value (+0.41) + POSITIVE Yield (+0.24). That's Index 1, which is equal-weighted — naturally tilts small + value.
Sign check: positive Size → small-cap · Positive Value → value · Positive Yield → high dividend. All three must align with Jones's profile.
2Mutual fund vs ETF comments
Three comments: (1) both on margin · (2) ETFs can short, mutual funds cannot · (3) same liquidity.
Wrong: picked #1 (both on margin) — only ETFs can be bought on margin, not mutual funds.
Correct: #2. ETFs allow short positions; mutual funds do not.
#1 FALSE — only ETFs can be margined #2 TRUE — ETFs can be shorted, mutual funds cannot #3 FALSE — different types of liquidity, not the same degree
3Factor strategies vs market-cap
Stapleton: "diversify risk + transparent + can be copied."
Wrong: said statement is correct or that "transparent" is wrong.
Correct: "diversify risk" is wrong. Factor strategies CONCENTRATE risk. "Transparent" and "can be copied" are both correct.
Anchor: any time you see "factor strategy + diversify" → red flag, likely wrong
4Brinson factor attribution %
Growth weight diff + Quality weight diff + Momentum return diff → what % of excess return is from factor weighting?
Wrong: gave the raw factor weighting contribution (−0.04%) instead of the percentage. Or gave the total effect (−0.22%).
Correct: divide factor weighting contribution by total effect → −0.04% / −0.22% = 18.18%.
Factor weighting contributions: Growth: (0.22 − 0.25) × 7.9% = −0.24% Quality: (0.29 − 0.26) × 6.7% = +0.20% Sum: −0.04% Security selection contribution: Momentum: 0.30 × (3.9% − 4.5%) = −0.18% Total effect: −0.04 + −0.18 = −0.22% % from factor weighting: −0.04 / −0.22 = 18.18%
5Parker's three factor claims
Which is correct? (a) fundamental overweights overpriced · (b) value factor lowers downside · (c) single-factor concentrates risk.
Wrong: picked value factor (confused with low-vol) or fundamental (the signs are reversed).
Correct: single-factor concentrates risk. (a) wrong — fundamental overweights UNDERpriced. (b) wrong — value ≠ low-vol.
Value factor = bet on mean reversion in valuations Low-volatility factor = bet on low-vol anomaly (downside protection) Fundamental weighting = built-in value tilt (underweight overpriced, overweight underpriced)
6Identifying blended stratified + optimization
Three replication managers. Which uses stratified sampling + optimization?
Wrong: picked Manager B (stratified only) because it has many holdings. Missed that B doesn't account for covariances.
Correct: Manager C. The giveaway is "accounts for covariances" = YES. This is the signature of optimization.
Manager A (498/500, TE 0.06%) → Full replication Manager B (800/928, TE 1.97%, covariances NO) → Stratified alone Manager C (1200/3000, TE 0.34%, covariances YES) → Stratified + Optimization ✓
7Parker's comments on Manager B
Three claims: (1) TE measures market volatility · (2) currency overlay levers returns · (3) excess return is luck.
Wrong: picked TE or currency overlay. Both contain errors.
Correct: excess return comment. A replication manager's JOB is to match the index, not beat it. Positive excess return with high TE → unintended deviation, luck more than skill.
TE measures std dev of (portfolio return − benchmark return), not market volatility Currency overlay hedges FX, doesn't lever For replication managers: excess return is a bug, not a feature
8Free-float and buffering statements
(1) Free-float lowers liquidity. (2) Buffering makes index more investable.
Wrong: thought free-float reduces the tradeable universe so must reduce liquidity.
Correct: #2 only. Free-float RAISES liquidity by restricting weights to actually-tradeable shares. Buffering IMPROVES investability by reducing turnover.
Both policies push toward more investable, more replicable indexes
9Method 1 = Full replication
"All index constituents available for trading + large commissions when index is large."
Keyword: "all constituents available". Full replication needs every single name to be tradeable. Stratified and optimization work with subsets.
"All constituents" → Full replication "Technically unsophisticated" → Stratified sampling "Accounts for covariances" → Optimization
10Highest TE among three ETFs
XIU (60 names, 0.18%) · SPY (506, 0.10%) · EFA (933, 0.33%). Which has highest TE under full replication?
Correct: EFA. More constituents = more tracking friction. Higher fees = constant drag. Both point same direction.
TE drivers: # constituents + expense ratio + liquidity of smallest names + international/FX exposure EFA loses on all four — it's international, has the most names, and highest fees
11Price-weighted index property
What characterizes the price-weighted large-cap benchmark? (A) unaffected by splits · (B) liquidity-weighted · (C) same shares of each.
Wrong: picked "unaffected by splits". Price-weighted is HIGHLY affected by splits — that's why divisor adjustments exist.
Correct: (C) same number of shares of each component. A price-weighted index is equivalent to holding 1 share of each constituent.
Price-weighted = "1 share of each" replication Splits DIVIDE the price → DIVIDE the weight with no economic change. Divisor adjustments compensate. Only DJIA and Nikkei 225 are major price-weighted indexes
1 / 11
Q1 · Jones small-cap value ✗ got wrong
Jones invests in small-cap securities with low P/B and high dividend yields. Three indexes with factor exposures given (Size, Value, Yield, Momentum, Quality). Best match?
A — Index 1 (equal-weighted): positive Size +0.33, positive Value +0.41, positive Yield +0.24
B/C — Index 2 & 3: negative Size and negative Value (large-cap growth tilt)
Read the signs: positive Size = small-cap tilt, positive Value = value tilt, positive Yield = dividend tilt. All three must align with the investor's style. Equal-weighted indexes naturally generate these tilts.
Trap: negative coefficient means OPPOSITE direction. Size −0.16 is a large-cap tilt, not a small-cap tilt.
Q2 · Mutual fund vs ETF comments ✗ got wrong
Three comments: (1) both can be purchased on margin · (2) ETFs can be shorted but mutual funds cannot · (3) same degree of liquidity. Which is most accurate?
B — Comment 2: only ETFs can be shorted
A — Comment 1 wrong: only ETFs can be margined
C — Comment 3 wrong: different types of liquidity
ETFs trade like stocks: margin, short, intraday pricing. Mutual funds redeem at NAV end-of-day only. The liquidity comment is the subtlest trap — "same degree" is wrong because the NATURE of liquidity differs.
Q3 · Factor strategies vs cap weighting ✗ got wrong
Stapleton's claim: factor-based strategies (a) diversify risk, (b) are transparent, (c) can be copied by others. Is her comment correct?
C — Incorrect regarding risk exposure
Factor strategies CONCENTRATE risk on the chosen factor. "Transparent" and "replicable by others" are both correct. The wrong word is "diversify".
This trap appears 3+ times in Index-Based Equity. If you see "factor-based + diversify" anywhere, it's almost always wrong.
Q4 · Brinson factor attribution % ✗ got wrong
River Valley fund vs benchmark. Growth weight diff, Quality weight diff, Momentum return diff. What % of excess return comes from active factor weighting?
C — 18.18%
A/B — wrong: these give the raw contribution, not the percentage
Factor weighting effects (weight diff, return same): Growth: (0.22 − 0.25) × 7.9% = −0.24% Quality: (0.29 − 0.26) × 6.7% = +0.20% Sum: −0.04% Security selection effect (weight same, return diff): Momentum: 0.30 × (3.9% − 4.5%) = −0.18% Total active return: −0.04 + −0.18 = −0.22% % from factor weighting: −0.04 / −0.22 = 18.18%
Two trap answers: (A) total effect itself · (B) absolute factor weighting amount. Neither is the PERCENTAGE of total. Always divide.
Q5 · Parker's three factor claims ✗ got wrong
(A) Fundamental weighting overweights overpriced · (B) value factor lowers downside · (C) single-factor concentrates risk. Which is correct?
B — Single-factor concentrates risk exposure
A — Wrong: fundamental weighting overweights UNDERpriced (value tilt)
C — Wrong: value factor seeks cheap valuations, NOT downside protection (that's low-vol)
Three distinct errors to know: fundamental weighting has a value tilt (not the reverse); value factor ≠ low-vol; single-factor concentrates risk.
Q6 · Stratified + optimization identification ✗ got wrong
Three replication managers. Which blends stratified sampling with optimization?
C — Manager C (1200/3000 holdings, TE 0.34%, accounts for covariances)
A — Manager A: full replication (498/500, TE 0.06%)
B — Manager B: stratified only (800/928, TE 1.97%, no covariances)
The single distinguishing feature is "accounts for covariances" = YES → optimization. Number of holdings alone is not decisive.
Reading the data: B has MORE holdings than C but HIGHER TE. That's the signature of stratified without optimization — it can't shrink TE by modeling correlations.
Q7 · Parker's three comments on Manager B ✗ got wrong
(A) High TE means volatile markets · (B) currency overlay levers returns · (C) excess return is luck.
B — Excess return is luck, not skill
A — Wrong: TE measures deviation from benchmark, not market volatility
C — Wrong: currency overlay HEDGES, doesn't lever
For a replication manager: the mandate is to match the index, not beat it. High excess return + high TE = unintended deviation. Skill for replication managers is measured by LOW TE, not positive excess return.
Q8 · Free-float and buffering ✗ got wrong
(1) Free-float adjustment lowers liquidity. (2) Buffering policy makes index more investable. Which is correct?
Statement 2 — correct (buffering improves investability)
Statement 1 — wrong (free-float RAISES liquidity)
Free-float restricts weights to actually-tradeable shares, so index-tracking funds can actually replicate. Buffering reduces turnover at inclusion/exclusion thresholds. Both push toward easier-to-replicate indexes.
Q9 · Method 2 replication process ✗ got wrong
"Large number of constituents, low AUM, straightforward and technically unsophisticated, fewer individual securities." Which method?
C — Stratified sampling
A — Optimization: explicitly sophisticated (factor model, covariances)
B — Full replication: requires ALL constituents, not fewer
Keyword "unsophisticated" eliminates optimization. "Fewer securities" eliminates full replication. Stratified sampling is the only method that is simple AND works with a subset.
Q10 · Highest tracking error among 3 ETFs ✗ got wrong
XIU (S&P/TSX 60, 60 names, 0.18%), SPY (S&P 500, 506, 0.10%), EFA (MSCI EAFE, 933, 0.33%). Full replication.
C — EFA (most constituents, highest fees, international)
TE drivers all point to EFA: largest constituent count (replication friction), highest expense ratio (constant drag), international (FX, settlements, time zones add noise).
Q11 · Price-weighted index property ✗ got wrong
The benchmark is price-weighted. Which is true? (A) unaffected by splits · (B) liquidity-weighted · (C) same number of shares in each stock.
C — Holds the same number of shares in each component
A — Wrong: HIGHLY affected by splits (needs divisor adjustment)
B — Wrong: liquidity-weighted is not a real index type
A price-weighted index is equivalent to holding 1 share of each constituent. Price = weight, regardless of shares outstanding or market cap.
Price-weighted is the MOST split-sensitive method — any split halves the price and halves the weight without economic change, forcing a divisor adjustment. "Unaffected by splits" is the trap answer.
The two big families of active management
Every active equity approach falls into one of two camps. The dichotomy is about how decisions are made — not what assets are bought.
DimensionFundamentalQuantitative
ProcessDiscretionary (human judgement)Systematic / non-discretionary
FocusDeep dive on a few companiesFactors applied across large groups
ForecastCompany-specific (earnings, mgmt, moat)Factor-level (returns to factors)
InformationQualitative + quantitativeQuantitative only
DecisionsConviction-based, concentratedRule-based, diversified
The 3 characteristics of quantitative investing
✓ Identifies factors driving security returns across large groups of securities (not deep dives on each) ✓ Is systematic / non-discretionary — same rules applied uniformly, no override ✗ Does NOT focus on forecasting prospects of underlying companies — that's fundamental
Exam trap (Drum): "characteristic of quantitative active investing = forecast underlying company prospects" → FALSE. That's the defining feature of fundamental, not quantitative. Quants look at factors across many stocks; they don't try to know each company deeply.
When you see these phrases on the exam
→ Fundamental: "deep understanding of companies" · "management quality" · "competitive moat" · "discretionary" · "high conviction" · "concentrated" → Quantitative: "factor model" · "systematic" · "across a universe of stocks" · "rule-based" · "non-discretionary" · "factor exposures"
Memory anchor: if the description says "company-by-company" → fundamental. If it says "factor-by-factor across many stocks" → quantitative.
The other dichotomy: where does the decision start?
Top-down vs bottom-up is about the direction of analysis — macro-first or stock-first. It's orthogonal to fundamental/quantitative (both styles can be top-down or bottom-up).
DirectionTop-downBottom-up
Starts withMacro / economic cycle / sectorsIndividual securities
Then narrows toCountry / sector / style buckets(aggregates up to sectors)
FinallyStocks within preferred bucketsPortfolio is sum of single bets
Typical signalGDP, rates, yield curve, sector rotationEarnings, valuation, balance sheet
The Drum exam trap: classify each fund
Three funds described. Which uses ONLY bottom-up?
FundProcess describedClassification
Fund AMacro analysis to identify sectors → security selection within themCombination (top-down dominant)
Fund BNews-source software to screen earnings surprises across 500 stocks; picks individual namesBottom-up ONLY ✓
Fund CSector forecasts + bottom-up stock selection inside each sectorCombination
Trap: even though Fund B uses sophisticated quantitative software, that doesn't make it top-down. The software is screening individual stocks based on stock-level signals (earnings surprises). The starting unit of analysis is the security, not the sector or macro environment → bottom-up.
Style rotation = top-down, even if you land in deep value
When a manager rotates style based on where we are in the economic cycle (e.g. "we're in late expansion → tilt toward defensives → tilt toward quality") that's top-down, period. The trigger is macro, not the stock.
Analyst 1 ✓: "Style rotation based on economic cycle = top-down" — CORRECT Analyst 2 ✗: "Style rotation = always growth at reasonable price (GARP)" — WRONG. GARP is one specific style; rotation is a process across styles. Analyst 3 ✗: "GARP is top-down" — WRONG. GARP is bottom-up — you compute P/E and PEG security by security.
The starting unit of analysis is the test. Macro context applied first → top-down. Stock characteristics applied first → bottom-up.
Quick decision tree
Q1: Does the manager start by analyzing macro/sectors/cycles? → Yes → top-down (regardless of what they end up buying) → No, starts with individual stocks → bottom-up Q2: Does the description mix both? → Yes → combination (note which dominates the entry point)
3 ways to classify a fund's style
MethodUsesBest whenAccuracy
Holdings-basedThe actual portfolio (every position)Full disclosure availableHighest
Returns-basedRegress fund returns on style indicesOnly return series availableModerate
Self-identificationProspectus / fund manager statementHedge funds, derivatives, long-shortRequired fallback
Why holdings-based beats returns-based
✓ Holdings-based looks directly at every stock in the portfolio and its characteristics (P/E, P/B, market cap). It captures the actual current style, including recent changes. ~ Returns-based infers style from past return correlations to style indices. It's a lagged inference — recent rotations don't show up until enough months have passed.
Lunnar exam trap: "Returns-based and holdings-based are equally accurate" → FALSE. Holdings-based is MORE accurate because it uses the actual portfolio. Returns-based is a statistical inference from history.
The hedge fund problem: why self-ID is required
Consider "Lunnar Hedge-X": long-short positions across asset classes plus derivatives overlay.
✗ Holdings-based fails: long positions don't represent net exposure when there are large shorts ✗ Returns-based fails: derivatives mean returns don't map cleanly to standard style indices ✓ Self-identification: rely on the manager's prospectus / disclosed strategy
Self-ID is not a fallback you choose because it's easier — it's the only method that works when holdings AND returns are both ambiguous. Hedge funds, market-neutral funds, and 130/30 strategies all fall here.
Identifying the most index-like fund — the 2-step method
"Style most consistent with its index" = smallest gap between the fund's actual style and the index style. The trick is knowing WHICH column to use.
Step 1: If both holdings-based AND returns-based columns are given → USE holdings-based (it's the actual portfolio, more accurate) Step 2: Compute |Holdings_value − Index_value| for each fund Step 3: Smallest absolute gap = most index-like fund
Note: the value and growth percentages sum to 100%, so comparing just the Value side is enough — the gap on Growth is identical.
Worked example — the Lunnar exam vignette
FundHoldings V/GReturns V/GIndex V/G|Holdings_V − Index_V|
Lunnar A68/3268/3275/25|68 − 75| = 7%
Lunnar B67/3368/3265/35|67 − 65| = 2% ✓ smallest
Lunnar C39/6134/6635/65|39 − 35| = 4%
Lunnar B wins with the smallest gap. Note: returns-based column is shown for context, but you IGNORE it when computing the answer. Holdings-based is the gold standard.
Common traps in this question: (1) comparing the fund's Holdings vs its own Returns columns (those measure the same fund — they're not the comparison). (2) Using returns-based when holdings is also available. (3) Picking Lunnar A because 68% Value "looks like" 75% Value (direction same, but the GAP is what matters).

Morningstar vs Lipper — two style scoring methods
AspectMorningstarLipper
InputsValue score + growth score (0-100 each)Z-scores on 6 characteristics
MethodSubtracts: growth score − value scoreSums Z-scores
Large positivePure growthPure growth
Large negativePure valuePure value
Near zeroCore (low signal)Core / blended
Both highBLEND (high value + high growth)(Doesn't appear — averaged away)
Asgard fund — the Morningstar vs Lipper divergence
A fund has Morningstar value score 75 AND growth score 70 (both high). Same fund: Lipper sums 6 Z-scores and gets a net −1.8 (clearly value-leaning).
Morningstar classification: Value 75, Growth 70 → both high Difference: 70 − 75 = −5 (near zero) But both scores >50 → BLEND (balanced exposure to value AND growth) Lipper classification: Σ Z-scores = −1.8 → value
The trap: thinking "near-zero difference = core". With Morningstar, when both component scores are HIGH simultaneously, the classification is BLEND (mix of value and growth stocks), not core. Core = both scores moderate/low. Blend = both scores high.
Lipper can disagree with Morningstar precisely because they use different methodologies. Both can be "correct" given their definitions — the exam expects you to know both definitions.

Company 14035Growth (higher than sector)
Company 21435Relative value ← lower than sector but absolute P/E not extreme
Company 3315Deep value ← extremely low absolute AND below sector
Common error: calling Company 2 deep value because P/E 14 is "much lower than 35". Wrong — P/E 14 is not extreme in absolute terms. Deep value requires BOTH: extreme absolute AND extreme relative.

PEG = P/E ÷ expected earnings growth rate (in %). Adjust the inputs to see how GARP screens different stocks.

Factor consistency check (Tokra trap)
A manager declares "value tilt" but the portfolio's P/B is HIGHER than the benchmark. Inconsistent — that's a red flag the manager's described style doesn't match the actual exposures.
Declared styleExpected portfolio charTokra's portfolioConsistent?
ValueLower P/B than benchmarkHigher P/B✗ NO — inconsistent
Low sizeSmaller mkt cap than benchmarkSmaller mkt cap ✓✓ consistent
Tokra exam trap: when asked which factor is inconsistent with the declared style, look at portfolio characteristics vs the style label. Higher P/B than benchmark contradicts a "value" claim — that's the red flag. Also: "price momentum" is NOT a growth metric (growth = earnings/revenue growth). Momentum is purely price-based.
Price momentum — its hidden tail risk
Price momentum strategies (buy recent winners) earn small steady positive returns most of the time, but suffer extreme negative tail events when the market reverses sharply (e.g. March 2009, March 2020).
Risk profile: long left tail (large losses, low frequency) NOT a "value trap" (that's value-specific) · NOT a "growth trap" (that's growth-specific) Distinct from market beta risk — momentum can blow up even when overall market is fine
Memory anchor: momentum = "skating on thin ice that holds 99% of the time" — when it cracks, the loss is large. Same factor concentrates the risk.
Event-driven strategies — what they trade and when
Event-driven strategies bet on price moves around corporate events. The horizon depends entirely on which event.
Event typeTypical horizonWhat you bet on
Merger arbitrageShort (weeks-months)Spread between deal price and current price closes
Acquisitions in consolidating industriesShort-to-mediumPredict next target before announcement
Distressed / control positionsLONG-TERM (1-3+ years)Restructuring or operational turnaround
ReorganizationsLONG-TERMPost-bankruptcy emergence, debt-for-equity, multi-year
Activist campaignsMedium-to-longGovernance / strategic changes play out over quarters
Fund B horizon trap
Question: "Fund B has a short-term horizon. Which event-driven strategies are appropriate?"
✓ Acquisitions in consolidating industries — predicting the next target → short-to-medium horizon → APPROPRIATE ✗ Distressed / control positions — restructuring takes years → INAPPROPRIATE for short horizon ✗ Reorganizations — multi-year post-bankruptcy → INAPPROPRIATE for short horizon
Common error: thinking all event-driven strategies are short-term because they're "tactical". Wrong — distressed and reorganizations are explicitly long-horizon strategies, often locked up for years. Match the horizon to the event TYPE.
Pairs trading: the core idea
A pairs trade goes long one stock and short another in the same sector/industry when their price ratio deviates from its long-term average. The bet is on mean reversion.
Setup: Spread_t = Price_A / Price_B (or log ratio) μ = long-term average spread σ = std dev of spread If spread_t > μ + 2σ → A is rich, B is cheap → SHORT A, LONG B If spread_t < μ − 2σ → A is cheap, B is rich → LONG A, SHORT B Exit: when spread reverts to ~μ
Kopernicus exam Q: which 3 criteria must hold for a valid pair?
✓ #1 — Current spread significantly different from long-term average (otherwise there's no opportunity) ✓ #2 — Spread is mean-reverting (statistical evidence: ADF/cointegration test) ✓ #3 — High correlation between the two stocks (or they're co-moving fundamentally)
All three conditions must hold. If any one fails, the pair is not tradeable.
Kopernicus pair evaluation table
PairSpread vs avgMean-reverting?High correlation?Valid?
Pair 1-2Similar to avgYesYes✗ No (no opportunity)
Pair 3-4Significantly different ✓Yes ✓Yes ✓✓ Valid pair
Pair 5-6Similar to avgNoNo✗ No (fails all three)
The exam often gives you 3 pairs and asks which is tradeable. Test each criterion individually — only the pair passing all 3 is valid.
Primary risk management tool for pairs trading
The main risk in pairs trading is structural divergence — when the spread keeps widening instead of mean-reverting (one stock fundamentally disconnects from the other, e.g. M&A news, accounting fraud).
Risk toolUse?Why
Stop-loss orders✓ PRIMARYCaps loss if spread keeps widening (structural divergence)
Asset identification✗That's pre-trade selection, not active risk management
Limit order book monitoring✗HFT-only technique, not pairs trading
Exam trap: "identification of the right assets" or "monitoring limit order book" — both are wrong answers. The PRIMARY risk tool is stop-loss orders, because they protect against the only risk you can't fully diversify away: structural divergence.
1Kopernicus — pairs trading risk management
What is the PRIMARY risk management tool used in pairs trading?
Wrong picks: "identification of the right assets" (that's pre-trade) · "monitoring limit order book" (HFT-only)
Correct: stop-loss orders. They cap losses if the spread keeps widening (structural divergence), which is the one risk pairs trading can't diversify away.
Anchor: "structural divergence" → stop-loss is the only practical defense
2Yarsley — Relative value vs Deep value classification
Company 2: P/E 14, sector P/E 35. Company 3: P/E 3, sector P/E 15. Which is relative value, which is deep value?
Wrong: calling both "deep value" because P/E is below sector in both cases.
Correct: Company 2 = relative value (P/E 14 below sector 35 but not extreme absolute). Company 3 = deep value (P/E 3 is extreme in absolute terms AND below sector 15).
Deep value requires BOTH: extreme absolute P/E + below sector P/E. Relative value only needs the relative criterion.
3Fund B horizon — event-driven appropriateness
Fund B has short-term horizon. Which event-driven strategies are appropriate?
Wrong: marked distressed/reorganizations as appropriate (they're long-term, not short).
Correct: acquisitions in consolidating industries YES (short-medium horizon). Distressed/control NO, reorganizations NO (both require multi-year holds).
Horizon mismatch is the trap. Match the event TYPE to fund's holding period.
4Lunnar — Holdings-based vs Returns-based + most index-like
Two parts: (a) is holdings-based or returns-based more accurate? (b) Which Lunnar fund is closest to the index style?
Wrong (a): said both equally accurate. Wrong (b): picked Lunnar A (highest variance, not lowest).
Correct (a): holdings-based MORE accurate (uses actual portfolio). Correct (b): Lunnar B = closest to index (~2% variance across P/E, P/B, mkt cap).
Lower variance from index style characteristics = more index-like fund
5Three analysts on style rotation (Drum)
Analyst 1: "style rotation based on economic cycle = top-down". Analyst 2: "style rotation = GARP". Analyst 3: "GARP is top-down".
Wrong: picked Analyst 2 or 3 thinking GARP is top-down because it involves growth.
Correct: only Analyst 1. Style rotation triggered by macro/cycle = top-down. GARP is bottom-up (P/E + growth computed stock by stock).
Starting unit of analysis is the test: macro first → top-down. Stock first → bottom-up.
6Hedge fund non-standard classification (Lunnar Hedge-X)
Long-short + derivatives. Which style classification method must be used?
Wrong: said holdings-based or returns-based.
Correct: self-identification via the prospectus. Holdings-based fails because longs don't represent net exposure. Returns-based fails because derivatives distort the regression.
Anchor: hedge funds + long-short + derivatives → self-ID is the ONLY method that works
7Price momentum risk profile
Which describes price momentum's risk: value trap, growth trap, or extreme tail risk?
Wrong: picked "value trap" or "growth trap" — both are factor-specific to those styles.
Correct: extreme tail risk. Momentum earns small steady gains most of the time but suffers large losses in sharp reversals (Mar 2009, Mar 2020).
Memory: "skating on thin ice that holds 99% of the time" — when it cracks, the loss is large
8Tokra — which factor is inconsistent with declared style?
Manager declares "value tilt". Portfolio shows P/B HIGHER than benchmark + price momentum signals. Which is inconsistent?
Wrong: picked "price momentum" thinking it's a growth metric.
Correct: higher P/B than benchmark contradicts the declared value tilt. Price momentum is NOT a growth metric (growth = earnings/revenue growth; momentum is purely price-based).
Factor consistency: portfolio characteristics must align with declared style Price momentum ≠ growth factor — they are distinct
9Asgard — Morningstar vs Lipper divergence
Asgard: Morningstar value 75, growth 70 (both high). Lipper sum of 6 Z-scores = −1.8. Classifications?
Wrong: said Morningstar = core because difference (70 − 75 = −5) is near zero.
Correct: Morningstar = BLEND (both value and growth scores high → balanced exposure to value AND growth stocks). Lipper = value (Σ Z-scores significantly negative).
Morningstar blend ≠ core. Blend = both scores high. Core = both scores moderate/low. Lipper sums; Morningstar subtracts. Different methods → can disagree.
10Quantitative investing characteristics
Three claims: (a) factors across large groups · (b) systematic/non-discretionary · (c) forecast underlying company prospects. Which is NOT a quant characteristic?
Wrong: picked (a) or (b) — both ARE quant characteristics.
Correct: (c) is NOT quantitative — that's the defining feature of FUNDAMENTAL. Quants don't dive deep on each company.
Quant signature: factors + systematic + breadth (not depth)
11Pairs trade selection — which pair is valid?
3 pairs evaluated on (1) spread vs avg, (2) mean reversion, (3) correlation. Which is tradeable?
Wrong: picked Pair 1-2 (similar to avg → no opportunity) or Pair 5-6 (fails all three criteria).
Correct: Pair 3-4 — passes all three: spread significantly different from avg + mean reverting + high correlation.
All 3 criteria must hold. If any fails, pair is not tradeable.
12New factor introduction — which classification methods affected?
A manager starts using a new factor. Which style classification approaches are affected?
Wrong: said only returns-based affected (the regression coefficients change), or only holdings-based.
Correct: BOTH are affected. Holdings-based detects the new portfolio characteristics; returns-based sees new return correlations to style indices. New style exposure shows up in both.
Style change = new exposure in BOTH the holdings AND the returns
1 / 12
Q1 · Kopernicus pairs trading risk ✗ got wrong
What is the primary risk management tool used in pairs trading by Kopernicus?
B — Stop-loss orders
A — Identification of the right assets (pre-trade, not risk mgmt)
C — Monitoring the limit order book (HFT technique, not pairs)
The main residual risk in pairs trading is structural divergence — the spread keeps widening rather than mean-reverting. Stop-loss orders cap that loss. Asset selection happens before the trade; limit-order-book monitoring is for HFT, not for pairs that hold positions for days/weeks.
Q2 · Yarsley value strategy classification ✗ got wrong
Yarsley analyzes three companies. Company 2 has P/E 14 vs sector 35. Company 3 has P/E 3 vs sector 15. Classifications?
Company 2 = Relative value · Company 3 = Deep value
Both deep value (wrong — Company 2's absolute P/E isn't extreme)
Deep value requires BOTH conditions: extreme low absolute P/E AND below-sector P/E. Company 3 (P/E 3) is extreme in absolute terms. Company 2 (P/E 14) is below sector but P/E 14 isn't extreme by itself — that's relative value, not deep value.
Don't classify "deep value" just because P/E is way below sector. Test BOTH the absolute AND relative criteria.
Q3 · Fund B event-driven horizon ✗ got wrong
Fund B has a short-term horizon. Which event-driven strategies are appropriate?
Acquisitions in consolidating industries — APPROPRIATE
Distressed / control positions — NOT appropriate (long-term)
Reorganizations — NOT appropriate (multi-year)
Acquisitions in consolidating industries play out over weeks-to-months — fits a short horizon. Distressed and reorganizations require multi-year holds for the restructuring to complete and the equity value to be realized.
Don't lump all event-driven strategies together. Match the HOLDING PERIOD to the event TYPE.
Q4 · Lunnar holdings vs returns + index-like fund ✗ got wrong
(a) Is holdings-based or returns-based more accurate? (b) Which Lunnar fund (A/B/C) is closest to the index style?
(a) Holdings-based MORE accurate · (b) Lunnar B (smallest variance ~2%)
Holdings-based reads the actual current portfolio characteristics. Returns-based infers style from past return correlations — a statistical lag. For "closest to index", the fund whose P/E, P/B, mkt cap all deviate by only ~2% from the index is the most index-like.
Q5 · Three analysts on style rotation ✗ got wrong
Which analyst is correct? A1: style rotation by cycle = top-down · A2: style rotation = GARP · A3: GARP is top-down
Analyst 1 only
A2 wrong — rotation is a PROCESS, not a single style like GARP
A3 wrong — GARP is bottom-up (P/E + growth computed per stock)
Style rotation triggered by economic cycle = top-down because the starting analysis is macro. Even if it lands in deep value, the macro entry makes it top-down. GARP computes ratios at the stock level, which is bottom-up by definition.
Q6 · Lunnar Hedge-X classification method ✗ got wrong
Lunnar Hedge-X is long-short + derivatives. Which classification method must be used?
Self-identification via prospectus
Holdings-based fails (longs ≠ net exposure when there are shorts)
Returns-based fails (derivatives distort regression to style indices)
For hedge funds, market-neutral, and 130/30 strategies, neither holdings nor returns can cleanly classify the style. The manager's prospectus is the only authoritative source for the strategy.
Q7 · Price momentum risk profile ✗ got wrong
Which risk profile describes price momentum strategies?
Extreme tail risk
Value trap (no — that's value-specific)
Growth trap (no — that's growth-specific)
Momentum earns small steady positive returns most of the time, then suffers extreme losses when the market reverses sharply (Mar 2009, Mar 2020). The risk distribution has a long left tail — the opposite of "safe" returns.
Q8 · Tokra factor consistency ✗ got wrong
Tokra declares value tilt. Portfolio: higher P/B than benchmark + uses price momentum signals. Which is inconsistent with the declared style?
Higher P/B than benchmark — contradicts value tilt
Price momentum is NOT a growth metric (growth = earnings/revenue growth)
A value tilt should produce LOWER P/B than benchmark. Higher P/B is the red flag. Price momentum is a separate factor entirely — it's purely price-based and isn't a "growth metric".
Don't confuse price momentum with growth. Growth = earnings/revenue growth metrics. Momentum = past price performance.
Q9 · Asgard Morningstar vs Lipper ✗ got wrong
Asgard: Morningstar value 75, growth 70 (both high). Lipper sum of 6 Z-scores = −1.8. What does each method classify Asgard as?
Morningstar = BLEND (both scores high) · Lipper = VALUE (sum negative)
Wrong: Morningstar = core (only true if both scores moderate/low)
Morningstar blend means the fund has substantial exposure to BOTH value AND growth stocks (both scores high). Core means neither score is high. Lipper sums Z-scores across 6 characteristics — a clearly negative sum points to value, despite Morningstar showing blend exposure.
The two methods can disagree because they use fundamentally different math. Morningstar subtracts; Lipper sums.
Q10 · Quantitative investing characteristics ✗ got wrong
Which is NOT a characteristic of quantitative active investing?
Forecasting underlying company prospects — that's FUNDAMENTAL, not quant
Identifying factors across large groups (IS a quant characteristic)
Systematic / non-discretionary (IS a quant characteristic)
Quantitative investing applies factor rules across many securities. Fundamental investors dive deep on individual companies. The "forecast underlying company prospects" phrasing is the textbook signature of fundamental investing.
Q11 · Pairs trade selection — which pair is valid? ✗ got wrong
Three pairs evaluated. Pair 1-2 spread similar to avg. Pair 3-4 significantly different + mean reverting + high correlation. Pair 5-6 fails all 3.
Pair 3-4 — passes all 3 criteria
Pair 1-2 — no opportunity (spread already at avg)
Pair 5-6 — fails all 3 criteria
Pairs trading requires ALL three: significantly different from long-term avg (the opportunity), mean-reverting (the trade thesis), and high correlation (the hedge). Any one missing → not tradeable.
Q12 · New factor changes classification — which method? ✗ got wrong
A manager introduces a new factor to their strategy. Which style classification methods will detect the change?
BOTH holdings-based AND returns-based
Wrong: only returns-based (the new factor shows up in BOTH)
A new factor changes which stocks are held (detected by holdings-based) AND changes the return pattern's correlation to style indices (detected by returns-based). Self-ID would also be affected if the prospectus is updated.
Don't think of holdings-based and returns-based as orthogonal. They capture different views of the same underlying portfolio — a style change affects both.
Approaches to portfolio construction — the big picture
Active equity managers can be classified along TWO dichotomies that combine into a 2×2 matrix:
Systematic vs Discretionary — is the process rule-based or judgement-based? Top-down vs Bottom-up — does analysis start from macro/factors or from individual securities?
Both dichotomies are orthogonal: a manager can be systematic top-down (e.g. macro factor timing model), systematic bottom-up (e.g. quant stock screen), discretionary top-down (e.g. sector rotation by judgement), or discretionary bottom-up (e.g. classic stock picker).
Part 1 · The 2×2 matrix (Figure P3.1)
Systematic · Top-Down
Rules + macro entry
  • Emphasizes macro rewarded factors
  • Factor timing possible but rare
  • Diversified across broad universe
  • Formal portfolio optimization used
  • Few managers in this category
Discretionary · Top-Down
Judgement + macro entry
  • Emphasizes macro rewarded factors
  • Most likely to use factor timing
  • Diversified or concentrated on smaller subset of securities
  • Less formal portfolio construction
Systematic · Bottom-Up
Rules + stock entry
  • Emphasizes security-specific factors
  • No factor timing
  • Diversified across broad universe
  • Formal portfolio optimization used
Discretionary · Bottom-Up
Judgement + stock entry
  • Emphasizes security-specific characteristics or factors
  • Potential factor timing
  • Diversified or concentrated on smaller subset of securities
  • Less formal portfolio construction
Pattern recognition across the matrix
FeatureSystematicDiscretionary
Portfolio constructionFormal optimizationLess formal
Universe breadthBroad, diversifiedBroad OR concentrated subset
Factor timingRare (top-down) or never (bottom-up)More common
FeatureTop-DownBottom-Up
Factor focusMacro rewarded factorsSecurity-specific factors / characteristics
Starting unitMacro / sectors / countriesIndividual stocks
Memory anchor: Systematic = formal optimization + broad universe. Discretionary = less formal + possible concentration. Top-down = macro factors. Bottom-up = security-specific factors.
Factor timing — who does it?
Discretionary top-down → MOST LIKELY to time factors (judgement + macro orientation = natural fit) Systematic top-down → POSSIBLE but RARE (rules can encode factor timing signals, but most quant strategies don't) Discretionary bottom-up → POTENTIAL factor timing (the manager may form macro views even if stocks are the entry) Systematic bottom-up → NO factor timing (rule-based stock screening doesn't time factors by definition)
Exam trap: "systematic bottom-up managers time factors" → FALSE. Systematic + bottom-up = the cell where factor timing is explicitly absent.
Part 2 · Objective functions & constraints (Figure P3.2)
Absolute vs Relative framework
Portfolio construction is an optimization problem with a GOAL (objective function) and a set of CONSTRAINTS. The framework choice (absolute or relative) flips both.
Absolute FrameworkRelative Framework
Objective FunctionMaximize Sharpe ratioMaximize Information ratio
Constraints
Sector / security weightsMaximum size in portfolioMaximum deviation from benchmark
RiskMaximum portfolio volatility specified as multiple (e.g. 0.9) of benchmark volatilityMaximum tracking error (active risk)
Market capitalizationMaximum / minimum set by mandateMaximum / minimum set by mandate
Same mandate, two different lenses: the absolute framework cares about the portfolio's own characteristics (its Sharpe, its volatility). The relative framework cares about deviation from benchmark (its IR, its tracking error).
Sharpe vs Information Ratio — the two objective functions
Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf) / σp ← absolute framework Information ratio = (Rp − Rb) / σ(Rp − Rb) ← relative framework = active return / tracking error
Sharpe measures excess return per unit of TOTAL risk → use when no benchmark or absolute mandate IR measures active return per unit of ACTIVE risk → use when benchmarked
When the question says "benchmark" or "tracking error", the framework is RELATIVE → IR is the right objective. When the question says "absolute return mandate" or "no benchmark", the framework is ABSOLUTE → Sharpe.
Other approaches to optimization
Risk-based objectives (instead of return-based): → Minimize portfolio volatility → Minimize downside risk (VaR, CVaR, semi-variance) → Minimize maximum drawdown Factor exposure objectives: → Maximize exposure to rewarded factors (size, value, momentum, quality, low-vol) Custom characteristic objectives: → Maximize exposure to a custom metric (e.g. deep value: significant undervaluation)
These risk-based and factor-based objectives can sit inside either framework (absolute or relative) — they're additional or alternative goals beyond pure Sharpe/IR maximization.
Part 3 · Heuristic vs Optimization
The two construction methods
AspectHeuristicOptimization
MethodLess scientific — rank securities by characteristicFormal mathematical maximization
BasisRanking on a desired metric (e.g. low P/B, high momentum)Maximize objective function subject to constraints
WeightingOften equal-weighted top N or rank-weightedComputed to maximize Sharpe / IR / factor exposure
ConstraintsInformal (rule of thumb caps)Formal (sector limits, TE, vol bands)
Common inDiscretionary + simpler quant strategiesSystematic strategies, especially top-down
Exam phrasing signals
→ Heuristic signals: "rank by", "less scientific", "based on weighting", "low P/B selection", "simple sort", "characteristic-based filter" → Optimization signals: "maximize Sharpe / IR", "formal mathematical", "subject to constraints", "covariance matrix", "tracking error minimization"
Memory anchor: heuristic = "rank and pick". Optimization = "maximize subject to constraints". The presence of constraints in the description is a strong signal toward optimization.
Where each fits in the 2×2 matrix
CellTypical method
Systematic · Top-DownFormal optimization
Systematic · Bottom-UpFormal optimization
Discretionary · Top-DownHeuristic or less formal optimization
Discretionary · Bottom-UpHeuristic (less formal portfolio construction)
"Less formal portfolio construction" is the recurring phrase in the discretionary cells. It means heuristic methods (or informal optimization) rather than the formal mathematical optimization characteristic of systematic strategies.
Active Share vs Active Risk — what each measures
MeasureWhat it capturesAffected by correlation?
Active ShareDifference in weights vs benchmark (pure mechanics)NO — weights only
Active Risk (tracking error)Volatility of (Rp − Rb)YES — weights + correlations + vols
Active Share = ½ × Σ |w(port,i) − w(bench,i)| Active Risk = σ(Rp − Rb) = standard deviation of active return
Same Active Share, different Active Risk: two managers can have identical Active Share (say 5%) but very different Active Risk depending on whether their active bets are on highly correlated stocks (low Active Risk) or uncorrelated stocks (high Active Risk).
The 6 manager styles — ordered by increasing Active Share + Active Risk
As you move from pure indexing to concentrated stock picking, BOTH Active Share AND Active Risk increase. Active risk increases as factor risk and idiosyncratic risk levels increase.
Pure indexing No active positions — portfolio equals benchmark
Active Share = 0Active Risk = 0
Factor neutral No active factor bets · idiosyncratic risk low if diversified
Low Active RiskLow Active Share (if diversified)
Factor diversified Balanced exposure to risk factors · minimized idiosyncratic risk through high # of securities
Reasonably low Active RiskHigh Active Share (many non-benchmark names)
Concentrated factor bets Targeted factor bets · idiosyncratic risk likely HIGH
High Active RiskHigh Active Share
Concentrated stock picker Targeted individual stock bets
Highest Active RiskHighest Active Share
Key insight: Factor diversified is the exception — it has HIGH Active Share (lots of off-benchmark names) but only REASONABLY LOW Active Risk because the many securities diversify away idiosyncratic risk, leaving only the balanced factor exposures.
Figure P3.3 — the visual map
* A closet indexer is a fund that advertises itself as actively managed but is substantially similar to an index fund in its exposures. Low Active Share + low Active Risk = closet indexing.
The critical exam point: Active Share ≠ Active Risk
Active Share looks ONLY at the weights. It ignores how stocks co-move. Active Risk depends on weights AND on the correlations + volatilities of the active positions.
Same Active Share, different Active Risk: Manager A: long +5% Apple, short −5% Microsoft (corr ≈ 0.9) → active positions move together → LOW Active Risk Manager B: long +5% Apple, short −5% utility stock (corr ≈ 0) → active positions independent → HIGH Active Risk Both: Active Share = 5%. But Active Risk very different.
Common exam trap: "Manager A and Manager B have the same Active Share, therefore the same Active Risk." → FALSE. The cross-correlation between active positions determines how much Active Risk you get from a given Active Share.
Memory anchor: Active Share = arithmetic on weights. Active Risk = statistics on returns (correlations matter).
Drivers of Active Risk
Factor risk — exposure to systematic factors that differ from the benchmark (e.g. value tilt, small-cap tilt) Idiosyncratic risk — stock-specific risk from concentrated single-name bets Active risk INCREASES as factor risk and idiosyncratic risk levels INCREASE Active risk DECREASES when the # of securities increases (idiosyncratic risk gets diversified away)
StyleFactor riskIdiosyncratic riskActive Risk result
Factor neutralLowLow (diversified)Low
Factor diversifiedBalanced/moderateLow (high N)Reasonably low
Concentrated factor betsHigh (targeted)HighHigh
Concentrated stock pickervariesHighestHighest
The core idea — match risk sources to your investment approach
An active manager should efficiently allocate their risk budget to sources that accurately represent their investment approach. The risk you take on should come from the bets you intend to make — not from accidental exposures.
Factor Diversified manager: balanced exposure to rewarded factors (size, value, momentum, quality, low-vol) → risk should come from FACTOR exposures across many securities Sector Rotator manager: concentrated sector and cash bets → risk should come from SECTOR positioning and the cash allocation
If a Factor Diversified manager has too much sector-specific risk, they have an "alignment problem" — their actual risk doesn't match their advertised strategy. Same for a Sector Rotator with hidden factor bets. The exam often tests this alignment.
Figure P3.5 — Comparative sources of risk & drivers of return
CharacteristicFactor DiversifiedSector Rotator
Number of securitiesHigh (in the hundreds)Low (in the tens)
Position concentrationLowHigh
Cash positionsVery lowHigh when allocated to cash
Market betaClose to one (diversified)Higher/lower than one — depends on risk targets
Absolute riskLowerHigher, though tempered by large cash allocation
Active riskLowerHigher — large idiosyncratic risks from concentrated positions & sector bets
Active ShareLowerHigher — consistent with higher security concentration
Average sector deviationLowerHigher — consistent with willingness to take sector bets
Sources of risk — where does the active risk come from?
SourceFactor DiversifiedSector Rotator
MarketHigherLower — consistent with higher security concentration
SectorsLowerHigher — consistent with sector bets
Styles (factors)Higher* — by designLower — concentrated positions, not style bets
Unexplained (idiosyncratic)Lower — diversified across many namesHigher — from sector rotation & concentrated positions
*Note: in the textbook table, "Source of risk: styles" is listed as Lower for Factor Diversified — this is because each individual style exposure is moderate (balanced across many factors). The factor RISK comes through clearly, but no single style dominates as a risk source.
Memory hook: think "where does the volatility live?" For Factor Diversified, it lives in MARKET beta (close to 1, broad exposure). For Sector Rotator, it lives in SECTOR bets and IDIOSYNCRATIC risk from concentrated names.
Why this matters — the alignment principle
✓ Risk budget allocated correctly: the sources of risk match the stated strategy ✗ Misallocation: e.g., a "factor diversified" fund whose risk comes mostly from sectors or single positions → the manager is making bets they didn't advertise → potential style drift
Diagnostic check (factor diversified fund): - Most active risk should come from factor exposures - Sector and idiosyncratic contributions should be LOW - Number of securities should be HIGH (hundreds) - Position concentration should be LOW → If any of these are off, the manager has a misalignment. Diagnostic check (sector rotator): - Most active risk from sector bets & concentrated positions - Style/factor contributions should be LOW - Number of securities LOW (tens) - Cash positions can be HIGH (tactical) → If factor risk dominates, the manager is closet factor-betting.
The 2 archetypes side by side — visual summary
Factor Diversified
Broad · diversified · factor-driven
  • Hundreds of securities
  • Low position concentration
  • Market beta ≈ 1
  • Active Share LOW, Active Risk LOW
  • Risk source: market & factors
  • Cash: very low
Sector Rotator
Concentrated · tactical · sector-driven
  • Tens of securities
  • High position concentration
  • Beta >1 or <1 (depends on tilt)
  • Active Share HIGH, Active Risk HIGH
  • Risk source: sectors & idiosyncratic
  • Cash: high when tactical (defensive)
Exam-ready cheat sheet
"Hundreds of securities, low concentration, beta ≈ 1" → Factor Diversified profile "Tens of securities, high concentration, high cash, sector bets" → Sector Rotator profile Active risk source dominated by SECTORS → Sector Rotator (or misaligned Factor Diversified) Active risk source dominated by MARKET → Factor Diversified (broad exposure) Active risk source dominated by IDIOSYNCRATIC/UNEXPLAINED → Sector Rotator (concentrated positions)
Common trap: confusing "high active risk" with "high factor exposure". A Sector Rotator can have very high active risk WITHOUT taking factor bets — the risk comes from idiosyncratic concentration, not from style tilts.
What makes a portfolio "well-constructed"
A well-constructed portfolio delivers the characteristics promised to investors in a cost-efficient and risk-efficient way. Four requirements:
✓ A clear investment philosophy and a consistent investment process ✓ Risk and structural characteristics as promised to investors (no style drift) ✓ Achieving desired risk exposures in the most efficient manner ✓ Reasonably low operating costs, given the strategy
"Risk-efficient" means you get the targeted exposures with as little extra (unintended) risk as possible. "Cost-efficient" means low fees AND low operating expenses for the type of strategy.
Comparing portfolios with the SAME desired characteristics
When two portfolios target the same exposures, three tie-breaker rules tell you which one is better-constructed:
ScenarioWhich portfolio wins?
Same desired exposures, but achieved with FEWER positions The one with fewer positions — more focus on risk management. Doesn't guarantee higher excess return, but indicates higher risk efficiency.
Similar risk factor exposures + similar costs Lower absolute volatility & lower active risk wins — same exposure, less noise.
Similar active risk + absolute risk + costs + alpha skill HIGHEST Active Share wins — leverages the manager's alpha skill more; higher expected return.
Memory anchor for the 3 tie-breakers: fewer positions → lower risk → higher Active Share. Each applies when EVERYTHING ELSE is equal.
Exam trap: the highest Active Share isn't always preferable. It's only preferable when the manager has REAL alpha skill AND when other risks/costs are similar. Without alpha skill, higher Active Share just means more uncompensated risk.
Part 2 · Long-Only, Long Extension, Long-Short, Market-Neutral
The four construction styles — at a glance
StyleLongShortNet exposureTypical
Long-only100%0%100%Traditional mutual funds, most active managers
Long extension130%30%100%130/30 funds — constrained long-short
Long-shortvariesvariesvariesGeneral — any portfolio that can short
Market-neutralvaries≈ longs≈ 0% (net beta ≈ 0)Stat arb, pairs trading, equity market neutral
Gross vs Net exposure — the two key metrics
Gross exposure = |Long| + |Short| (as % of capital) Net exposure = |Long| − |Short| (as % of capital)
Worked example (textbook): fund raises $100M. Invests $80M long, shorts $30M.
Long position: $80M = 80% of capital Short position: $30M = 30% of capital Gross exposure = 80% + 30% = 110% Net exposure = 80% − 30% = 50% Cash balance = $20M uninvested + $30M short sale proceeds = $50M
The short sale proceeds sit as cash (collateral with the lender). The "uninvested" portion is what wasn't put into longs. Both contribute to the cash balance.
The 130/30 long extension — the classic example
A long extension portfolio is a long-short fund constrained to 100% net exposure. The most common version: 130% long + 30% short = 130/30 fund.
→ Net exposure: 100% (130 − 30) — same market beta as a long-only fund → Gross exposure: 160% (130 + 30) — higher than long-only's 100% → Manager has no discretion over net exposure (it's fixed at 100%) → But can use 30% shorting to express negative views & finance the 130% long
Who picks 130/30? Investors who want full market exposure (100% beta) AND want the manager to be able to short. They get the upside of shorting without giving up the market risk premium.
Market-neutral portfolios — net beta ≈ 0
Market-neutral funds aim to remove market exposure by balancing long and short positions. Two ways to think about this:
Net beta zero: weighted average of long and short betas cancels out Equal beta-weighted longs & shorts: not just $-equal, but β-equal
Textbook example: Long $200M of assets with β = 0.9 → β-weighted long = $180M Short $150M of assets with β = 1.2 → β-weighted short = $180M → Net market beta = 0 ✓ → Gross exposure = $350M (much larger than longs alone) → If positions had EQUAL betas (size/value/etc.), net exposure = 0
Market-neutral isn't $100M long + $100M short. It's β-weighted long = β-weighted short. The example shows you can be net-beta-zero with UNEQUAL dollar amounts when betas differ.
In practice it's hard to maintain a zero beta over time because correlations between exposures change continually. Market-neutral funds rebalance frequently.
Market-neutral construction methods — pairs trading & stat arb
Pairs trading: buy and short securities of similar companies to exploit perceived mispricings (the relative bet hedges market exposure) Statistical arbitrage (stat arb): quantitative pairs trading — same idea but driven by quantitative signals across many pairs
Market-neutral funds are often used for diversification (low correlation with other strategies), not for high returns. They should have lower volatility than long-only strategies.
Part 3 · Benefits & drawbacks of long-short
Benefits of long-short strategies
BenefitWhy it matters
Express negative viewsLong-only manager: max underweight = security's benchmark weight. Long-short: no cap on negative bets → higher transfer coefficient (TC) → higher IR (fundamental law)
Leverage long ideasShort proceeds finance additional long positions → gear into high-conviction longs
Remove market riskMarket-neutral construction → diversifying investment against other strategies (low correlation)
Better control of factor exposuresMost rewarded factors (size, value, momentum) are long-short by construction. Shorting allows cleaner factor exposures.
The transfer coefficient point is key for the fundamental law of active management: IR ≈ IC × √breadth × TC. Removing the long-only constraint raises TC.
Drawbacks of long-short strategies
DrawbackWhat it means
Unlimited losses on shortsStock prices have NO upper bound → potential losses are unlimited; also reduces long-term exposure to market risk premium
Leverage magnifies lossesSome long-short strategies require significant leverage → both gains AND losses are amplified
Borrowing costsCost of borrowing securities can be high — especially for hard-to-borrow names
Collateral & forced liquidationLosses on shorts → lender demands more collateral → may force liquidation at unfavorable prices. Short squeeze risk: heavily-shorted stocks rise sharply, forcing covers that push prices even higher. Lenders can also recall shares at inopportune times.
RegulationsSome countries ban short selling in periods of financial instability
Transactional complexitySource borrow + post collateral + manage recalls + prime broker counterparty risk (if PB goes bankrupt, collateral may be lost)
Higher costsManagement fees + operational expenses higher than long-only
Personal ideologySome investors morally object to profiting from another company's failure
Exam trap: forgetting that short squeezes and share recalls are SEPARATE risks. Squeeze = price action forces you out. Recall = lender pulls the shares back. Both can disrupt the strategy at the worst moment.
Part 4 · The merits of long-only investing
Why some investors stay long-only
FactorLong-only advantage
Long-term risk premiumsMarket risk premium is earned by NET LONG investors. Long-term holders should be net long; short sellers suffer negative expected returns over long horizons. Long-only naturally captures the equity risk premium.
Capacity & scalabilityLong-only capacity = liquidity of underlying securities. Short strategies' capacity is limited by availability to borrow — typically much smaller than long-only capacity, especially for large-cap funds.
Limited legal liabilityMax loss for long investor = price paid (stock falls to zero, you lose 100%). For short seller: unlimited loss since prices have no ceiling. "Naked" short selling (no hedge) is riskier than long-only by definition.
Regulation & restrictionsMany institutional mandates and retail products don't permit shorting at all
Lower costs & complexityNo borrowing fees, no collateral, no prime broker counterparty risk
Short horizon investors worried about negative returns may PREFER strategies with short exposure (market-neutral, long-short). Long horizon investors should generally lean toward long-only or constrained long-short (130/30) to retain equity risk premium exposure.
Part 5 · Which approach for which investor?
Decision matrix — matching strategy to investor profile
Investor characteristicBest suited to...
Long-term horizon, wants market risk premiumLong-only (or 130/30 if wants shorting flexibility with full market exposure)
Wants 100% net market exposure + manager flexibilityLong extension (130/30)
Wants alpha without market risk; diversifierMarket-neutral
Short horizon, downside-sensitiveMarket-neutral or long-short
Moral / ideological objection to shortingLong-only
Strong manager alpha skill + similar risks across optionsHigher Active Share variant (long-short usually allows higher AS than long-only)
When selecting equity managers for a multi-asset fund: combine managers so the overall equity allocation is well-constructed. A risk factor exposure that's desired but missing in one manager can be added via a different manager that specializes in that factor.
The scale problem — why size impairs strategy
As a fund's AUM grows, the manager must own more dollars of each name. But each security has limits:
Index weight floor: strategy may forbid investing in tiny index names (below e.g. 0.02%) Position weight cap: maximum portfolio weight a single security can have (e.g. 10× index weight or +100bps) Liquidity cap: can't own more than X% of a security's average daily volume (ADV) without crippling market impact
When the fund grows large enough that the dollar position dictated by the weight cap exceeds the dollar amount allowed by the liquidity cap, the strategy is impaired — you can't fill the position without moving the price.
Small-cap focused funds hit this wall earlier than large-cap funds (smaller ADV, smaller market cap). Solutions: limit AUM, diversify further, lower turnover, or change trading style.
Worked example — Issues of Scale (textbook)
A diversified multifactor fund: $200M AUM, 350 positions. Benchmark = large-to-mid-cap index, 1,000 constituents, total market cap ≈ $20 trillion. Smaller index securities trade ~1.5% of shares daily.
#Constraint
1No investment in any security with index weight < 0.02%
2Max fund position = lesser of (10 × index weight) or (index weight + 100 bps)
3Absolute position size cannot exceed 5% of ADV (trailing 12 months)
Question: at what AUM is the strategy impaired by illiquidity?
Step-by-step walkthrough — click "Next step" to animate
Step 0 / 5
1What's the SMALLEST market cap I'm allowed to invest in?
Constraint 1 says: no security with index weight < 0.02%. The smallest allowed has weight exactly 0.02% of the index.
Smallest mkt cap = 0.02% × total index mkt cap = 0.0002 × $20 trillion = $4 billion
→ Smallest allowed market cap = $4 billion
2What's the ADV of that smallest name?
The smaller securities trade 1.5% of shares outstanding daily. For a $4bn cap stock:
ADV = 1.5% × $4 billion = 0.015 × $4,000,000,000 = $60 million
→ Daily trading volume ≈ $60 million
3What's the MAX dollar position I can hold (liquidity limit)?
Constraint 3 caps the position at 5% of ADV — beyond this, market impact becomes punishing.
Max position $ = 5% × ADV = 0.05 × $60 million = $3 million
→ Max dollar position in the smallest cap holding = $3M
4What does the STRATEGY tell me to hold (weight cap)?
Constraint 2: max position weight = lesser of (10 × index weight) or (index weight + 100 bps). For the smallest stock at 0.02% index weight:
Option A: 10 × 0.02% = 0.2% Option B: 0.02% + 1.00% = 1.02% Lesser of the two = 0.2%
→ Strategy wants up to 0.2% of fund in the smallest holding
5At what AUM does the strategy break?
Set the two binding constraints equal: the dollar position the strategy wants (0.2% × AUM) cannot exceed the $3M liquidity cap.
0.2% × AUM ≤ $3,000,000 0.002 × AUM ≤ $3,000,000 AUM ≤ $3,000,000 / 0.002 AUM ≤ $1.5 billion
→ Strategy is impaired when AUM exceeds $1.5 billion
Above $1.5bn, the manager is constrained by small-cap illiquidity and CAN'T hold the maximum 0.2% weight allowed by the strategy. They'll have to underweight small caps relative to the model — style drift.
Visual logic chain
Interactive — change the parameters
Adjust any input below. The maximum AUM updates live.

Min index weight (%)0.02%
Daily volume (% of shares)1.5%
Max position vs ADV (%)5%

Try lowering total mkt cap to $5T (e.g. an emerging market index) — the AUM ceiling drops dramatically. Or raise the daily volume to 5% (more liquid market) and watch capacity expand.
Exam-ready memory anchors
The chain: min index weight × total mkt cap = smallest stock's mkt cap → × daily volume % = ADV → × position-vs-ADV cap = max $ position Then: max $ position ÷ max portfolio weight = AUM ceiling Why this matters: if a fund's AUM exceeds this ceiling, it physically can't hold its smallest names at the weight the strategy specifies → style drift forced by liquidity Small-cap funds hit the ceiling EARLIER than large-cap funds because ADVs are smaller and prices move more on the same trade size Solutions for funds approaching capacity: limit AUM (close fund to new investors) · diversify into more names · lower turnover · adapt trading strategy (slower execution, dark pools)
Exam trap: "higher market impact cost is associated with lower AUM" → FALSE. Higher AUM = need to trade more $ at once = more market impact. Also: large-cap securities have LOWER impact cost (more liquid). Higher portfolio TURNOVER = more trades = more impact cost.
Your errors are not 11 isolated mistakes — they're 4 patterns
I analyzed your 11 wrong answers. They cluster into 4 recurring error types. Fix the patterns, fix the questions.
Pattern 1 · Confusing similar-sounding concepts
You mix up concepts that look alike but mean different things.
ConfusionAffected Qs
Alpha vs Active ReturnQ19 (Fraser, you said −0.17%, correct = −0.20%)
Active Risk vs Active Share vs Total VolatilityQ14 (Fund A/B), Ash/Blue/March
What reduces volatility vs what reduces active riskAsh/Blue/March — low covariance reduces volatility but you need HIGH covariance to reduce active risk
Top-down vs Bottom-up when description has BOTHQ Soar (occasional macro doesn't make it top-down)
Diagnostic: when you see two words that "feel close" in a question, STOP and write the formula or definition for each before answering.
Pattern 2 · Variance/Covariance contribution formula
You missed the multi-factor variance decomposition 3 times — same formula, different vignettes.
QuestionWhat was askedCorrect answer
Q20 HerrickCountry A's contribution to portfolio variance47.5%
Q25 LSMEMarket factor's contribution to variance9%
Q30 Fund 1Market factor's contribution to total risk87%
The formula every time: Contribution of factor k = w_k × Σ_j (w_j × Cov(k, j)) (sum across ALL other factors, including itself) Then: Proportion = Contribution / Total portfolio variance (= σ²_portfolio)
Memory anchor: it's a row of the covariance matrix × the weight vector, then × the weight of factor k again. Never just w_k × Cov(k,k) — that's the trap that gives wrong answers.
Pattern 3 · Classifying a strategy from a description
You misclassify fund descriptions when the wording is ambiguous.
FundYour answer (wrong)CorrectThe key signal
SoarTop-down systematicBottom-up systematic"Security-specific factors" = bottom-up. Low idiosyncratic + low concentration = systematic.
FraserBalanced factor exposureFirm-specific (pricing power)"Discretionary" → firm-specific. Balanced factor = systematic.
AE vs CCMomentum tiltAE = concentrated stock-picking, CC = concentrated factor-bettingCC has R²=0.98 (factors dominate). AE has R²=0.72 + 42 names (idiosyncratic dominates).
Decision tree: (1) Does it use security-specific or macro factors? → bottom-up vs top-down. (2) Rule-based or judgement? → systematic vs discretionary. (3) Concentrated or diversified? → tells you stock-picker vs factor-better.
Pattern 4 · Scale & liquidity arithmetic
You got the chained calculations right (40 days for Reed) but you missed the strategic ANALYSIS in the Voyager question.
For Voyager: 2 concerns were (1) cash size vs total market cap of holdings ($1.1bn vs $800M), (2) daily volume vs shares outstanding (<0.1% means high impact for any large trade) You said "cash has low correlation with benchmark" — that's not a recognized issue. Cash is uninvested capital; the issue is whether you can DEPLOY it without market impact.
Memory anchor: when you see new contributions vs current holdings, ALWAYS compare to (a) total market cap of current positions and (b) average daily volume of those positions. These are the two capacity constraints.
Pattern 1 deep-drill · The concept confusions
a. Alpha vs Active Return
DefinitionFormula
Active ReturnPortfolio return minus benchmark returnR_A = R_p − R_b
AlphaReturn NOT explained by rewarded factorsα = R_p − Σ(β_k × F_k)
Q19 Fraser walkthrough: R_p = 0.55%, R_b = 0.72%. Factor return = (0.91×0.61) + (0.15×0.17) + (0.60×0.18) + (0.08×0.72) = 0.75%. So active return = 0.55 − 0.72 = −0.17% BUT alpha = 0.55 − 0.75 = −0.20%. Different concepts, different math.
b. Active Risk vs Active Share vs Volatility
What it measuresReduces if...
Active ShareWeight difference vs benchmarkPortfolio weights closer to benchmark
Active Risk (tracking error)Volatility of (R_p − R_b)Higher COVARIANCE with benchmark
Total Volatilityσ(R_p) — standalone portfolio riskLower correlation between holdings
Ash/Blue/March walkthrough: To minimize ACTIVE risk of total Amity fund after substitution → pick fund with HIGH covariance with Amity (Ash). Low covariance (Blue, March) reduces total volatility but NOT active risk.
c. Sector bets affect which?
Sector bets → Active Risk (yes) → Active Share (yes, only if weights differ) But: same Active Share + very different Active Risk = different sector/idiosyncratic profile Fund A active risk 3× Fund B with same Active Share → A makes sector bets, NOT B
Pattern 2 deep-drill · The variance contribution formula
This formula appears in 3 different forms but it's always the same logic. Learn it once.
FORMULA: Contribution of factor k to portfolio variance = w_k × [w_k × Var(k) + Σ_{j≠k} w_j × Cov(k,j)] = w_k × [Σ_j w_j × Cov(k,j)] ← combines into one clean form Where the bracket [...] is the covariance of factor k with the WHOLE portfolio: Cov(k, portfolio) = Σ_j w_j × Cov(k,j) So: Contribution_k = w_k × Cov(k, portfolio) Proportion_k = Contribution_k / Var(portfolio)
Q20 Herrick worked example: For Country A with weight 30%, the covariance with portfolio (given) = 0.0276. Contribution = 0.30 × 0.0276 = 0.00828. Portfolio variance = 0.132² = 0.01742. Proportion = 0.00828 / 0.01742 = 47.5%.
Q30 Fund 1 worked example: Market factor β = 1.080. Sum all 4 covariance terms (×βs):
1.080×0.00109×1.080 = 0.001271
1.080×0.00053×0.098 = 0.000056
1.080×0.00022×(−0.401) = −0.000095
1.080×(−0.00025)×0.034 = −0.0000092
Sum (Contribution) = 0.001223
Total variance = 0.0374² = 0.001399. Proportion = 0.001223 / 0.001399 = 87%.
Common errors: (a) using just w_k² × Var(k) without the cross-terms → wrong. (b) Forgetting to multiply by w_k at the end → gives the bracket value alone. (c) Forgetting to square σ → gives wrong denominator.

Signal in descriptionPoints to

"Macro / sectors / countries first"Top-down

"Discretionary / judgement / firm-specific (e.g., pricing power)"Discretionary

AE vs CC walkthrough: AE has R²=0.72 (factors explain only 72% of variance, idiosyncratic dominates) + 42 names + Active Share 0.92 → concentrated stock-picking. CC has R²=0.98 (factors explain 98%) + 124 names + Active Share 0.71 → concentrated factor-betting. The R² is the deciding signal.
Pattern 4 deep-drill · Capacity & cash deployment
Two questions you have to ask when new contributions arrive:
Q1: Is the new cash large relative to the total market cap of current holdings? → If yes, the strategy might not be able to deploy the cash within its current universe Q2: Is the daily trading volume large enough to absorb the deployment? → If daily volume is <0.1% of shares outstanding, even modest position sizes will move the price
Voyager numbers: Current portfolio holdings total mkt cap = 500 + 200 + 100 = $800M New cash contribution = $1,100M (= $1.1bn) → New cash > total mkt cap of existing holdings ✗ capacity issue → ADV of A,B,C all < 0.1% of shares outstanding ✗ impact issue
When asked "discuss concerns about new contributions", the 2 answers should always be: (1) size relative to holdings' market cap (can you deploy?) and (2) liquidity relative to ADV (can you trade without impact?). Don't reach for "correlation" or "active variance" — those aren't the structural issues.

Reference prices — what they are and why we need them
A reference price is a benchmark price used to (1) determine expected trading costs before trading, (2) select the optimal trading strategy, and (3) calculate the actual cost of trading for post-trade evaluation.
A trade's "cost" = execution price minus reference price. Choice of reference price drives what you measure. 4 categories based on WHEN the reference is set: Pre-trade, Intraday, Post-trade, Price target.
The category dictates the manager's INTENT: pre-trade = "what did I expect when I decided?", intraday = "how well did I participate?", post-trade = "tracking the close", price-target = "earn alpha vs fair value".
Animated trading day — click "Reveal next" to see each benchmark in order
0 / 8 benchmarks shown
PRE-TRADEDecision price
Price of the security at the moment the portfolio manager made the investment decision. The earliest "anchor" in the workflow.
Use case: standard benchmark for measuring implementation shortfall.
PRE-TRADEPrevious close
Yesterday's closing price. A proxy for decision price often used by quantitative systematic managers running rule-based, data-driven strategies (decisions are made overnight from data ending at prior close).
Use case: quant funds where the decision is generated by the data of D−1.
PRE-TRADEOpening price
Today's open. Often used as a proxy for decision price by subjective fundamental managers chasing long-term alpha — it doesn't punish or reward traders for overnight news.
Use case: long-term fundamental managers who want a "neutral" reference unaffected by overnight news.
Trap: if the TRADE itself goes into an opening auction, then the opening auction price IS affected by the trade → opening price is NOT a good benchmark in that case.
PRE-TRADEArrival price
Price at the exact moment the order is sent to the market for execution. Active managers trying to generate alpha will often pick arrival price as the benchmark.
Use case: alpha-driven active managers; tightest implementation shortfall measure.
INTRADAYVWAP — Volume-Weighted Average Price
Average price of all trades, weighted by volume, over the trading horizon. Managers use VWAP when they want to participate with normal volume patterns.
Use case: rebalancing over a day · using sell-side cash to fund buy-side · low-information urgency trades.
Why VWAP fits rebalancing: you're not pursuing alpha, you're trying to be representative of how the market actually traded that day.
INTRADAYTWAP — Time-Weighted Average Price
Equal-weighted average price across the trading horizon — ignores volume. Managers use TWAP to remove the impact of outlier trades (large blocks at highs/lows) and during highly volatile volume conditions.
Use case: thinly traded names · highly fluctuating volume · when manager can't participate in extreme block trades.
VWAP vs TWAP: same averaging idea, but VWAP weights by volume, TWAP weights by time. If volume is steady, they converge. If there's a giant block, VWAP gets pulled toward it; TWAP doesn't.
POST-TRADEClosing price
End-of-day price. Most frequent post-trade benchmark. Often used by managers who execute AT the close to reduce tracking error vs the benchmark index (which is also marked to close).
Use case: index funds / index-tracking strategies that fundamentally want zero tracking error.
Drawback: the closing price isn't known until AFTER trading is done → manager cannot assess trading performance DURING the day. Post-trade only.
PRICE TARGETPrice target benchmark
A price reflecting the manager's view of fair value. Profit-seeking managers chasing short-term alpha will use a price target benchmark.
Example: Current price: $10 Manager's fair value: $10.50 Strategy: buy as many shares as possible BELOW $10.50
Use case: short-term alpha extraction · "buy under fair value" or "sell over fair value" tactical strategies.
