Exam traps to remember
Opening auction trap: opening price is normally a good pre-trade benchmark, but if the trade is executed AS PART of the opening auction, the trade itself moves the auction price → it's no longer a clean benchmark.
Closing price post-trade drawback: the closing price benchmark is unknowable until trading ends → managers can't evaluate trading performance during the horizon, only after.
VWAP vs TWAP confusion: VWAP weights by volume; TWAP weights equally over time. TWAP is the right choice when you want to avoid being dragged by large blocks at the highs/lows.
Memory anchor for category → use: Pre-trade = "how good was my decision-vs-execution?" · Intraday = "how well did I participate?" · Post-trade = "where did the day close?" · Price target = "did I beat fair value?"
The selection framework — match trading strategy to the trade's purpose
Every trade has a purpose. The trading strategy (urgency level, reference price benchmark, execution method) should fit that purpose.
Urgency is not a single number — it's the result of 4-5 underlying drivers. Each card below shows the drivers so you see WHY each trade type has its urgency level.
The 5 urgency drivers — what makes a trade urgent or not
DriverRaises urgency when...Lowers urgency when...
Market liquidityLiquid market (you can move fast)Illiquid market (forces patience to avoid impact)
Time horizonShort window (intraday, fixed deadline)Long window (weeks, months)
Directional exposureOne-sided trade (open risk during execution)Two-sided rebalance (no directional risk)
Alpha decay riskFast decay (mispricing closes in minutes)Slow decay (thesis plays out over months) or N/A
Information leakage costLiquid market absorbs your trades anonymouslyDealers see your size and front-run you
Drivers can conflict (e.g. illiquid market raises leakage cost AND raises impact cost — both push toward LOW urgency / slow execution). The dominant driver determines the overall urgency.
Reveal the 5 trade types one by one
0 / 5 trade types shown
URGENCY: HIGH Short-term alpha
Objective: Trade short-term mispricing in a liquid equity market (e.g. overreaction to news flow).
⚙️ Why urgency is HIGH — the drivers
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid equity)
Time horizon→VERY SHORT (intraday)
Directional exposure→YES — one-sided alpha bet
Alpha decay risk→FAST — minutes to hours
Information leakage cost→Tolerable (liquid market absorbs)
Reference price: Price target benchmark (manager's fair value) + Arrival price for orders placed in the market
Execution method: Computer algorithm (fast, automated, low-latency)
URGENCY: LOW Long-term alpha
Objective: Trade over the long term due to changes in fundamental conditions (e.g. sell average-sized positions in illiquid bonds expected to experience deteriorating credit over the next year).
⚙️ Why urgency is LOW — the drivers
Market liquidity→LOW (illiquid bonds)
Time horizon→LONG (weeks to a year)
Directional exposure→YES but slow-moving thesis
Alpha decay risk→SLOW — months
Information leakage cost→HIGH (dealers move prices on you)
Reference price: Difficult to use in practice (no clean anchor over weeks/months)
Execution method: Sell securities gradually over a few weeks in small parts to avoid information leakage and pressure on dealer's prices
Key tension: liquidity is LOW (which would normally raise urgency to "do it quickly before market moves") but leakage cost is HIGH (which forces patience). Patience wins → low urgency, slow execution.
URGENCY: LOW Risk rebalance
Objective: Rebalance or hedge risk exposure (e.g. reduce risk in liquid FX markets by liquidating long AND short positions to bring fund volatility down to a target level).
⚙️ Why urgency is LOW — the drivers
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid FX markets)
Time horizon→FLEXIBLE (a couple of days)
Directional exposure→NO — both buying AND selling
Alpha decay risk→N/A — not an alpha trade
Execution risk→LOW (two-sided neutralizes risk)
Reference price: TWAP
Execution method: Algorithmically target TWAP over the next couple of days
Key insight: even though it's a "trade", a two-sided rebalance has NO directional exposure → very low execution risk. One-sided rebalances would carry higher urgency because the trader IS exposed during execution.
URGENCY: DAY-END DEADLINE Cash flow driven · Client redemption
Objective: Liquidate holdings to meet client redemptions (e.g. liquidate small-cap fund to meet redemptions calculated using the closing prices of portfolio securities). The fund bears the risk that liquidations are NOT made at the closing prices used to calculate the redemption.
⚙️ Why urgency is DAY-END — the drivers
Market liquidity→VARIABLE (small-cap → low)
Time horizon→FIXED to TODAY's close
Directional exposure→YES — must SELL to fund payout
Alpha decay risk→N/A — not an alpha trade
NAV tracking risk→HIGH if missing close price
Reference price: Closing price
Execution method: Execute a reasonable amount of liquidity in the closing auction; execute the remainder before the close of trading (e.g. at VWAP)
Risk to watch: if the close auction can't absorb all the volume, the rest is traded earlier in the day → may not hit the close benchmark → tracking error to NAV calculation.
URGENCY: IMMEDIATE EXPOSURE Cash flow driven · New trade mandate
Objective: Invest new client funds (e.g. invest large amount with a mandate to track a small-cap index with 3% tracking error). Performance measurement begins at today's closing price.
⚙️ Why urgency is IMMEDIATE — the drivers
Market liquidity→LOW in underlying (small-cap)
Market liquidity (futures)→HIGH (index futures)
Time horizon→EXPOSURE: NOW · Build: weeks
Directional exposure→YES — must BUY the index
Cash drag risk→HIGH if uninvested
Tracking error budget→3% (limits how slow you can go)
Reference price: Closing price
Execution method: (1) Obtain immediate exposure to the index via a LONG position in index futures to eliminate cash drag; (2) build underlying stock positions OVER TIME to reduce market impact; (3) simultaneously unwind the futures position as cash is deployed
Two issues: (1) there may not be a closing auction for the futures contract, so the futures trade has to be done as close to the market close as possible; (2) the mandate must allow derivatives positions.
The split urgency is the key insight: the EXPOSURE is immediate (so futures bridge), but the underlying BUILD is slow (small-cap illiquidity). Two different speeds, one trade.
Side-by-side comparison — drivers visible for each trade type

Quick diagnostic — given a vignette, identify the urgency
If the trade description says...Driver signal→ Urgency→ Strategy hint
"Exploiting overreaction / mispricing in liquid market"High liquidity + fast alpha decayHIGHAlgorithm + arrival/price target
"Sell over the next year due to deteriorating credit"Long horizon + illiquid + leakage riskLOWSmall slices, no clean benchmark

Exam traps for trading strategy selection
High urgency ≠ always bad: short-term alpha REQUIRES high urgency. Slowing down kills the alpha. Don't recommend TWAP for an alpha-extraction trade.
Rebalance ≠ urgent: even though it's a "trade", a two-sided risk rebalance has LOW urgency because there's no directional exposure. Recommending arrival-price aggressive execution would be wrong.
Long-term alpha has NO clean reference price: this is intentional — over weeks, no single benchmark works. The strategy is about avoiding leakage, not about hitting a price.
Cash flow redemption AND new mandate both use closing price but for different reasons: redemption = NAV strike, new mandate = performance start. Same benchmark, different urgency profiles.
Memory anchor by urgency level: High → short-term alpha · Low → long-term alpha + risk rebalance · End-of-day → cash flow redemption · Immediate via derivative → new mandate.
Two big families of trade execution
Once you've picked the strategy (urgency + reference price), you still need to choose HOW to execute. Two broad approaches: high-touch (human-intensive) vs electronic (computer-driven).
High-touchElectronic
Human involvementHIGH — traders, dealers, brokersLOW — algorithms + systems
Best forLarge trades (block trades), illiquid marketsMore liquid markets, smaller trades
Why high-touch?Finding the OTHER side of large/illiquid trades requires discretion + relationshipsOrder book + algos can find counterparties efficiently
Market typeQuote-driven (dealers post quotes)Order-driven (limit orders in CLOB)
Same trade, two paths: large illiquid → high-touch. Small liquid → electronic. The trade size relative to market liquidity is the master variable.
High-touch sub-types — Principal vs Agency
When you go high-touch, there are 2 ways the broker can act:
PRINCIPAL · BROKER RISK Principal trade (broker risk trade)
Mechanism: The dealer/market maker takes the OTHER side of your trade onto their own book — they assume the risk. Their compensation is baked into the bid-ask spread.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Market structure→Quote-driven · OTC · off-exchange
Urgency→HIGH (need immediate fill)
Liquidity→LOW or fragmented
Risk transfer→Broker absorbs execution risk
Also used in: Request-for-quote (RFQ) markets — market makers don't post continuous quotes but provide them on request
AGENCY Agency trade
Mechanism: The broker SEARCHES for the other side of the trade. They earn a commission but the execution risk stays with the portfolio manager/trader.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Urgency→LOWER (can wait for natural counterparty)
Risk transfer→PM still bears execution risk
Cost structure→Commission (often tighter than spread)
Discretion→Broker uses judgement / network
Memory anchor: PRINCIPAL = broker BUYS your risk (urgent, illiquid). AGENCY = broker FINDS your buyer (patient, less urgent).
Electronic trading basics
Order-driven markets: buyers and sellers post limit orders to a Central Limit Order Book (CLOB). Trades match when orders cross. Limit order: trade only at a specific price OR BETTER. Buy with limit $20 → execute up to $20. Sell with limit $20 → execute at $20 or higher. Direct Market Access (DMA): buy-side traders access the order book DIRECTLY through a broker's technology infrastructure (no broker manual intervention). Algorithmic trading: programmed rules execute orders electronically (covered in the next tab).
Why electronic dominates in liquid markets: low cost, fast, transparent, scalable. Why it fails for blocks: a large limit order on the book reveals your hand and moves the price against you (information leakage).
Quick decision matrix
Trade profileApproachSub-type
Large block, illiquid market, urgentHigh-touchPrincipal (broker risk)
Large block, illiquid market, can waitHigh-touchAgency
Small order, liquid market, urgentElectronicArrival price algo or SOR
Small order, liquid market, can waitElectronicScheduled algo (VWAP/TWAP/POV)
OTC derivatives, FX dealer marketHigh-touchPrincipal (RFQ)
Algorithmic trading — the 2 big purposes
Algorithmic trading = programmed rules to electronically trade orders. Two purposes:
Profit-seeking algos: use real-time market data to decide what to buy/sell. Used by electronic market makers, quant funds, HFTs. Execution algos: trade according to manager rules to meet the manager's objectives. This is what the exam focuses on.
All 5 algo types below are EXECUTION algos. They don't decide WHAT to trade — the manager already decided. They decide HOW to slice it.
The 5 execution algorithm types — animation
0 / 5 algorithms shown
SCHEDULED Scheduled algorithms — POV, VWAP, TWAP
Execute according to rules based on historical volumes or specified time periods. Trade passively throughout the day.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL relative to ADV
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid market)
Urgency→LOW (longer horizons tolerated)
Concern→Minimize market impact
3 sub-types:
POV (Percent of Volume / participation): send orders to be e.g. 5% of traded volume. Advantage: auto-exploits liquidity when available. Disadvantage: trades at any (potentially adverse) price; may not fill if volume is low.
VWAP (time-slicing on volume profile): carves up trade based on HISTORICAL intraday volumes — more at open/close, less midday. Advantage: ensures specified shares executed in specified time. Disadvantage: may force trades in low liquidity, miss high liquidity windows.
TWAP (time-slicing equal): equal shares per time period (e.g. each hour). Same advantage/disadvantage as VWAP but volume-insensitive.
LIQUIDITY-SEEKING Liquidity-seeking algorithms (opportunistic)
Take advantage of favorable liquidity when it's offered. For a buyer: wait until a large seller appears, then enter a market order. Use BOTH lit and dark venues.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→LARGER
Market liquidity→LESS LIQUID (sporadic episodes)
Urgency→HIGHER
Information leakage concern→HIGH (don't want to display limit orders)
Market impact concern→Mitigated by trading only when liquidity is offered
Memory anchor: "I'm hungry, I'll wait for the buffet" — only trades when the other side shows up.
ARRIVAL PRICE Arrival price algorithms
Seek to trade close to market prices prevailing at the time the order is entered. Trade MORE AGGRESSIVELY (faster) than other algos, with more shares executed close to the arrival price.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL (less than 15% of expected volume)
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid market)
Manager view→Prices likely to MOVE AGAINST during horizon
Profile→Profit-seeking OR risk-averse minimizing execution risk
Memory anchor: "lock in the price NOW before it gets away" — aggressive, frontloaded execution.
DARK / AGGREGATOR Dark strategies / liquidity aggregators
Execute trades in dark pools with aggregator algorithms optimizing across multiple dark venues. No order book exposure → no information leakage.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→LARGE
Market liquidity→ILLIQUID lit markets
Execution speed→LOWER probability of immediate fill
Urgency→CAN WAIT (no need for immediate full fill)
Alternative algos→Arrival/scheduled would cause high impact
Memory anchor: "hide and seek in private rooms" — patience trades anonymity for completion risk.
SMART ORDER ROUTER Smart Order Routers (SORs)
Determine the BEST DESTINATION (lit or dark venue) to route an electronic order. For market orders → best price. For limit orders → highest probability of execution.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL
Market impact→LOW
Market dynamics→Fast-moving market (for market orders)
Multi-venue→Multiple potential execution venues
Info leakage→LOW concern (small orders don't move markets)
Memory anchor: "GPS for your order" — find the cheapest/fastest route across many venues.

SFDL → Liquidity-seeking algorithm
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→50% (HIGH — big order)
Liquidity→LOW (ADV 20k is small)
Urgency→HIGH
Market impact concern→HIGH (must minimize)
Why this algo: trades only when liquidity is offered by the other side → minimizes market impact for a large order in a thin market. High urgency means execution should still occur relatively quickly when liquidity appears.
TWEL → Scheduled algorithm (POV, VWAP, or TWAP)
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→5% (LOW)
Liquidity→RELATIVELY HIGH
Urgency→LOW
Adverse price concern→LOW (long horizon OK)
Why this algo: low urgency means we can tolerate longer trading horizons. Low order size + high liquidity means a scheduled algo can passively trade throughout the day → minimizes market impact cost. Perfect fit.
UDSL → High-touch principal approach
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→100% (= entire daily volume)
Information leakage→EXTREME risk if displayed
Market impact→PROHIBITIVE for any algo
Discretion needed→YES — find a natural counterparty
Why this approach: 100% of ADV = an algorithm would either dump the price (information leakage) or take days to fill (and still leak). Need a human intermediary with relationships to find the other side of a block trade discreetly. The dealer takes on the principal risk and prices it into the spread.

Trade profileBest algo

Large + less liquid + higher urgency + leakage concernLiquidity-seeking

Recent developments — ML in algorithmic trading
Clustering
Machine learning technique where a computer learns to identify which algorithm is optimal for different trade types, based on key features.
How it works: groups trades together with similar attributes (e.g. order size as a fraction of ADV). Then quantitatively tests factors for their impact on the performance of different algorithms.
Key value: clustering can identify features that a human manager hadn't previously considered important.
High-frequency market forecasting
Attempts to model short-term market direction. Challenge: too many potential explanatory variables.
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) = machine learning technique that reduces the number of explanatory variables to a manageable number of significant ones.
Memory anchor: LASSO = "shrink the variable list to the ones that matter".
5 key markets — each with its own trade implementation pattern
Different asset classes have different market structures → different ways trades get done. The exam asks you to know what's typical for each.
Equity markets
Venues: stock exchanges (lit markets) + dark pools Tech level: MOST advanced of all asset classes Execution: mostly electronic; algorithmic trading is commonplace Order type: order-driven (CLOB)
Memory anchor: equities = the gold standard for electronic + algorithmic execution.
Fixed-income markets
Structure: large number of heterogeneous securities (many issues per issuer) Liquidity: generally LOW per security, but typical order size is LARGE Market type: dealer-based, quote-driven Electronic RFQ: growing, but algorithmic trading is mostly limited to on-the-run U.S. Treasuries + futures contracts Corporate bonds: electronic trading is growing but still a small fraction
⚙️ Execution method depends on urgency
Urgent trades→Principal (broker risk) trade
Less urgent→Broker-agent approach
Exchange-traded derivatives (options & futures)
Electronic trading: COMMON Algorithmic trading: NOT as common as in equities — and is used MORE for futures than for options DMA: buy-side traders generally use Direct Market Access
Memory anchor: futures > options for algo adoption (futures are simpler, more standardized).
OTC derivatives
Market type: dealer quote-driven Execution: implemented through high-touch approaches Regulation shift: since 2008 credit crisis, regulators pushed for transparency + central clearing of basic OTC derivatives (e.g. interest rate swaps via Dodd-Frank Act 2010 in the US)
OTC = the most "high-touch" asset class. Discretion + dealer relationships matter more here than in any other market.
Spot foreign exchange (FX)
Venue: OTC market Execution: BOTH electronic AND high-touch broker approaches
3-tier structure (decreasing trade size, increasing spreads):
1. Interbank — largest trades, tightest spreads 2. Interdealer — middle tier 3. Bank-to-client — smaller trades, widest spreads
⚙️ FX execution method by trade type
Large urgent→RFQs with brokers
Large non-urgent→Scheduled algorithms OR high-touch agency
Small trades→DMA
5 markets side by side — quick comparison
MarketTech levelPrimary typeAlgo trading?Typical method
EquityHighestOrder-drivenYES — commonplaceElectronic + algos + dark pools
Fixed incomeModerateQuote-driven (dealer)Limited (on-the-run UST + futures only)High-touch principal or agency

Exam traps for key markets
Trap 1: "Algorithmic trading is widespread in fixed income" → FALSE. Only on-the-run U.S. Treasuries and futures contracts. Corporate bonds are still mostly high-touch.
Trap 2: "OTC derivatives are quote-driven order book markets" → FALSE. Quote-driven, yes. But NOT an order book — dealers quote on request, no CLOB.
Trap 3: "Options have more algo adoption than futures" → FALSE. Reversed: futures > options for algos.
Trap 4: "FX spot is purely electronic" → FALSE. It's BOTH electronic AND high-touch. Large urgent trades use RFQs with brokers.
Memory anchor: liquidity + standardization drive algo adoption. Equity wins on both → most algo. OTC derivatives lose on both → least algo.
Trade Governance — why it exists
Asset managers must have a formal written trade policy that clearly spells out trade procedures. This is BOTH good practice AND usually required by regulation. The policy protects clients from conflicts of interest and ensures consistent execution.
Trade policy has 4 key areas. Each is examinable on its own. Together, they describe how the firm finds, evaluates, and monitors execution.
The 4 pillars of trade policy — animation
0 / 4 pillars shown
PILLAR 1 Meaning of best execution
Definition: "Best execution" is a regulatory term — the duty of asset managers to seek the best possible RESULT for clients when trading. The trade policy must define best execution within the applicable regulatory framework.
⚙️ Factors that determine best execution
Execution price→Achieved vs benchmark
Trading costs→Explicit + implicit
Speed & likelihood of execution→Settlement included
Order size & liquidity→Size relative to ADV
Nature of the trade→Urgency, motivation
Critical exam point: Best execution does NOT simply mean seeking the best price or trading at the lowest cost. It means the best RESULT for the client overall.
Example: a manager with a large stake in a company they expect to file for bankruptcy might get a better RESULT by selling a BLOCK to a trusted dealer at a discounted price — even if there are higher bids for small quantities on lit venues. Why? Because hitting lit bids would cause information leakage and adverse market movements that would tank the bigger position.
PILLAR 2 Factors that determine the optimal execution approach
The trade policy needs to communicate the criteria that determine HOW each trade gets executed. These factors:
⚙️ The criteria the policy must spell out
Urgency & size of order→From the PM's mandate
Liquidity of security (ADV)→+ standardized vs customized
Characteristics of venues→Lit / dark / quote-driven
Investment strategy objectives→Long-term vs short-term
Reason for the trade→Alpha / rebalance / cash flow
Regulatory context: different asset classes have different trading conventions. The policy must reflect both the relevant regulations AND the conventions used by the manager.
MiFID II trap: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID II) in Europe has effectively prohibited soft-dollar arrangements.
Soft-dollar arrangements = an asset manager pays for goods or services using REBATES from client commissions in return for executing high volume with a broker. This may jeopardize best execution if the manager uses the client's soft dollars for the manager's OWN benefit (e.g. buying research that helps the manager, not the specific client).
Memory anchor: asset classes match methods. Equities + exchange-traded derivatives = algorithms. Fixed income = high-touch. The policy must reflect these conventions.
PILLAR 3 List of eligible brokers and execution venues
The policy includes a list of approved brokers + the process used to create it. Best practice = establish a Best Execution Monitoring Committee (BEMC).
⚙️ BEMC composition
Portfolio execution→Traders / PMs
Compliance→Regulatory oversight
Risk personnel→Counterparty risk view
BEMC duties: maintaining, updating, and distributing the list to all parties involved in trade execution.
Why due diligence matters MOST for OTC trades: no exchange rules protection, low transparency, no central clearing → counterparty risk is huge.
6 principles for broker approval:
⚙️ Criteria the BEMC checks
Service quality→Execution price, speed, capacity
Financial stability→Mitigates counterparty risk
Ethical reputation→Good behavior history
Settlement facilities→Adequate infrastructure
Explicit costs→Competitive commissions
Capital commitment→Willing to take principal risk in illiquid trades
PILLAR 4 Process for monitoring execution arrangements
The approved broker list must be constantly monitored. Brokers that fail the standard are removed promptly.
⚙️ What's monitored continuously
Reputational issues→News, allegations, regulatory actions
Trading error frequency→Mistakes that cost clients
Criminal actions→Investigations, charges, convictions
Financial stability→Ongoing creditworthiness
Execution quality→vs benchmarks, ongoing
Record-keeping: trading records must be kept to (1) facilitate execution quality analysis, (2) address client concerns, (3) respond to regulator inquiries about executions and trade allocations.
Memory anchor: pillar 3 = onboarding (who's allowed in). Pillar 4 = ongoing surveillance (are they still good enough?). Both work together to enforce best execution.
4 pillars at a glance
#PillarWhat it covers
1Meaning of best executionDefine best RESULT (not lowest price) + the 5 factors that determine it
2Factors determining optimal approachUrgency, liquidity, venue, strategy, reason for trade + MiFID II / soft dollars
3Approved broker list + BEMCComposition (PM/compliance/risk) + 6 approval criteria + OTC due diligence
4Monitoring processContinuous tracking + record-keeping for regulators/clients
"Best execution" — the most misunderstood concept
Best execution ≠ Best price Best execution ≠ Lowest cost Best execution = Best RESULT for the client The "best result" is a function of: Execution price + Trading costs + Speed + Likelihood of fill + Order size + Liquidity + Nature of the trade A worse price can be the BEST execution if: - Selling a small piece at a high lit bid would leak info - The lit market would move against the larger remaining position - A block trade with a trusted dealer protects the bigger value
This is a classic CFA exam construction: "manager A got a worse price but better best execution because..." The right answer is the manager who protected the client's overall position, not the one who hit the highest visible bid.
Exam traps for Trade Governance
Trap 1 · "Best execution = best price". FALSE. Best execution = best RESULT for the client. A worse price can be the right choice if it preserves overall value.
Trap 2 · Soft dollars allowed everywhere. FALSE. MiFID II in Europe effectively PROHIBITED soft-dollar arrangements. The exam might test US vs EU regulatory differences.
Trap 3 · BEMC = just the PM. FALSE. BEMC = portfolio execution + compliance + risk personnel. It's cross-functional by design to prevent conflicts of interest.
Trap 4 · Due diligence equally important everywhere. FALSE. Due diligence on brokers is PARTICULARLY important for OTC trades (no exchange protection, low transparency, no central clearing).
Trap 5 · One-time broker approval. FALSE. Approved broker list must be CONSTANTLY monitored and updated. Pillar 4 = ongoing surveillance.
Memory anchor: governance has 4 verbs — DEFINE (pillar 1) → DETERMINE (pillar 2) → APPROVE (pillar 3) → MONITOR (pillar 4).

Fix the patterns, fix the questions. Each pattern has its own drill section.
Pattern 1 · IS & cost calculations (the BIG one — 7 errors)
You miss the sign convention for SELL orders and you mix up the components of expanded IS.
CalculationWhat you missed
Arrival cost (SRM)132 bps. Formula : Side × [(Avg − Arrival)/Arrival] × 10,000
IS for TS sell$35,450 (you picked $21,650 — forgot opportunity cost or sign for sell)

Decision price for ACME$79.90 (Tuesday close), NOT $80 (limit) — decision is observed, not chosen
The key trap: for SELL orders, shares are NEGATIVE. If you forget the sign, your numbers will be wrong but plausible-looking.
Second key trap: the decision price ≠ limit price. Decision price is the market price OBSERVED at the moment of decision (previous close if before open, arrival if intraday, today's close if after close). Limit price is just an execution constraint chosen by the PM.
Drill: 4 separate interactive calculators (Arrival Cost / IS / Expanded IS / Market-Adjusted) preset with each question's numbers.
Pattern 2 · Trade urgency drivers (3 errors)
You confuse execution risk (price moves against you while you trade) and market impact (you push the price). They move in OPPOSITE directions with speed.
StatementTruth
"Trading with greater urgency → lower execution risk"✓ TRUE (faster = less time exposed to volatility)
"Wide bid-ask spread + longer time → lower execution risk"✗ FALSE (longer = MORE exposed to vol)
"Larger size + higher urgency → reduces market impact"✗ FALSE (urgency + size → MORE impact)
"High alpha decay → less aggressive trading"✗ FALSE (high decay = MUST trade fast, accept impact)
"Info leakage minimized by fast exchange execution"✗ FALSE (info leak → dark pools + limit orders)
Memory anchor — the inverse relationship: FASTER trading → LOWER execution risk → HIGHER market impact SLOWER trading → HIGHER execution risk → LOWER market impact You can't minimize BOTH simultaneously. You pick which to prioritize.
Pattern 3 · Algo selection (3 errors)
You pick the wrong algo when the dominant driver isn't "urgency" but something else (info leakage, completion guarantee).

Dynopax (illiquid, must complete in 1 day)VWAP or POVTWAPCompletion guarantee in time window
Music Plus open marketClosing auction or passiveOpen market (active)HIGH urgency on intraday alpha
Decision tree: Order size > 15% of vol? → Liquidity-seeking. Must complete in fixed window? → TWAP. High intraday urgency? → Active open market (NOT closing auction).
Pattern 4 · Trade policy themes (mineur — 2 erreurs)
You miss what's INAPPROPRIATE in a trade policy.
Theme statementAppropriate?
"Disclose ALL trade errors to clients"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — errors go to compliance, priority = no adverse impact for client
"Lowest possible trading cost only"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — best execution ≠ lowest cost
"Same execution approach for all asset classes"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — depends on asset class & market structure
"Pre-approved broker list, reviewed regularly"✓ APPROPRIATE
"Pro-rata allocation for partially-executed pooled orders"✓ APPROPRIATE
Trap: "treatment of trade errors" policy is NEEDED (errors must be documented in trade error log + reported to compliance) — but NOT necessarily disclosed to clients. Two different things.

Expanded IS = Delay cost + Trading cost + Opportunity cost + Fees Delay cost = (shares × arrival price) − (shares × decision price) Trading cost = (shares × execution price) − (shares × arrival price) Opportunity cost = unfilled shares × (current − decision price) Fees = commission × executed shares For SELL orders: number of shares is NEGATIVE. Market-Adjusted Cost calculator
Market-adjusted cost = Arrival cost − (β × Index arrival cost) This isolates the cost CAUSED BY the trade (vs cost caused by general market movement). Step 1: Compute trade's arrival cost (in bps) Step 2: Compute index's arrival cost (in bps) over the trade horizon Step 3: Market-adjusted cost = Step 1 − (β × Step 2) A NEGATIVE market-adjusted cost = the trade looks BETTER than the index move suggests. The trade outperformed the broader market move.

Urgency drivers drill — true or false?
Click on a statement to reveal the truth. Each one is a statement you got wrong.
The fundamental tradeoff — memorize this
FASTER trading → LOWER execution risk → HIGHER market impact SLOWER trading → HIGHER execution risk → LOWER market impact You can't minimize BOTH simultaneously. Which to prioritize depends on: • Alpha decay rate (fast decay → trade fast → accept impact) • Information leakage concern (high → use dark pools, NOT exchanges) • Bid-ask spread (wide spread + long horizon = high execution risk) • Order size vs ADV (large = unavoidable impact)
The exam frames the same idea 5 different ways. Once you know the tradeoff, you can spot any reformulation.

Order > 15% of expected volume + leakage concern?Liquidity-seeking
Must complete entirely in a fixed time window?TWAP
Order ≤ 15% vol + price moves against expected?Arrival price
Low urgency + just track market volume profile?VWAP / POV
Order ≈ 100% of ADV?High-touch principal (not algo)
High urgency + small order + multi-venue?SOR
Large + don't need immediate fill?Dark pool
Common mistake: defaulting to POV when "volume" is mentioned. POV chases volume but CAN'T guarantee completion. Use TWAP if completion in a window matters.
Why you panic on essays — and how to stop
You don't panic because you don't know the content. You panic because you have NO PROCEDURE. Once you have a 4-step procedure, the page is never blank.
The 4-step universal procedure: 1. SCAN the question → identify the instruction KEYWORD 2. HUNT the vignette → underline 2-4 signal facts the examiner planted 3. PICK the concept(s) the question refers to → define them in 1 line each 4. WRITE the 3-block answer: CHOICE → DEFINITION → APPLICATION
When you can write definitions in 5 seconds and you've highlighted your signals, the writing starts immediately. No more blank page.
The 3-block answer template
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 1 · DIRECT CHOICE │ │ One bold sentence that answers the question. │ │ Don't preamble. Don't hedge. State the answer. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 2 · DEFINITION │ │ One or two sentences defining the concepts named │ │ in the question. Shows theoretical mastery. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 3 · APPLICATION (the most important) │ │ 2-3 reasons drawn FROM THE VIGNETTE. │ │ Each reason: [vignette fact] → [theoretical effect] │ │ Examiners reward you for connecting facts to theory.│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
If you skip Block 2, you sound like you guessed. If you skip Block 3, you sound like you wrote a textbook. You need BOTH.
Quality checklist — before you stop writing
✓ Did I make a clear choice in the first sentence? ✓ Did I define the key concept(s) named in the question? ✓ Did I cite at least 2 specific facts from the vignette? ✓ Did each fact connect to a theoretical effect (driver → consequence)? ✓ Did I close with a synthesis sentence?
If you can't answer YES to all 5, your essay is incomplete. Add what's missing before moving on.
Common reasons you block (and the fix)
Block reasonFix
"I don't remember the definition perfectly"Write what you DO remember + apply the procedure. Partial definition + good application beats no answer.
"I'm searching for the 'right' wording"There's no right wording. There's a right STRUCTURE. Use the 3-block template.
"I don't know which concept they want"The question NAMES the concept(s) explicitly. "Trade urgency and alpha decay" = those are the two concepts.
"I don't have enough to say"Re-read the vignette. Each unusual detail is a planted signal. 3-year holding, persistent mispricing, etc.
"I want to write more but I'm not sure if it adds points"Stop. Concise + structured beats long + rambling. The graders use a rubric.
Decode the instruction keyword first — it dictates your format
Different keywords expect different response formats. Mismatching = lost points even if your content is correct.
Determine / Identify
Examiner wants: one clear choice in the first sentence, then justification.
Format: "X is the [most likely / most appropriate / correct] choice because..." [2-3 reasons drawn from vignette]
Examples: "Determine the most appropriate algorithm." "Identify which fund has higher trade urgency."
Calculate
Examiner wants: formula + numbers + result with units.
Format: Formula: [write the formula clearly] Substitution: [plug in numbers from vignette] Result: [final answer with currency or bps unit]
Show your work even if you have it right — partial credit if final number is wrong but steps are correct.
Discuss / Justify
Examiner wants: 2-3 reasons with evidence from the vignette.
Format: [Topic sentence stating the position] Reason 1: [vignette fact] → [theoretical consequence] Reason 2: [vignette fact] → [theoretical consequence] (Reason 3 if relevant)
"Justify" = give reasons FOR something already chosen. "Discuss" = present analysis (often pros AND cons or multiple sides).
Recommend
Examiner wants: a specific choice + at least 2 justifications based on vignette evidence.
Format: "I recommend [X] because..." Justification 1: [vignette evidence] Justification 2: [vignette evidence] (Optionally: "[X] is preferred over [alternative] because...")
Compare / Contrast
Examiner wants: a side-by-side comparison, ideally as a table.
Format: Build a 2-column or 2-row structure. For each dimension: state the difference clearly. Example dimensions: urgency, liquidity, risk appetite, time horizon
If a table isn't feasible, use parallel sentences: "X has [feature A], while Y has [feature B]."
Evaluate / Critique
Examiner wants: your assessment with reasoning — often "is X appropriate / correct?"
Format: "X is [appropriate / inappropriate / incorrect] because..." [Reason 1] [Reason 2] [What should be done instead, if relevant]
For "evaluate the firm's trading policy" or similar, scan for the LOS-required components and check each.
Drill Mode — build your essay step by step
For each question: read the vignette, then progressively reveal the signals, structure, and full answer. Train yourself to spot signals BEFORE reading the answer.
Essay 1 / 5
All essays — pick one to review
LOS 1.a · The 7-step process to formulate CME
Capital Market Expectations are forward-looking estimates of return, risk, and correlation for asset classes. This is the standardized procedure to build them.
1
Determine the SPECIFIC CMEs needed
Based on investor's allowable asset classes and investment horizon(s). Time horizon is particularly important in determining which CMEs are needed (e.g. short-horizon investor doesn't need 30-year return forecasts).
2
Investigate historical performance + drivers
Identify what DROVE past performance, then forecast forward. Establish a plausible range for future performance. Compare forecast to past results — does it pass the sanity check?
3
Identify valuation model + requirements
E.g. comparables-based / relative value used in US may NOT work for emerging markets. The model must FIT the asset class and market.
4
Collect the best data possible
Faulty data → faulty conclusions. Financial publications + commercial databases = best sources for reliable asset class data.
5
Use experience & judgment for inputs
Interpret current investment conditions; decide which values to assign. Verify inputs are consistent ACROSS asset classes (e.g. same inflation assumption everywhere).
6
Formulate CMEs — RECORD assumptions
Any assumption or rationale used in the analysis should be DOCUMENTED. Without this, you can't audit later or improve the process.
7
Monitor performance + refine the process
If actual performance varies significantly from forecasts, both the process AND the model should be refined. Continuous learning loop.
Information needed to support the investment process
Geography: individual countries, economic blocks (e.g. EU), nondomestic vs domestic, regional, global.
Major asset classes: fixed income, equity, real assets.
Sub-asset classes:
• Equity: industries, sectors, size, style
• Fixed income: nominal vs TIPS, floating vs fixed, credit quality, maturities
• Real assets: commodities, real estate, timber
What makes a GOOD forecast?
✓ Unbiased — no systematic over/under estimation ✓ Objective — driven by data, not opinion or wish ✓ Well researched — supported by evidence and analysis ✓ Efficient — small forecasting error ✓ Internally consistent — inputs align across asset classes
Rule of thumb: at least 30 observations are needed to test a hypothesis. Less = unreliable.
Memory anchor — DICCUM FM
Step 1: Determine CMEs (asset classes + horizon) Step 2: Investigate history (drivers) Step 3: Identify valuation model Step 4: Collect data Step 5: Use judgment for inputs (consistent across classes) Step 6: Formulate CMEs (record assumptions) Step 7: Monitor & refine
Mnemonic: D-I-I-C-U-F-M · "Determine, Investigate, Identify, Collect, Use, Formulate, Monitor"
LOS 1.b · 9 problems in developing capital market forecasts
Poor forecasts → inappropriate asset allocations. Click each problem to expand.
1. Economic data limitations ← data is slow / revised / rebased 2. Data measurement errors + biases ← survivorship, appraisal smoothing 3. Limitations of historical estimates ← regime changes, nonstationary data 4. Use of ex post for ex ante ← past low risk ≠ future low risk 5. Nonrepeating data patterns ← data mining, time-period bias 6. Conditioning information ignored ← beta varies by regime 7. Misinterpretation of correlations ← causality, spurious, nonlinear 8. Psychological biases ← 6 sub-biases (anchoring, etc.) 9. Model uncertainty ← MOST SERIOUS · 3 types
PROBLEM 1 Limitations to using economic data ▶
Economic data has 3 main issues that distort analysis:
• Time lag — IMF reports data with a lag of up to 2 years. By the time you have it, conditions changed. • Revisions — data is revised AFTER initial publication. Definitions and methodology change over time (e.g. CPI basket updated every few years). • Rebasing — base period of indexes changes. Unaware analysts compute % changes incorrectly.
Mitigation: use multiple data sources, know revision schedules, adjust for rebasing before comparing.
PROBLEM 2 Data measurement errors and biases ▶
Transcription errors misreporting
Misreporting or incorrect recording of information. Most serious if BIASED (systematic, not random).
Survivorship bias selection
Managers / securities deleted from historical record. Deletions tied to POOR performance → biases historical return UPWARD.
Appraisal (smoothing) data illiquid assets
Returns for illiquid assets (e.g. real estate, private equity) appraised infrequently → return path appears SMOOTHER than reality. Effect:
• Biases standard deviation DOWNWARD
• Makes returns appear LESS correlated (closer to 0) with liquid assets
Big problem for alternatives.
PROBLEM 3 Limitations of historical estimates ▶
Values from historical data must often be ADJUSTED going forward as economic, political, regulatory, and technological environments change. These changes are regime changes and result in nonstationary data.
Example: the 2007–2009 financial crisis produced returns data markedly different from the previous 5 years. Pre-crisis data has different statistical properties than post-crisis data.
Two questions to decide if a long period is INAPPROPRIATE:
1. Is there a reason to believe the entire (longer) period is not appropriate?
2. If yes, does a statistical test confirm a regime change exists AND identify where?
If both = yes → use judgment to pick the relevant SUBPERIOD.
Long vs short period tradeoff:
• Long = more obs, more precise stats — BUT risks regime changes / nonstationarity
• Short = avoids regimes — BUT tempts you to use HIGHER FREQUENCY data (weekly) → asynchronous data, missing values, distorted correlations. More frequent ≠ more precise.
Fat tails & skewness: asset returns historically exhibit them, which adds complexity to statistical tests. Sometimes the cost of modeling nonnormality outweighs the benefit.
PROBLEM 4 Using ex post data for ex ante estimates ▶
Ex post = after the fact (historical). Ex ante = before the fact (forward-looking). Using ex post to determine ex ante can mislead.
Example (Fed scenario): investors feared Fed would raise rates → depressed stock prices. Inflation abated without Fed intervention → stocks recovered. Ex post: returns look high. The analyst would conclude returns will be HIGH going forward — blind to the PRIOR RISK that was faced. Net: UNDERESTIMATES risk, OVERESTIMATES return.
Inverse case — VaR overestimation: if the data subset INCLUDES outliers / rare negative events, the historical VaR distorts upward, suggesting rare negatives occur MORE frequently than they actually do.
PROBLEM 5 Nonrepeating data patterns (data biases) ▶
Data mining false patterns
Random patterns mistaken for real ones. At 5% significance with 40 random variables, ~2 will appear statistically significant by chance alone.
Time-period bias window cherry-picking
Results depend on the chosen time span. E.g. small-cap US stocks beat large-cap "always" — UNTIL you exclude 2000–2010, then the advantage disappears.
3-step antidote:
1. Ask if there's an ECONOMIC basis for the variable to relate to returns
2. Scrutinize the modeling process for susceptibility to bias
3. Test out-of-sample (split data: build on one portion, test on another)
PROBLEM 6 Failing to account for conditioning information ▶
The relationship between security returns and economic variables is NOT constant over time. Historical data reflects MANY different business cycles and conditions. Analysts must account for CURRENT conditions.
Example: A firm's beta is 1.2 using all historical data. But split the data:
• In expansions: beta = 1.0
• In recessions: beta = 1.4
Going forward, beta forecast should reflect WHICH regime you expect: 1.0 if expansion expected, 1.4 if recession expected. Using the blended 1.2 is wrong.
PROBLEM 7 Misinterpretation of correlations ▶
Correlation ≠ causality. Three common misinterpretations:
Causality direction wrong
Example: corn prices correlated with rainfall in Midwest. Reasonable: rainfall influences corn prices. Unreasonable: corn prices influence rainfall.
→ Rainfall = EXOGENOUS variable (arises outside the model)
→ Corn price = ENDOGENOUS variable (arises within the model)
Spurious correlation — two variables look correlated but neither causes the other; possibly a 3rd variable drives BOTH.
Nonlinear relationships — correlation only captures LINEAR relationships. A strong nonlinear relationship can produce near-zero correlation.
PROBLEM 8 Psychological biases (6 sub-biases) ▶
CFA categorizes biases as cognitive (faulty reasoning) or emotional (feelings override logic).
Anchoring bias cognitive
First information received is overweighted. In a debate on the economy, if the first speaker forecasts a recession, that view is given greater credence.
Counter: consciously question the first input; re-evaluate against fresh data.
Status quo bias emotional
Predictions strongly influenced by recent past. If inflation is 4% today, the forecast becomes 4% — rather than making an active "error of commission" by choosing different.
Counter: require justification for "same as last year" forecasts.
Confirmation bias cognitive
Only information SUPPORTING existing beliefs is considered; contrary evidence is ignored or actively avoided.
Counter: give all evidence equal scrutiny; actively seek out CONTRARY opinions.
Overconfidence bias emotional
Past mistakes are ignored, the lack of comments from others is taken as agreement, and forecast accuracy is overestimated.
Counter: consider a RANGE of potential outcomes, not point estimates.
Prudence bias cognitive
Forecasts overly CONSERVATIVE to avoid the regret of extreme forecasts being wrong.
Counter: consider a range of outcomes (same antidote as overconfidence — symmetry of error).
Availability bias cognitive
What is EASIEST to remember (often an extreme event) is overweighted. Example: many believed the 1929 crash depressed equity values for 30 subsequent years.
Counter: base predictions on OBJECTIVE DATA, not emotions or recollections.
Cognitive vs Emotional cheat-sheet:
• Cognitive (4): anchoring, confirmation, prudence, availability
• Emotional (2): status quo, overconfidence
PROBLEM 9 Model uncertainty (3 types — MOST SERIOUS) ▶
Three types of uncertainty, but ONE is the most serious:
Model uncertainty which model?
Unsure whether to use DCF model or relative value model to evaluate expected stock return. Wrong choice of model → invalid conclusions.
Parameter uncertainty estimation errors
Estimation errors in model parameters (e.g. the beta in CAPM is itself an estimate, not a truth).
Input uncertainty knowing correct inputs
Knowing the CORRECT input values for the model. Even if DCF is appropriate, the correct growth rate and discount rate are still needed and may be wrong.
Exam trap: MODEL UNCERTAINTY is the MOST serious of the three. Reasoning: an incorrect model will likely lead to invalid conclusions, regardless of how accurate your parameters or inputs are. Wrong tool, wrong answer.
LOS 1.c · How exogenous shocks affect economic growth trends
Economic growth has two components: cyclical variations (short-term) and growth trends (long-term, what matters for CME). Both can be disrupted by shocks.
The fundamental distinction — EXOGENOUS vs ENDOGENOUS
TypeDefinitionBuilt into prices?
EXOGENOUSUnanticipated events outside the normal course of the economyNOT priced in (because unanticipated)
ENDOGENOUSNormal trends within the economyAlready in market prices
Critical implication: Exogenous shocks cause statistical regime changes (the same issue covered in Problem 3 of forecasting problems). This is why historical data may suddenly become inappropriate after a shock.
Memory anchor: Exogenous = OUTSIDE the model + UNANTICIPATED + NOT priced. Endogenous = INSIDE the model + EXPECTED + PRICED.
The 5 causes of exogenous shocks (memorize these)
1. Changes in government POLICIES → fiscal, free markets, infrastructure, tax 2. POLITICAL events → geopolitical tensions, defense spending 3. TECHNOLOGICAL progress → new markets, products 4. NATURAL disasters → short-term ↓, possibly long-term ↑ 5. Discovery of NATURAL RESOURCES → enhances growth (more supply)
Mnemonic: P-P-T-N-N · "Policies, Political, Technology, Natural disasters, Natural resources"
Decision cards — which type of shock is this?
Click each scenario to reveal the answer.
Special case · Financial crises
Financial crises are a separate category mentioned in the text. Shocks to the financial system lead to a crisis of confidence among market participants.

• Short-term effect: reduce economic output
• Long-term effect: may also decrease the TREND rate of growth (not just cyclical)
Exam trap: a financial crisis affects BOTH cyclical AND trend growth. Many candidates think it's only short-term. The long-term trend can be permanently lowered (think: 2008 productivity slowdown debate).
Natural disasters — the counterintuitive case
Natural disasters likely reduce short-term growth, but may (arguably) encourage long-term growth if more efficient capacity replaces previous capacity.
Professor's Note counter-argument: the owners of capital ALREADY replace old facilities with newer/more efficient ones when the time is right. A natural disaster forcing this acceleration isn't necessarily a "free" growth boost — the replacement would have happened anyway.
LOS 1.d · Why the trend rate of growth matters for CME
→ DCF models incorporate trend growth as an anchor for long-term forecasts → Higher trend growth may lead to higher stock returns (if not already priced in) → Higher trend growth = economy can grow faster before inflation becomes a concern → influences monetary policy → Higher trend growth tends to generate higher government bond yields
Trend growth is relatively stable in developed economies. In emerging economies it's less predictable and can include longer periods of rapid catch-up growth.
The basic forecasting model — 3 components
Trend Growth = Labor Input + Capital per Worker + Total Factor Productivity
1. Labor INPUT
Based on growth in the labor force AND labor participation.
• Labor force growth = population growth + demographics
• Labor participation = % of population working, affected by real wages, work/leisure decisions, social factors
2. CAPITAL per worker
Increases labor productivity. Each worker has more tools/equipment/technology to use.
3. TOTAL FACTOR PRODUCTIVITY (TFP)
Reflects technological progress and changes in government policies. The "residual" — output growth not explained by labor or capital alone.
Worked example — long-term projected growth rate
Given: Population growth = 2.00% Labor force participation growth = 0.25% Capital input growth = 2.50% Total factor productivity (TFP) = 0.50% Long-term growth = 2.00% + 0.25% + 2.50% + 0.50% = 5.25%
All components ADD. No multiplication. Each one is just summed to give the total trend growth rate.
Quick variant — the "labor input growth" formulation
Some questions combine population + participation into "labor input growth":

Labor input growth = labor force growth + labor participation growth

Example: labor input growth = 0.4% means population + participation already aggregated.
Then: Real GDP growth = labor input growth + labor productivity growth
(where labor productivity growth absorbs both capital per worker AND TFP)
Watch for this trap: if the question gives "labor input growth" AND "labor productivity growth" separately, just add those two (don't double-count). If it gives population, participation, capital, and TFP separately, add all four.
Worked example — Cindy Navaro real GDP
Given (Exhibit 1): Annual labor input growth = 0.4% Annual labor productivity growth = 1.4% Real GDP growth = 0.4% + 1.4% = 1.8% Then to get NOMINAL GDP, add inflation: Nominal GDP = Real GDP + Inflation = 1.8% + 3.8% = 5.6%
This 5.6% nominal GDP becomes the input to the equity return calculator (next sub-tab).
Asset Returns and Trend Growth — the equity decomposition
Market value of equity = Nominal GDP × (Earnings/GDP) × (P/E) Long-term: profits/GDP and P/E cannot continuously increase or decrease. Thus, long-term growth in equity value = growth in nominal GDP. Equity total return = Capital gains + Dividend yield Capital gains = ΔNominal GDP + Δ(profits/GDP) + Δ(P/E) Over long horizons, Δ(profits/GDP) ≈ 0 and Δ(P/E) ≈ 0 → Capital gains ≈ nominal GDP growth → Total equity return ≈ nominal GDP growth + dividend yield
The high-growth trap: "High growth rates in capital investment → high economy growth → but NOT necessarily high equity returns." Why? Because growth is already factored into equity prices. Additional reason: if capital growth rate > economic growth rate, return on capital may DECREASE.
Equity Return Calculator
Walk through the Cindy Navaro example — preset gives the textbook 8.2% answer.
Labor input growth (%)
Labor productivity growth (%)
Inflation (%)
Δ profits/GDP (%) — usually 0 long-term
Δ P/E multiple (%) — usually 0 long-term
Dividend yield (%)
How to read the formula: capital gains comes from nominal GDP growth + any expansion of profits/GDP + any expansion of P/E. Long-term, the last two = 0 (they can't grow forever). Add dividend yield to get TOTAL return.
Dividend yield breakdown (useful side-formula)
Dividend yield = Annual dividends / Market value = (Dividend payout ratio) / (Profit multiple) = (Dividends / Profit) / (Market value / Profit)
If a question gives you payout ratio and P/E multiple but not dividend yield directly, this lets you compute it.
LOS 1.e · 3 approaches to economic forecasting
Each has tradeoffs. Exam will test which approach fits a given situation, and which advantage/disadvantage matches each.
Approach 1 · Econometric analysis
Statistical methods to explain economic relationships and formulate forecasting models.
Two sub-types:
• Structural models — based on economic theory
• Reduced-form models — compact versions of structural approaches

Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression is most common.
Advantages:
✓ Can incorporate MANY variables
✓ Once specified, model can be REUSED
✓ Output is QUANTIFIED, based on consistent relationships
Disadvantages:
✗ COMPLEX and time-consuming to construct
✗ Data difficult to forecast, relationships can CHANGE
✗ Output may need interpretation or be UNREALISTIC
✗ Does NOT work well for turning points (key exam trap)
Approach 2 · Economic indicators
Available from governments (e.g. OECD) and private sources (e.g. Conference Board).
Three types of indicators:
TypeTimingUse
LEADINGMove ahead of business cyclePredict what comes next
COINCIDENTMove with business cycleConfirm what's happening NOW
LAGGINGMove after business cycleConfirm what just happened
Two ways to use them:
• Composite — combine into an index. 3 consecutive months of increase/decrease signals start of expansion/contraction (Conference Board's 10 leading indicators for US)
• Diffusion index — count of indicators pointing toward expansion vs contraction
Advantages:
✓ Simple, intuitive, easy to interpret
✓ Data readily available from third parties
✓ Lists can be TAILORED to specific forecasting needs
Disadvantages:
✗ Forecasting results have been INCONSISTENT
✗ Have given FALSE SIGNALS
✗ Indicators are revised frequently → can make them appear to fit PAST cycles better than they actually did when first released
Approach 3 · Checklist approach
More subjective. Analyst considers a series of questions (e.g., to forecast GDP: "What was the latest employment report? What is the central bank's next move?"). Uses judgment + some statistical modeling to interpret.
Advantages:
✓ LESS complex than econometrics
✓ FLEXIBLE — mixes objective statistical analysis with judgment to incorporate changing relationships
Disadvantages:
✗ SUBJECTIVE and time-consuming
✗ Complexity must be limited (manual process)
Summary comparison — when to use which
If you need...Use
Quantified output, many variables, reusableEconometric
Simple, fast, third-party dataIndicators
Flexibility to adapt to changing relationshipsChecklist
To forecast TURNING POINTSNOT econometric (its key weakness)
Classic exam trap: "Which approach is BEST for forecasting turning points?" → Indicators (leading), NOT econometric. Econometric models fail at turning points because relationships change at those moments.
LOS 1.f · The 5 phases of the business cycle
Click on any phase dot on the curve to see its full profile. Toggle overlays to see what each asset class does at each phase.
Overlay what to focus on
Memory anchors — the cycle's 3 inflection points
PEAK of GDP → between Phase 3 (Late Exp) and Phase 4 (Slowdown) PEAK of inflation → between Phase 4 (Slowdown) and Phase 5 (Contraction) TROUGH of GDP → between Phase 5 (Contraction) and Phase 1 (Recovery) Inflation PEAKS LATE — it lags GDP. Inflation is "topping out" only as the economy enters contraction. Inflation TROUGHS EARLY — it decelerates as we approach recession and continues falling into early recovery.
Key insight: stocks lead the real economy. They START RISING in late contraction (anticipating recovery) and START FALLING in slowdown (anticipating contraction).
The yield curve morphs across the cycle
As the cycle progresses through its 5 phases, the yield curve transforms shape. Click any phase to see its typical curve plus the policy combination that drives it.
Interactive — phase → yield curve shape
The 4-state morphing cycle (memorize)
BOTTOM of cycle (Recovery) → STEEP curve EXPANSION (Early → Late) → Curve tends to FLATTEN TOP of cycle (Late Exp / Slowdown) → FLAT to INVERTED CONTRACTION → Curve RE-STEEPENS Then back to STEEP → cycle repeats.
Why this works: at the bottom, central bank policy is stimulative (short rates LOW) but long rates already price in eventual recovery → curve is STEEP. As the economy expands and the central bank tightens, short rates rise faster than long rates → curve flattens. At the peak, restrictive policy + recession expectations push short above long → INVERSION. As recession unfolds, central bank cuts aggressively → short rates drop → curve re-steepens.
The exam connection — Module 1.3 × Module 1.4
The yield curve shape AT EACH PHASE is determined by the COMBINATION of monetary + fiscal policy stance prevailing in that phase. This is where Module 1.3 (the cycle) connects to Module 1.4 (policy matrix).
PhaseMonetaryFiscalCurve shape
1·RecoverySTIMULATIVEStimulative (deficits still high)STEEP
2·Early ExpBecoming less stimulativeLess stimulative (deficits narrowing)Still steep, beginning to flatten
3·Late ExpRESTRICTIVELess stimulative / restrictiveFLAT
4·SlowdownRESTRICTIVE (peak)RestrictiveFLAT to INVERTED
5·ContractionBecoming stimulative (easing)Becoming stimulativeRE-STEEPENING
Caution from the textbook: these relationships may NOT always hold. The yield curve has produced false signals (inversions that didn't lead to recession). Use it as a PREDICTOR but don't treat it as deterministic.
Common exam questions on yield curve + cycle
Q1 · Click to reveal
"The yield curve is flattening. Which phase of the cycle?"
Late Expansion (Phase 3). Flattening occurs as monetary policy becomes RESTRICTIVE — short rates rising while long rates plateau or rise slower. Confirms the cycle has moved past the early-expansion sweet spot.
Q2 · Click to reveal
"The yield curve has inverted. What does this predict?"
Economic contraction ahead. Inversion typically occurs at the TOP of the cycle (Slowdown / Phase 4) when both monetary AND fiscal policies are restrictive. Historically a reliable but not infallible recession predictor.
Q3 · Click to reveal
"The yield curve has been inverted and is now re-steepening. Which phase?"
Contraction (Phase 5) in progress. The central bank has started easing aggressively → short rates falling fast → the inverted curve begins to re-steepen. Stock prices may also be starting to rise in anticipation of recovery.
Q4 · Click to reveal
"The yield curve is sharply steep. Which phase?"
Initial Recovery (Phase 1) — also possible in mid-Contraction as steepening begins. Stimulative monetary policy keeps short rates low while long rates already price in recovery. Classic bull-steepener signal.
Q5 · Click to reveal
"Yield curve is flat. What can you say about policy and the economy?"
Implications LESS CLEAR. A flat curve typically signals monetary restrictive + fiscal stimulative (or vice versa) — the two are pushing against each other. Could correspond to Late Expansion. Need other signals (inflation direction, confidence, output gap) to confirm.
All 5 phases side-by-side
Use this as your reference table when answering "what does X do in Y phase" questions.
Dimension 1·Recovery 2·Early Exp 3·Late Exp 4·Slowdown 5·Contraction
Duration Few months Year → several years — Few months → year+ 12–18 months
Confidence Rising Increasing HIGH Declining Declining (low)
Output gap LARGE Narrowing ELIMINATED · overheating risk Reopening Widening
Inflation Decelerating LOW INCREASING Still rising Topping out
Monetary policy STIMULATIVE Becoming less stimulative Becoming RESTRICTIVE Becoming less restrictive EASING
Short-term rates Low / falling Increasing Increasing At PEAK Declining
Bond yields Bottoming → bond prices PEAK Bottoming / rising · prices ↓ Rising · prices ↓ Peaking · then ↓ · prices ↑ Declining · prices ↑
Stock prices RISING Rising Rising/peaking · ↑ volatility FALLING Rising late-stage (anticipating end)
Yield curve Normal/steepening Normal Flattening Possible INVERSION Steepening
Best assets Small-cap, HY bonds, cyclicals Equity (broad) Late-cycle plays · commodities Treasuries · defensive equity Treasuries · gold · early stocks late
Pattern to memorize: as you progress through phases 1→5, short rates trace an arch (low→rising→peaking→falling). Inflation lags by about one phase. Bond prices are INVERSE to yields. Stock prices lead the real economy by one phase.
3 reasons why business cycle ≠ CME (the nuance)
1. Business cycles vary in duration and intensity; turning points are difficult to predict. Variations may result from interactions of many SUBCYCLES with different frequencies. 2. Distinguishing what's CYCLICAL (short-term) vs what's TREND (long-term) is hard in real time. 3. Capital market returns depend on REAL economy + INVESTOR EXPECTATIONS + RISK TOLERANCES — not just economic data.
Application: Business cycle analysis is most useful for trades within a TYPICAL CYCLE horizon. For longer investment horizons that include one or more full cycles, current state of the economy is LESS valuable as input.

+ POSITIVE if rates bound by 0%
+ POSITIVE · fixed CF have ↑ purchasing power
− NEGATIVE · activity & business decline
− NEGATIVE · property values decline
Professor's Note: these generalizations don't hold in every case. They're a starting point for the forecaster taking a MACRO approach. Even if the generalizations always held, it's not easy to determine when a business cycle phase starts, how long it lasts, or when it ends.
Memory anchors for the matrix
"Within expectations" row: everything is largely PRICED IN. Cash earns the real rate. Equity/RE are neutral. Bonds have shorter end more volatile (expectations of changes to short-term policy rate dominate).
"Above/below expectations" row: the SURPRISE drives volatility. Now it's the LONGER end of curve that's more volatile (expectations of long-run inflation dominate). Equity suffers (central bank tightening). Real estate WINS (real asset hedge against inflation).
Critical trap to memorize: bond yield curve volatility location FLIPS based on whether inflation is within vs off expectations.
• Within → SHORT end more volatile
• Above/below → LONG end more volatile
"Deflation" row: bonds and cash WIN (fixed CF have higher purchasing power; cash benefits from real rate when nominal can't go below 0). Equity and RE LOSE (economic activity declining, property values declining).
3 inflation terms — know the differences
TermDefinitionCPI exampleTiming in cycle
InflationGenerally RISING pricesCPI 100 → 105 = +5%Accelerates LATE in cycle (near peak)
DisinflationDECELERATION in rate of inflation (still positive, just slower)CPI 105 → 108 = +3% (slower than +5%)Decelerates approaching recession
DeflationGenerally FALLING prices (negative inflation)CPI 108 → 106 ≈ −2%Severe threat — usually in recession
Common confusion: disinflation ≠ deflation. Disinflation = inflation still positive but slowing. Deflation = inflation actually negative (prices falling).
Why deflation is uniquely dangerous
Deflation is a severe threat to economic activity for two main reasons:
Reason 1 · Encourages debt default
Real burden of debt INCREASES as prices fall. Consider a homeowner:
• Home worth $100,000, mortgage $95,000 → equity = $5,000
• Decline of >5% in home prices → NEGATIVE EQUITY
• Triggers panic sales (further depressing prices) and defaults
→ Vicious cycle, debt-deflation spiral.
Reason 2 · Zero Lower Bound (ZLB) on nominal rates
With negative inflation, interest rates decline toward zero. Once at the ZLB, central banks CAN'T further lower rates to stimulate.
→ Traditional monetary policy loses traction.
→ Need unconventional tools: Quantitative Easing (QE).
Quantitative Easing (QE)
Central bank monetary policy used when traditional rate cuts are exhausted (e.g. post-2007-2009 crisis).
Traditional Open Market OpsQuantitative Easing
ScaleSmaller, temporaryMuch LARGER
SecuritiesHigh-quality fixed incomeWider range: MBS, corporate bonds, etc.
IntentShort-term liquidityLONG-term increase in bank reserves
DurationTemporarySustained
Central banks generally target SLIGHTLY POSITIVE inflation
Why not target 0% inflation?
• Moderate inflation creates only MODERATE costs for the economy • Slightly positive inflation gives policy ROOM ABOVE the ZLB • Investors expect equity and bond prices to reflect SOME positive inflation level
Why this matters for CME: 0% target would be too close to deflation territory. Targeting ~2% provides a buffer.
Phase Identification Drill
Read each scenario, then pick the phase. The drill randomizes order each time you click "New round".
Drill strategy — how to identify a phase fast
Step 1: Look at INFLATION first → Decelerating = Recovery → Low and stable = Early Expansion → Rising = Late Expansion or Slowdown → Topping out = Contraction Step 2: Confirm with SHORT-TERM RATES direction → Low/falling = Recovery → Rising = Early or Late Expansion → At peak = Slowdown → Declining = Contraction Step 3: Confirm with CONFIDENCE → Rising = Recovery or Early Expansion → High = Late Expansion → Declining = Slowdown or Contraction Step 4: Look for SPECIFIC TELLS → "Output gap eliminated, overheating risk" = Late Expansion → "Yield curve possibly inverting" = Slowdown → "Stocks rising in latter stages" = Contraction (anticipating recovery) → "Government stimulus, low rates, deficits" = Recovery
LOS 1.h · Monetary policy as a countercyclical force
Central banks attempt to optimize economic performance by balancing price stability against growth. The goal: keep growth near the long-run sustainable rate.
Late-expansion risk: as expansion matures, inflation typically rises → central banks tighten. The risk is overtightening → recession. Many recessions are policy-induced.
The transmission mechanism — how monetary policy works
CUT short-term rates → SPUR GROWTH: ↓ rates → ↑ consumer spending → ↑ business spending → ↑ stock prices → ↑ bond prices → ↓ currency value → ↑ exports RAISE short-term rates → SLOW GROWTH: ↑ rates → opposite effects on all 5 channels
Currency channel is often overlooked. Lower rates → weaker domestic currency → cheaper exports abroad → higher export volumes → stimulates the economy from a 5th angle.
Direction of change AND level both matter
An exam trap: rates increasing is NOT automatically restrictive — depends on where they start.
Example: Rates raised from 2% to 4% to combat inflation.
If the country's average rate is 6%, the 4% level is still LOW.
→ The rise in rates may begin to dampen inflation, BUT the absolute level may still be low enough to allow growth.
Memory anchor: "Is it tight?" depends on direction (going up) AND level (vs neutral rate / vs historical norms).
The Neutral Rate
The equilibrium interest rate at which a balance between growth and inflation is achieved. It's what most central banks STRIVE to achieve.
Neutral rate = Inflation component + Real growth component + Judgment from policymakers
Example: Inflation target = 3% · Economy expected to grow at 2% → Neutral rate ≈ 5%
→ If inflation too HIGH → central bank raises ABOVE neutral (restrictive) → If growth too LOW → central bank lowers BELOW neutral (stimulative) → At neutral → policy neither stimulative nor restrictive
The Taylor Rule
Embodies the neutral rate concept. Prescriptive tool (what the central bank SHOULD do) and fairly accurate at predicting central bank action.
n_target = r_neutral + i_expected + [0.5 × (GDP_expected − GDP_trend) + 0.5 × (i_expected − i_target)] where: n_target = target NOMINAL short-term interest rate r_neutral = neutral REAL short-term interest rate i_expected = expected inflation rate i_target = target inflation rate GDP_expected = expected GDP growth rate GDP_trend = long-term trend GDP growth rate
Interactive Calculator + Twist Analyzer
Click "Preset: Textbook 7%" to load the worked example. Modify inputs to see how the twist analyzer identifies whether INFLATION or GROWTH concern dominates.
Neutral real rate (r_neutral) %
Inflation target (i_target) %
Expected inflation (i_expected) %
GDP long-term trend %
Expected GDP growth %
How to read the twist analyzer:
• If INFLATION gap pushes target UP more than growth gap pushes it DOWN → inflation overrides growth concern (raise rates)
• If GROWTH gap pushes target DOWN more than inflation gap → growth overrides inflation concern (cut rates)
• If both push in same direction or cancel → balanced policy stance
The textbook example — why net effect is the neutral case
In the preset (3% neutral, 2% target inflation, 4% expected inflation, 2% trend GDP, 0% expected growth):

• Weak growth: 0.5 × (0% − 2%) = −1% (calls for CUT)
• High inflation: 0.5 × (4% − 2%) = +1% (calls for HIKE)
• Net adjustment: 0%
• Target = 3% (neutral) + 4% (expected inflation) + 0% = 7%
Trap: the 7% might LOOK like an arbitrary high number. It's actually neutral + expected inflation — the central bank is neither tightening nor easing relative to its rule, because the growth concern and inflation concern cancel.
Real-rate version (Professor's Note)
By moving expected inflation to the left-hand side, you get the real Taylor target:
n_target − i_expected = r_neutral + [0.5(GDP_expected − GDP_trend) + 0.5(i_expected − i_target)]
Useful when you want to compare to the neutral REAL rate directly without nominal inflation noise.
