What changed: college & campaign goals were funded and dropped out; only scholarship remains as the aspirational goal (now 24%). Fewer consumption years left → minimum subportfolio shrinks 65%→60%, aggregate equity rises 25%→35%.
Professor's note: the specific allocations are somewhat arbitrary — there is no formula. Your task is to see the logic behind choosing higher/lower equity, bond, cash in one subportfolio vs another.
Regulatory & External Constraints — Insurance Companies
Investment returns are a large contributor to insurer performance. The largest allocation is fixed income, reflecting the need to match assets to projected cash flows of the risks insured.
Book-value accounting: Local accounting laws often allow assets stated at book value, so the insurer focuses primarily on the pattern of cash-flow receipts rather than the volatility of market value.
Main risk considerations — maintaining enough capital to meet policyholder claims + factors affecting financial-strength metrics:
▪ Risk-based capital measures ▪ Liquidity ▪ Yield levels ▪ Credit ratings ▪ Potential to liquidate assets to meet claims
Allocation caps: local legislation often limits allocations — equity may be limited to as little as 10%, with caps also on private equity and high-yield bonds.
Pension Funds
Beyond capping allocations to certain asset classes, local legislation places a wide range of tax, accounting, reporting, and funding constraints on pension funds.
▪ Tax incentives may encourage investing in domestic assets. ▪ Accounting rules may allow deferred recognition of losses. ▪ Final allocation considers anticipated funding cost + the pension expense reported in financial statements.
Funding as a constraint — the risk/return trade-off
The fund compares the risk of funding cost exceeding a threshold (to minimize) against the PV of expected contributions (also to minimize).
The tension: higher allocation to equities (vs bonds) → ↑ volatility of returns → ↑ risk that low returns increase required contributions. But the higher expected return decreases the PV of expected contributions.
The fund decides the optimal combination of risk (contributions exceed a level) and return (measured by PV of expected contributions), subject to external regulatory requirements and allocation limits.
Endowments & Foundations
▪ Assumed infinite time horizon → very few regulatory constraints vs other entities. ▪ Some countries: a minimum required annual distribution or socially responsible investing requirement to keep tax-exempt status. ▪ Long horizon usually allows investing in risky assets. ▪ Caveat: if the endowment funds an organization, lender covenants on that organization may constrain the portfolio's activities.
Sovereign Wealth Funds
▪ Government-owned entities investing on behalf of the state. ▪ Typically not looking to match assets and liabilities (unlike insurers/pensions). ▪ But: subject to scrutiny from citizens → this may reduce the level of risk their long horizon would otherwise allow.
Self-governance: each fund self-governs by capping allocations. Constraints may include: minimum investment in socially/ethically acceptable assets; maximum in risky assets such as alternatives; limits on investment in certain currencies. ESG investing is usually not part of the initial allocation — rather, an allocation is set aside and invested in acceptable assets.
LOS 5.b — Tax considerations in allocation & rebalancing
With taxation, pretax vs after-tax risk and return characteristics may differ significantly. Taxable entities should use after-tax characteristics during allocation — adjusting for taxes after the fact may lead to suboptimal allocations.
Common tax characteristics
▪ Interest income — usually taxed at the highest rate, often progressively. → tax-exempt bonds (e.g. US munis) may form a large part of a taxable investor's fixed-income allocation. ▪ Dividends — usually taxed lower than interest. → some investors hold preferred stock instead of bonds. ▪ Capital gains — usually taxed lower than income; capital losses can offset capital gains elsewhere. ▪ Tax-deferred / tax-exempt accounts — place the least tax-efficient (most heavily taxed) assets in the most tax-advantaged accounts.
Key: Return & risk must be considered on both a pretax and after-tax basis — but correlations are unaffected by taxes.
EXAMPLE — Simple after-tax return (bond held to maturity)
Investor taxed 40% on interest, considering a 5% coupon bond held to maturity. Input for allocation:
After-tax = 0.05 × (1 − 0.40) = 0.03 = 3%
EXAMPLE — Multi-step after-tax return (equity)
Stock: 16% pretax return, of which 10% is dividend income and 90% is price appreciation. Dividend tax 30%, capital gains tax 20% (realized annually).
Pretax dividend income: 16% × 0.1 = 1.6% After-tax dividend income: 1.6% × (1 − 0.3) = 1.12% Pretax capital gain: 16% × 0.9 = 14.4% After-tax capital gain: 14.4% × (1 − 0.2) = 11.52% After-tax return: 1.12% + 11.52% = 12.64%
Equity returns include both dividend income and capital gains → the after-tax calc must adjust each component with its own tax rate, then sum.
Embedded gains / losses — cost basis ≠ market value
Cost basis below market value → unrealized gain (embedded tax liability). Cost basis above market value → unrealized loss (embedded tax asset). Three ways to adjust current market value:
(1) Subtract the embedded capital-gains tax from current market value as if sold today. (2) Assume sold in the future, discount the tax liability to PV using the asset's after-tax return as the discount rate. (3) Assume sold in the future, discount the tax liability to PV using the after-tax risk-free rate.
After-tax standard deviation
Risk must also be adjusted for tax. Capital gains tax reduces gains on price appreciation, and the ability to use losses to offset gains reduces losses on price declines → use a posttax standard deviation as the allocation input.
σAT = σPT × (1 − t)
EXAMPLE
Pretax σ = 12%, capital gains tax = 20%.
σAT = 12% × (1 − 0.20) = 9.6%
Effect on the frontier: using after-tax return + after-tax risk shifts the efficient frontier. Allocations to tax-inefficient assets (e.g. high-yield bonds) usually decrease — but they can still feature in the optimal allocation if they have low correlations with other assets.
Portfolio rebalancing under tax
To maintain the SAA, all portfolios rebalance periodically. Taxable owners realize taxable gains at each rebalancing → must balance maintaining the SAA against avoiding taxable gains via frequent rebalancing.
Rebalance less frequently in taxable portfolios — taxation reduces volatility (while correlations remain unaltered), so the allowable deviation band can be wider.
Two distinct tax effects — don't confuse them
Effect on σ of return: taxes cushion the upside & downside → decrease after-tax σ of the asset.
σAT = σPT × (1 − t)
Effect on allowable deviation from target weight: because taxes lower return volatility, they increase the allowable deviation band.
deviationAT = deviationPT / (1 − t)
Trap: one effect multiplies by (1−t) [σ shrinks], the other divides by (1−t) [band widens]. Opposite directions.
EXAMPLE — Pretax vs after-tax rebalancing range
Tax-exempt-style SAA: 40% fixed income, ±5% → range 35%–45%. Fixed-income returns taxed 30%. Equivalent after-tax range?
Pretax allowable deviation = 45% − 40% = 5% Posttax deviation = 5% / (1 − 0.30) = 7.14% Range = 40% ± 7.14% = 32.86% – 47.14%
Two strategies to reduce the impact of taxation
▪ Tax loss harvesting — deliberately realizing losses to offset gains elsewhere. ▪ Strategic asset location — most efficient use of tax-advantaged accounts.
Two tax-advantaged account types:
Tax-exempt accounts — assets not subject to taxation. No adjustment to market value before inclusion in allocation; use pretax risk/return inputs. Tax-deferred accounts — assets appreciate tax-free but are taxed upon distribution. (grow tax-free → use pretax inputs.)
Strategic asset location — general rules:
▪ Assets subject to the lowest tax rates (typically equity) → first allocated to taxable accounts.
▪ Assets subject to frequent trading & high tax rates → allocated to tax-advantaged accounts.
▪ Inputs: tax-deferred/tax-exempt (grow tax-free) → pretax; taxable vehicle → after-tax.
Account-expansion logic: 2 accounts (1 taxable, 1 tax-deferred) × 2 asset classes (FI + equity) → the optimization should use four account "types," depending on whether each class sits in the taxable or tax-deferred account.

LOS 5.c — Revising the strategic asset allocation
The initial optimal allocation is unlikely to be applicable for the entire lifetime of any portfolio. In practice it is reevaluated annually, or whenever a change in goals, constraints, or beliefs suggests a revision is required.
Three triggers for revision: change in goals · change in constraints · change in beliefs.
1 · Change in Goals
▪ For institutions, the business cycle may trigger goal changes. ▪ Example — airlines: facing competition from low-budget rivals + uncertain revenue → may reduce risk exposure in their pension fund to smooth the volatility of contributions. ▪ Pension funds facing increasing deficits in recent years → triggers reexamination of the allocation. ▪ Individuals: change in employment status or starting a family → impacts both willingness and ability to take on risk.
2 · Change in Constraints
A change in any constraint discussed earlier necessitates a review. Examples:
▪ Government regulations requiring increased distributions to maintain tax-exempt status. ▪ Large unexpected cash flows to cover one-off events. ▪ Increased funding requirements for the beneficiary of an endowment. ▪ Forced early retirement of an investor due to illness.
The liquidity rule: any change requiring increased cash outflows → shift to more liquid assets. Conversely, a large inflow (e.g. donation to a foundation) → more flexibility to take on risk.
3 · Change in Beliefs
Investment activities are guided by a set of principles/beliefs — no guarantee these stay fixed.
▪ Investment committee: a change in committee makeup can change beliefs. New members are walked through an asset allocation study to understand the adopted approach. ▪ Economic environment: changes have a major impact on optimization. Key inputs = expected returns, volatility, and correlation. If macro forecasts for a major asset class change → the optimal allocation will likely change.
Example: an allocation exercise on fixed-income performance done pre-2008 would use very different expectations than one done post-2008 (interest-rate environment shift).
Predetermined revisions — target-date funds
Allocations may also change at predetermined dates without detailed reexamination. Target-date mutual funds adjust by investor age using a glide path — shifting from equity to more conservative investments (nominal and inflation-protected bonds) as the target date approaches.
LOS 5.d — SAA vs TAA
SAA (strategic): the long-term allocation specified in the IPS — target asset weightings for the portfolio. TAA (tactical): short-term deviations used to exploit cyclical conditions or a perceived mispricing in an asset class.
Objective
Increase risk-adjusted returns by exploiting short-term opportunities.
Key assumptions: TAA assumes short-term returns are predictable (rather than a random walk, as assumed for long-term returns). Success depends on market or factor timing — NOT individual security selection.
TAA still respects the risk constraint in the IPS, but does not consider specific goals or liabilities.
Constraints
▪ Success judged against the SAA benchmark. ▪ Size of deviations often limited to a range around the SAA. ▪ May also have an allowable range of predicted volatility or a tracking-error budget vs the SAA.
Evaluation — measuring TAA success
▪ Compare Sharpe ratios under TAA vs SAA. ▪ Information ratio or t-statistic of excess realized returns relative to the SAA. ▪ Compare realized risk/return of TAA to portfolios on the SAA's efficient frontier (may be less optimal than other frontier portfolios). ▪ Attribution analysis on excess return → identify contribution of specific under/overweightings.
Drawbacks
▪ Additional trading costs and taxation (for taxable investors). ▪ Overweighting concentrates risk within the portfolio and reduces diversification benefits.
Discretionary TAA — qualitative interpretation
Relies on qualitative interpretation of macroeconomic variables. A skillful manager aims to enhance returns in a rising market and hedge risks in a falling market by forecasting short-term deviations from expected returns. Uses a combination of macroeconomic, fundamental, and sentiment indicators.
Data inputs
▪ Macroeconomic: bond yields & credit spreads, monetary policy, GDP growth, earnings & inflation predictions, leading economic indicators. ▪ Fundamental: deviation of P/E, P/B, dividend yield from their historic means. ▪ Sentiment: consumer confidence index.
Market sentiment indicators
1 · Margin borrowing — ↑ purchases on margin drives up prices → bullish. BUT if margin buying gets too high → bearish sign (investors overenthusiastic). 2 · Short interest (aggregate short selling) — the opposite. ↑ short interest drives prices down → bearish. BUT very high levels could indicate the market is at/near a low. 3 · Volatility indexes — level of fear in the market, from bid-ask spread on index options. ↑ with more put purchases, ↓ with more call purchases.
Note: although the data is quantitative in nature, the individual manager decides which indicators to use and how to prioritize/interpret them — hence "discretionary."
Systematic TAA — quantitative
A more quantitative view. Attempts to capture excess returns using strategies that have historically been predictable and persistent. Two main exploitable factors: value and momentum.
Value approach
Exploits the excess return of value stocks over growth stocks. Value measured by dividend or cash-flow yields.
▪ Equities: Shiller's earnings yield (E/P) — 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings vs market price. ▪ Currencies: short-term interest-rate differentials. ▪ Commodities: roll yields. Backwardation → positive roll yield to the long; contango → negative. ▪ Fixed income: yield spreads over risk-free rates identify value.
Momentum approach
Assumes trends will persist → recent price movements indicate whether to overweight/underweight an asset class.
▪ Most recent 12-month trend — assumed to persist for the next 12 months. ▪ Moving-average crossover — shorter-term MA crossing above longer-term MA → uptrend (and vice versa).
LOS 5.e — Behavioral biases in asset allocation
Behavioral biases cause problems during the allocation process. Awareness that the bias exists is crucial to dealing with every bias.
Loss aversion
Investors dislike losses more than they like gains → hard to maintain discipline when returns are negative; strong temptation to alter the allocation.
Overcome: goals-based investing. Goals are prioritized & subportfolios used — high-priority goals funded with less-risky assets; riskier assets used as goal priority declines. Risk analysis focuses on downside measures such as shortfall risk.
Illusion of control (+ overconfidence)
Tendency to overestimate the ability to control events. Combined with overconfidence → investors fail to diversify, trade too frequently, or both. Common signs:
▪ Frequent trading & tactical shifts attempting market timing (over-confidence after correctly calling one reversal). ▪ Active security selection by institutions believing their resources give superior selection skills. ▪ Above-average use of short selling and leverage. ▪ Shifting allocations despite lack of consensus (an individual trustee thinks they know better than the market). ▪ Concentrated positions exposing the portfolio to diversifiable risk. ▪ Biased risk/return forecasts → allocations inappropriately different from the market portfolio → undiversified extreme corner portfolios (too heavy in 1-2 classes).
Hindsight bias exacerbates it: looking back at past strategies as having led to predictable outcomes.
Overcome: use the market portfolio (CAPM mean-variance) as the starting point; shifts away from it should be subject to a formal review process.
Mental accounting (+ endowment effect)
Separating assets & liabilities into different "buckets" based on subjective criteria → suboptimal allocations. E.g. spending a tax refund on luxury goods while savings are inadequate; keeping low-interest savings while paying high credit-card interest; an entrepreneur emotionally attached to a founded company, irrationally holding it in a high-risk aspirational bucket even after losing control.
Endowment effect also leads to mental accounting: ownership of an asset causes an investor to overvalue it.
Overcome: goals-based investing.
Professor's note: mental accounting ≠ goals-based investing. Goals-based has some elements of mental accounting, but it is primarily a rational effort to differentiate goal priority and use subportfolios to increase the chance of meeting goals.
Representative / recency bias
Attaching more importance to recent data than old data. Result: shift allocations toward assets that performed well recently. E.g. 1990s real-estate "flipping" by a generation who had only experienced rising house prices — the past trend can and did change.
Overcome: strong governance & objective asset allocation processes.
Framing bias
The way information is presented affects the decision. If risk is presented as standard deviation, most prefer the lower risk — but downside risk measures may be more useful in specific situations:
▪ VaR — amount of loss at some probability over a time. ▪ Conditional VaR — average loss within the VaR tail. ▪ Shortfall probability — directly states the probability of an adverse outcome occurring.
Overcome: provide a full range of relevant information, not selectively framed information.
Availability bias (+ familiarity & home bias)
Personally experienced or easily recalled events disproportionately influence decisions. E.g. an investor who lost heavily in the tech bubble won't buy tech / high-P/B stocks again. Also: benchmarking your portfolio to other investors without regard to whether they have comparable goals & constraints.
▪ Familiarity bias — offshoot: what is familiar/easy to recall is given too much weight. ▪ Home bias — offshoot: overallocate to domestic securities, missing international diversification.
Overcome: start the allocation process with the global market portfolio.
Investment Governance
Investment governance is essential to keeping behavioral biases under control. An effective framework should incorporate:
▪ Clearly stated long-term and short-term objectives. ▪ Logical allocation of responsibility for allocation decisions based on skills and workload. ▪ Documented processes for developing and approving the investment policy statement. ▪ Documented processes for developing and approving the SAA. ▪ A framework to monitor and report performance relative to specified goals and objectives. ▪ Periodic audits.
THE TRIAD — lock this distinction
Goals = change in risk appetite / risk capacity (employment status, starting a family, illness affecting willingness/ability to take risk). Constraints = change in time horizon, liquidity needs, asset size, or regulatory/external limits. Beliefs = change in optimization inputs or guiding principles (macro forecasts, committee makeup, expected returns/vol/correlation).
You missed this triad in opposite directions (Phase 4 → called beliefs "goals"; Young → called constraints "goals"). Drill the table above until the mirror-image trap disappears.

Refresher — calls, puts, parties
▪ Call = a right to buy the underlying. ▪ Put = a right to sell. ▪ Buyer (long) pays the premium and holds the right. ▪ Seller (short) receives the premium as payment for taking on the contingent liability: a short call must deliver the underlying if exercised (receiving the strike); a short put must take delivery (paying the strike). ▪ European = exercisable only at expiration. ▪ American = exercisable any trading day up to and including expiration (the labels are not about geography).
Symbols (curriculum notation)
X = exercise (strike) price S = underlying (stock) price c, p = call premium, put premium subscripts: 0 = position entry, T = expiration e.g. S_T = underlying price at expiry
Intrinsic value + time value
An option's total premium decomposes into two parts:
▪ Intrinsic value = value of immediate exercise; the degree to which the option is in-the-money (ITM). Zero if not ITM. ▪ Time value = the extra value reflecting what might happen over the option's remaining life. Driven by volatility, time to expiry, the risk-free rate, and any yield — which is why the first pricing formula (BSM, 1973) was needed.
Two principles to remember (all else equal): higher volatility → higher premiums (calls AND puts); less time to expiry → lower premiums (calls AND puts).
Trap: intrinsic value is NOT profit. An option can be ITM yet still produce a loss for the long if intrinsic value < premium originally paid. "ITM" only means exercise (ignoring premium) would yield a gain.
Implied vs historical volatility
▪ Implied volatility = the consensus volatility backed out of the current option price through a pricing model (forward-looking). ▪ Historical (realized) volatility = the square root of the actual realized variance of returns to date (backward-looking). The two are not the same.
ITM / ATM / OTM and intrinsic value
OptionITM whenIntrinsic value (if ITM)OTM when
CallS > XS − XS < X
PutS < XX − SS > X
▪ ATM: S = X (zero intrinsic value). ▪ OTM: zero intrinsic value as well.
Call ITM logic: the right to pay less than market for the underlying; gain = S − X (buy at X, sell at market S). Put ITM logic: the right to receive more than market; gain = X − S (buy at market S, sell at X).
Twist: at expiration there is only intrinsic value (no time value) — that intrinsic value is the option's payoff. Before expiry, even an OTM option has positive value (all time value).

The golden rule of payoff diagrams
Profit line = value line shifted by the net initial premium: down if the net premium was an outflow (you paid), up if it was an inflow (you received). The profit line always has the same shape as the value line. Long and short of the same option have identical breakevens; their max profit/loss just swap (zero-sum).
Long call  |  Short call
Long call: max loss = premium paid (expires OTM); breakeven = X + c₀; unlimited max profit. Motivation: profit from a rise, downside limited to the premium. Short (naked) call: max profit = premium received; breakeven = X + c₀; unlimited max loss. Limited upside (premium) balanced against unlimited loss if the underlying rises.
XYZ MAY 50 call, c₀ = 6.26 S=40 → value 0, profit = 0 − 6.26 = −6.26 (max loss) S=60 → value 10, profit = 10 − 6.26 = +3.74 Breakeven = 50 + 6.26 = 56.26
Long put  |  Short put
Long put: max profit = X − p₀ (when S→0); breakeven = X − p₀; max loss = premium paid. Note max profit equals breakeven here. Short put: max profit = premium received; max loss = X − p₀ (= breakeven); large but limited downside (stock can't fall below zero). Profile looks like a covered call.
XYZ JUN 50 put, p₀ = 4.88 Max profit = max loss of the short = 50 − 4.88 = 45.12 Breakeven = 50 − 4.88 = 45.12 (= max profit for the long put)

Synthetic long forward (LOS 16.a)
Long call + short put (same underlying, same strike, same expiration) = a synthetic long forward position. Value at expiration = S_T − X.
Above X: the long call is ITM (positive value); the short put is OTM. Below X: the short put is ITM — exercised by the counterparty (negative value); the long call is OTM.
Either way the position ends as if you bought the stock for X — the same payoff as a long forward struck at X. (A cash-secured short put deposits X; a naked short put does not.)
Put–call parity
Buying the call & selling the put must cost the same as buying the stock and borrowing PV(X), since both end with value S_T − X:
c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − PV(X) rearranged: S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X) XYZ check (MAY 50, rf 3%, 61 days): c₀ − p₀ = 6.26 − 3.87 = 2.39 PV(50) = 50 / 1.03^(61/365) = 49.75 S₀ − PV(X) = 52.14 − 49.75 = 2.39 ✓
Put–call FORWARD parity: substitute PV(F₀(T)) for S₀ → PV(F₀(T)) + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). For an underlying paying no yield, the fair forward = FV(S₀), so it's just a restatement of standard parity.
Note: this parity assumes the underlying pays no yield over the life. If PV(X) exactly equalled S₀, call and put would have identical premiums and X would be the fair forward price.

Covered call (LOS 16.b)
Structure: long stock + short call. The short call is hedged by ownership of the stock. Above the strike, the increasingly negative call value exactly offsets the stock's gain, capping the upside.
Max profit at expiry = X − S₀ + c₀ Breakeven = max loss basis = S₀ − c₀ (loss increases one-for-one below breakeven; stock floored at 0)
Three motivations — told apart by strike vs spot
UseStrike vs spotIdea
Yield enhancementOTM (possibly far)Stock has limited upside; pocket premium as extra yield.
Reduce position at favourable priceITMPlan to sell; if exercised, sell at strike + keep premium → more than selling at market now.
Target price realizationmarginally OTMHappy to sell slightly higher; calls struck just above market.
Exam hook: the observable difference between the three uses is purely the strike relative to the current stock price. A question describing intent (income vs disposal vs target) is testing whether you map it to OTM / ITM / marginally-OTM.
Example (yield enhancement)
Long XYZ @ 52.14, short APR 55 call, c₀ = 2.52 Max profit = 55 − 52.14 + 2.52 = 5.38 (cap at 55: stock gain 2.86 + premium 2.52) Breakeven = max loss basis = 52.14 − 2.52 = 49.62 Worse off than just holding only if S_T > 55 + 2.52 = 57.52

Protective put (LOS 16.c)
Structure: long stock + long put. The classic options hedge for a long position — protects against the underlying falling while retaining full upside.
Max loss at expiry = S₀ − X + p₀ Breakeven = S₀ + p₀ Max profit = unlimited (stock keeps rising; put just expires)
XYZ example: long @ 52.14 + MAY 50 put @ 3.87. Stock loss capped at 52.14 − 50 = 2.14; net max loss = 2.14 + 3.87 = 6.01. Breakeven = 52.14 + 3.87 = 56.01.

Options as a hedge of a SHORT position (LOS 16.e)
A short seller gains if the price falls, loses if it rises. The two option overlays mirror the long-position hedges:
Buy a call (likely OTM): hedges the short against the price rising — the positive call value above the strike offsets short-stock losses. Analogous to a protective put on a long position. Caps the loss, keeps downside gain. Sell a put (likely OTM): sells off part of the benefit of the price falling, in the same way a covered call sells off the upside of a long position. Collects premium, caps the gain.
Underlying positionHedge upside-cap (sell premium)Hedge protect (buy insurance)
Long stockCovered call (short call)Protective put (long put)
Short stockShort putLong call
Mirror map: short-stock ↔ long-stock swaps calls and puts. Buy-call-on-short ≙ buy-put-on-long (protection); sell-put-on-short ≙ sell-call-on-long (income, capped benefit).
The Collar — protective put + covered call
A collar is best thought of as a combination of a protective put and a covered call, held on an existing long position in the underlying. Also known as a fence or a hedge wrapper.
▪ Long the underlying + buy a put (usually OTM) → hedges the stock's downside. ▪ Sell a call (usually OTM) → sells off the upside and subsidizes the cost of the put.
Zero-cost collar
Usually the put strike is set first, then an appropriate call strike is chosen so the call and put have the same premium.
If the options are OTC (rather than exchange-traded), matching premiums is easy → no net inflow or outflow at initiation → a zero-cost collar.
Profile (LOS 16.f)
Objective: hedge an existing long position cheaply by giving up upside. Structure: long stock + long put (OTM) + short call (OTM). Max profit: rise from initial price up to the call strike. Max loss: fall from initial price down to the put strike. Breakeven: the initial stock price (for a zero-cost collar — no net premium).
The stock value is hedged beyond the strikes — value capped above the call strike, floored at the put strike.
EXAMPLE — XYZ zero-cost collar (20 March, price = $52.14)
Buy a June 50 put (premium $4.88) and sell a June 55.87 call (premium $4.88). Same premium → zero net cost.
Max profit
$3.73
Max loss
$2.14
Breakeven
$52.14
Max profit = call strike − initial price = $55.87 − $52.14 = $3.73 Max loss = initial price − put strike = $52.14 − $50.00 = $2.14 Breakeven = initial stock price = $52.14 (zero net premium)
Chart note: the "stock profit + option values" line is the same as the net profit line because the zero net initial premium means there's nothing to subtract.
Payoff regions
Stock at expirationOutcome
Below put strike ($50)Floored — put protects; loss capped at $2.14
Between strikes ($50–$55.87)Profit/loss tracks the stock; both options expire worthless
Above call strike ($55.87)Capped — short call caps upside; profit capped at $3.73

The Straddle — the classic volatility play
A long straddle involves the purchase of an equal number of calls and puts on a given underlying. All options have the same expiry date and strike.
Distinction: unlike covered call / protective put / collar, the straddle (and the spreads) do not involve a position in the underlying — they use options only.
Strangle (currency reading): like a straddle, but the call and put have different strikes.
At expiration — only one leg is ITM
Either the call or the put will be ITM, but not both. With strike 52.50: call is ITM for prices above 52.50, put is ITM for prices below 52.50.
The value line is always V-shaped, centered on the strike, where both options expire worthless so total value = 0.
EXAMPLE — Long XYZ June 52.5 straddle
Stock at $52.14 → go long both the June 52.5 call and June 52.5 put (strike close to ATM). Call premium $6.22 + put premium $6.19, both paid at initiation.
Total outlay = Max loss
$12.41
Upside breakeven
$64.91
Downside breakeven
$40.09
Total outlay = $6.22 + $6.19 = $12.41 (max loss, at the strike) Upside BE = strike + outlay = $52.50 + $12.41 = $64.91 Downside BE = strike − outlay = $52.50 − $12.41 = $40.09
Profit profile: larger profits the further the underlying moves either way. No maximum profit on the long call (unlimited upside). Max profit on the long put = strike price − cost of the options.
Short Straddle — the neutrality play
A short straddle involves selling instead of buying — it is a neutrality play.
▪ Makes more profit the closer to the strike the underlying ends up. ▪ No limit on potential loss (mirror of the long straddle's unlimited profit).
Trap: long straddle = volatility play (wants a big move, either way); short straddle = neutrality play (wants the underlying to stay near the strike). Loss is unlimited on the short.

Spreads — the building blocks
Bull and bear spreads are positions with equal numbers of long options on one strike and short options on a second strike. A spread is constructed using either calls or puts.
▪ Bull spreads = "Buy Low" — long options on the lower strike, short options on the higher strike. ▪ Bear spreads = short options on the lower strike, long options on the higher strike.
Key identity: a bear spread is just a short bull spread.
Debit vs Credit
TypeStrategiesNet premiumWhy
DebitBull call · Bear putNet outlay (pay)The bought (more valuable) option costs more than the sold one
CreditBear call · Bull putNet inflow (receive)The more valuable option is sold
Professor's note: by default assume a bull spread uses calls and a bear spread uses puts (debit spreads preferred over credit spreads) unless the question states otherwise.
Bull Call Spread (debit) — bullish, limited
Buy XYZ June 50 call ($7.40), sell XYZ June 55 call ($5.20). Net outlay = $7.40 − $5.20 = $2.20.
Max loss

At 55+: value = diff between strikes = $5 (max value; further upside hedged by short call) Max loss = net premium paid = $2.20 (value = 0, below lower strike) Breakeven = lower strike + net premium paid = $50 + $2.20 = $52.20 Max profit = diff strikes − net premium paid = $5 − $2.20 = $2.80
Below 50 → both OTM, value = 0. Between strikes → only long call ITM, value = stock − lower strike. Similar to a covered call, but with a long call taking the place of the stock.
Bear Put Spread (debit) — bearish, limited
Sell a lower-strike put, buy a higher-strike put. Buy XYZ May 55 put ($6.61), sell XYZ May 50 put ($3.87). Net outlay = $6.61 − $3.87 = $2.74.
Max loss

Max loss = net premium paid = $2.74 Breakeven = higher strike − net premium paid = $55 − $2.74 = $52.26 Max profit = diff strikes − net premium paid = $5 − $2.74 = $2.26
Both OTM above the higher strike → value 0. Between strikes, value reflects the moneyness of the long 55 put. At the lower strike (50), value is maxed and hedged for any lower price. Exposure is bearish but limited vs just a long put at 55.
Bear Call Spread (credit) — using calls for a bear position
Short XYZ June 50 call ($7.40), long XYZ June 55 call ($5.20). Net initial inflow = $7.40 − $5.20 = $2.20.
Max profit = net premium received = $2.20 (at 50 and below) At 55+: net intrinsic value = −$5 Max loss = diff strikes − net premium received = $5 − $2.20 = $2.80 Breakeven = lower strike + net premium received = $50 + $2.20 = $52.20
Bull Put Spread (credit) — using puts for a bull position
Reverse of the bear put spread: short XYZ May 55 put ($6.61), long XYZ May 50 put ($3.87). Net inflow.
Max profit = net premium received Breakeven = higher strike − net premium received Max loss = diff strikes − net premium received
Beware credit spreads with American-style options: the short option may go ITM while the long option is still OTM → the counterparty might exercise early, disrupting the strategy.
Generalized at-expiration formulas
"Net premium" = absolute value of the difference between the premiums.
Debit spreads (bull call & bear put)
Max loss = net premium paid Max profit = difference between strikes − net premium paid
Credit spreads (bear call & bull put)
Max profit = net premium received Max loss = difference between strikes − net premium received
Breakeven (by option type)
Call spreads: breakeven = lower strike + net premium Put spreads: breakeven = higher strike − net premium

The Greeks — each is a ratio of absolute changes
So far we considered values/profits at expiration (simple one-for-one with intrinsic value). During their lives, options respond to changes in the underlying (and other factors) in a more complex way. The Greeks describe that.
You won't be asked to calculate the Greeks — if needed they'd be provided. What matters is the meaning and significance of each.
The four Greeks
GreekDefinitionSign (long call)Sign (long put)
Delta (Δ)Δ option price per +1 change in stock pricepositivenegative
Gamma (Γ)Δ option delta per +1 change in stock pricepositivepositive
Theta (θ)daily change in option price (effect of time passing)negativenegative
Vega (ν)Δ option price per +1% change in volatilitypositivepositive
Memory anchor: long options are long gamma and long vega (both positive), but short theta (time decay hurts). Delta is the only one whose sign flips between calls (+) and puts (−).
Delta — slope of the value line
Delta measures the change in option price for a +1 change in the underlying (all else constant — the change must be instantaneous).
XYZ stock $52.14. MAY 55 call delta = 0.47. If stock rises $1 to $53.14, the call rises ~$0.47: $4.02 + $0.47 = $4.49 (predicted).
Why the pricing model gives $4.51, not $4.49: the option price line is curved (except at expiration), with curvature measured by gamma — so delta itself varies with the underlying. Delta is only accurate for infinitesimal moves.
Time value
The vertical distance between the (total) value line and the intrinsic value line = time value. It is greatest around ATM and diminishes the more an option is ITM or OTM (time value reflects uncertainty about whether the option expires ITM/OTM — deeply ITM/OTM = less uncertainty).
Delta sign & magnitude rules
▪ Long calls: positive delta. ▪ Long puts: negative delta (line slopes downward).
Simple rule (ignoring the sign), all else equal:
▪ The more ITM an option → the higher its absolute delta (closer to 1). ▪ The more OTM an option → the lower its absolute delta (closer to 0).
Delta ranges: Long call 0→+1 · Short call 0→−1 · Long put 0→−1 · Short put 0→+1.
Gamma — curvature of the value line (slope of delta)
Gamma = change in delta per +1 change in the underlying. It's the slope of the line representing delta, and changes with the underlying too.
MAY 55 call gamma = 0.031. If the share price rises $1, the call's delta rises 0.031: 0.470 + 0.031 = 0.501.
Gamma adjustment improves the delta estimate: if delta is 0.470 at $52.14 and 0.501 at $53.14, the average delta = (0.470 + 0.501)/2 = 0.486. Predicted call value $1 up = $4.02 + $0.486 = $4.506 — much closer to the model's $4.51 than using initial delta alone.
When is gamma highest?
Gamma tends to be higher the closer an option is to ATM, and is at its greatest for ATM options close to expiration.
Why: with little time left, the option premium line is crammed into a narrow range either side of the strike (low time value), so delta swings sharply from ~0 to ~1 across that range → gamma is highest there. ATM + near expiry = max gamma.
Gamma table — XYZ at $52.14 (20 March)
StrikeCall γ (APR/MAY/JUN)Put γ (APR/MAY/JUN)
500.041 / 0.030 / 0.0240.041 / 0.030 / 0.024
52.50.044 / 0.031 / 0.0250.044 / 0.031 / 0.025
550.043 / 0.031 / 0.0260.043 / 0.031 / 0.026
Note gamma is higher for the nearer expiry (APR > MAY > JUN) and peaks around the ATM strike (52.5). Call gamma = put gamma at the same strike/expiry.
LOS 16.d — Position (portfolio) delta
The overall delta for a combination of options and positions in the underlying = sum of the individual deltas (being careful with signs).
▪ Long position in 1 unit of the underlying: delta = +1. ▪ Short position in 1 unit of the underlying: delta = −1. ▪ Futures/forwards on a no-yield underlying are proxies → delta +1 (long) / −1 (short).
Contract multiplier: a traded option contract is usually a right over 100 shares. A long XYZ call with delta +0.65 → position delta = 100 × +0.65 = +65.
Worked examples
100 shares of XYZ → delta = 100 × +1 = +100 (stock +$1 → value +$100) 1,000 shares + 10 long put contracts (put delta −0.6): = (1,000 × +1) + (10 × 100 × −0.6) = 1,000 − 600 = +400 → stock falls $1: shares lose $1,000, but net position only falls $400
Full forward hedge: long stock + short forward on the same number of shares → delta = shares × (+1 + −1) = 0 → completely hedged against price moves.

Protective put pre-expiry
At expiration we thought of a protective put as retaining full stock exposure above the strike and fully hedging below it. Before expiration, it's better seen as modifying the delta of the long stock from its unhedged +1.
▪ Large stock rises → put moves substantially OTM → position delta → +1 (almost same as unhedged stock). ▪ Large stock falls → put moves substantially ITM → position delta → 0 (downside protected).
Stock + protective put has a net exposure equivalent to a long call.
Contrast — forward hedge: a forward-based hedge (short forward on the same shares) gives position delta = shares × (+1 + −1) = 0 → completely hedged. The put hedges asymmetrically (keeps upside), the forward hedges both directions.
Covered call pre-expiry
As with the protective put, the covered call's position delta varies with the underlying:
▪ Call deeply OTM (stock low) → position delta close to +1 (you still have nearly full stock exposure). ▪ Call deeply ITM (stock high) → position delta close to 0 (virtually all the stock's upside is hedged away by the short call).
Both covered call and protective put mute the exposure of the underlying — the bull/bear spread pre-expiry behaves similarly (highly muted vs the at-expiration profile).
MQ 16.9 #1 — likely deltas just after establishment (3 months out)
A covered call (long stock + short OTM call) and a protective put (long stock + long OTM put), both newly established with time to expiry.
▪ Covered call: long stock (+1) + short OTM call (small negative, e.g. −0.55) → net position delta around +0.4 to +0.45 (positive, <1). ▪ Protective put: long stock (+1) + long OTM put (small negative) → net positive but <1 as well.
Trap: both deltas are positive and between 0 and 1 just after establishment — neither is zero, and the protective put's delta is NOT negative (the long-stock +1 dominates the small negative put delta).
Theta — speed of time-value decay
Theta measures how quickly an option loses value as time passes (all else equal). For a long option position theta is always negative: less time to expiration means less time value.
Call ThetaStrikePut Theta
APRMAYJUNPriceAPRMAYJUN
−0.058−0.042−0.03550−0.054−0.038−0.031
−0.061−0.043−0.03652.5−0.056−0.039−0.031
−0.059−0.043−0.03655−0.055−0.039−0.031
▪ All negative: long calls AND long puts both lose time value as expiry nears. ▪ Shorter-dated = larger |theta|: APR (nearest) thetas are more negative than JUN (furthest) — the near-dated option bleeds time value fastest. This is the engine behind calendar spreads.
ATM behaviour: options close to ATM have the highest |theta|, and |theta| increases (becomes more negative) as expiration approaches → ATM options lose time value at an increasing rate. A 1-month-to-expiry ATM option loses far more time value over a month than an otherwise-identical 3-month option does over the same period.
Contrast — deep OTM / deep ITM: for options far from the money, the decline in time value slows down as maturity approaches (the curve flattens), the opposite of ATM. Don't assume "closer to expiry → faster decay" universally; it's true for ATM, false for deep OTM/ITM.
Calendar Spreads (LOS 16.g)
Calendar spreads are the only strategy where the two options have different expirations (same underlying, same strike). The motivation: exploit the difference in theta between a close-to-expiry and a more-distant option.
For options near ATM, the nearer-dated option has a higher absolute theta (more negative) than the longer-dated one. The calendar spread monetises that gap.
Long calendar spread
Structure: buy longer-dated option + sell shorter-dated option (same strike & underlying). Logic: shorter-dated premium falls faster than longer-dated → more value gained on the short leg than lost on the long leg → net profit. Conditions: options near ATM (so thetas are the right way round); want little movement in the underlying over the near option's life (large moves undermine profit). Calls or puts? reflects longer-term view — calls if bullish, puts if bearish. Benefits from: a stable market or an increase in implied volatility.
Short calendar spread
Structure: reverse — sell longer-dated + buy shorter-dated. Vulnerable when: the underlying stays still so the options end up ATM as the short-dated option expires → longer-dated premium rises (a loss, since we're short it) unless implied vol also falls. Benefits from: a big move in the underlying or a decrease in implied volatility.
Unifying idea: in both cases the strategy sells the option expected to lose value (theta) relatively faster as time passes.
Example — Jenkins long calendar spread
20 March, XYZ = $52.14. Long-term bullish but expects little movement next month.
Buy 4 XYZ June 52.5 calls @ 6.22 Sell 4 XYZ April 52.5 calls @ 3.53 Net premium outlay = 2.69 × 4 × 100 = $1,076 At April expiry, stock still $52.14: • Both calls OTM → April call expires worthless (good, we're short it) • June call now worth $5.00 (from pricing model) Position value = 5.00 × 400 = $2,000 (paid $1,076 a month earlier)
Profit would be even higher if implied volatility rose — that drives the June call value up.
Vega — sensitivity to a +1% change in volatility
Vega measures the effect of a 1% increase in implied volatility on the option's value. Vegas are always positive: a more volatile underlying makes every option on it more valuable (more uncertainty about the expiry outcome → more time value).
Call VegaStrikePut Vega
APRMAYJUNPriceAPRMAYJUN
0.0570.0810.098500.0570.0810.098
0.0600.0840.10252.50.0600.0840.102
0.0590.0840.103550.0590.0840.103
▪ More time → higher vega: JUN vegas > MAY > APR. Longer-dated options are more sensitive to vol. ▪ Diminishes deep ITM / deep OTM: vega peaks near ATM and falls away as the option moves far in- or out-of-the-money. ▪ Call vega = put vega at the same strike/expiry (put–call parity).
Aside — converting volatility between periods
To convert a volatility (standard deviation) from one period to another, multiply by the square root of the ratio of the period lengths.
σ(target) = σ(source) × √(days_target / days_source) Annual 57% → two-monthly (42 trading days, 252-day year): 57% × √(42 / 252) = 23.27% Monthly (21 days) → annual: σ_monthly × √(252 / 21)

Straddle value before expiration
At expiry a long straddle has the familiar V-shape. Before expiry the value curve is smoother (U-shaped) but the same idea holds: value increases the further the underlying moves from the strike.
▪ Delta near the strike ≈ 0 (the curve is flat at the bottom). ▪ Delta → +1 as the underlying rises far above strike; → −1 as it falls far below.
Long volatility: at a given underlying price, a higher level of volatility lifts the whole curve — the long straddle gains value even if the underlying doesn't move. This is the real reason a long straddle is called "going long volatility."
Long straddle — Greeks profile
Delta: long call (+δ) + long put (−δ) → delta-neutral (≈0 near strike) — we don't much care about small moves in the underlying. Vega: positive — value rises if vol rises. Theta: negative — two long options bleed time value. Vol must rise quickly enough to offset the decay.
Short straddle — Greeks profile
Delta: delta-neutral as well. Vega: negative — a bet on falling volatility. Theta: positive — collects time decay.
Twist: "delta-neutral" describes BOTH long and short straddles — the distinguishing Greek is vega (long = +vega = long vol; short = −vega = short vol). A question that hinges on delta to tell them apart is a trap.
Volatility Skew & Smile (LOS 16.h)
The XYZ option prices throughout this reading assumed a single volatility of 30% for all strikes and expirations — a simplification. In practice, implied volatility computed from actual traded options varies by strike and by expiration (and differs between calls and puts). Holding expiration constant, two patterns appear:
Smile vs Skew
▪ Volatility SMILE: further-from-ATM options (both sides) have higher implied vol → a U-shaped (smiling) curve when IV is plotted against strike. Less common. ▪ Volatility SKEW: implied vol increases for more OTM puts and decreases for more OTM calls. Explanation: OTM puts are desirable as insurance against market declines, so they're bid up by higher demand (higher value ⇒ higher implied vol); demand for OTM calls is comparatively low. More common.
Memorise the skew direction: OTM puts → IV UP; OTM calls → IV DOWN. The reversed wording ("IV up for OTM calls, down for OTM puts") is a classic distractor (it describes neither standard pattern).
Reading sentiment from skew deviations
▪ Bearish signal: a sharp increase in the level of the skew plus a surge in the absolute level of implied vol → market sentiment turning bearish. ▪ Bullish signal: higher implied vols (vs historical) for OTM calls → investors bullish, demand to take on upside exposure is strong.
Deviations expected to correct can form the basis of trading strategies — which might use risk reversals (next tab).
Two more terms
▪ Term structure of volatility: implied vols differ across maturities. Contango (longer-dated options having higher implied vol) is quite common. ▪ Implied volatility surface: a 3-D graph examining the joint influence of maturity (x-axis) and strike price (y-axis) on implied volatility (z-axis).
Risk Reversal
A long (short) risk reversal combines long (short) calls and short (long) puts on the same underlying. It's used to exploit a skew that has deviated anomalously from historical levels.
Long risk reversal: if a trader believes put implied vol is relatively too high vs calls → buy the OTM call (seen as relatively underpriced) + sell the OTM put (seen as relatively overpriced), same expiration. Aim: profit if the anomalous IV relationship corrects — long the options that should gain value, short those that should lose. NOT a directional bet on the stock.
Problem: long call + short put both create long exposure to the underlying → the position is "broadly long" the stock, which is problematic if you didn't want directional risk.
Example — PQR risk reversal & delta hedge
PQR = $50. Buy call (strike 60, IV 50%) + sell put (strike 40, IV 70%). The 20-point IV differential is substantially greater than seen in the past → trade the anomaly.
At the current price ($50) the risk reversal delta ≈ 0.3 (well below 1). Position = 10 call contracts + 10 put contracts (each on 1,000 shares). For each $1 fall in the stock: loss ≈ $1 × 0.3 × 1,000 = $300 (the net long exposure)
To remove the unwanted long exposure → delta hedge: sell 300 shares. Why 300? A short position of that size produces equal-and-opposite P&L to the risk reversal's stock exposure.

1,000 shares' worth of options with delta 0.3 are delta-hedged by 1,000 × 0.3 = 300 shares. (The hedge size = the other side's notional × its delta.)
Dynamic hedge: the delta of the risk reversal does not stay constant — it changes as the stock price moves and as time passes. So the size of the delta hedge must be adjusted periodically (rebalanced). This is typical of all delta hedges.

★ Two-leg decomposition — why stock+option formulas look the way they do
The #1 trap on stock+option strategies: forgetting the stock leg. Profit always = (stock leg) + (option leg). The stock you bought at S₀ contributes its own gain/loss separately from the option. Always split them before reaching for a formula.
Master identity: at any expiry price, total profit = (S_T − S₀) from the stock + option payoff ± premium. The maxima below are just this, evaluated at the best/worst S_T.
Covered call — long stock + short call (strike X, receive c₀)
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Short call leg+c₀ − max(S_T − X, 0)
BEST CASE: stock ends at (or above) X — say S₀=52.14, X=55, c₀=2.52, S_T=60 Stock leg : 60 − 52.14 = +7.86 Call leg : +2.52 − (60 − 55) = 2.52 − 5 = −2.48 Total : 7.86 − 2.48 = 5.38 Above X the two legs cancel $1-for-$1 → profit is CAPPED. At the cap, S_T = X, so plug in: (X − S₀) + c₀ = (55 − 52.14) + 2.52 = 2.86 + 2.52 = 5.38
Why NOT just c₀? c₀ alone ignores the stock gain from S₀ up to the strike (the 2.86). You bought at 52.14 and effectively sold at 55 — that appreciation is yours, PLUS the premium. c₀ would be the answer only for a naked call (no stock leg).
Max profit = (X − S₀) + c₀ → stock gain up to strike + premium kept.
Max loss / breakeven = S₀ − c₀ → stock falls to 0; effective cost was S₀ minus the cushion c₀.
Protective put — long stock + long put (strike X, pay p₀)
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Long put legmax(X − S_T, 0) − p₀
WORST CASE: stock ends at (or below) X — say S₀=52.14, X=50, p₀=3.87, S_T=40 Stock leg : 40 − 52.14 = −12.14 Put leg : (50 − 40) − 3.87 = 10 − 3.87 = +6.13 Total : −12.14 + 6.13 = −6.01 Below X the put gain offsets further stock losses → loss is FLOORED. At the floor, S_T = X, so plug in: (S_T − S₀) + (X − S_T paid premium) = (X − S₀) + p₀ as a loss S₀ − X + p₀ = 52.14 − 50 + 3.87 = 2.14 + 3.87 = 6.01
Max loss = S₀ − X + p₀ → stock fall down to strike (S₀ − X) + premium spent on insurance.
Breakeven = S₀ + p₀ → stock must rise to cover the put's cost.
Max profit = unlimited → you still own the stock; the put just expires.
Collar — long stock + long put (X_p) + short call (X_c), net = p₀ − c₀
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Long put leg (X_p)max(X_p − S_T, 0) − p₀
Short call leg (X_c)+c₀ − max(S_T − X_c, 0)
The collar is just covered call + protective put on the same stock. • Below X_p: put protects → floored. • Above X_c: call caps → ceilinged. • Net premium = p₀ − c₀ (a cost if put dearer than call). CEILING (S_T = X_c): (X_c − S₀) − net FLOOR (S_T = X_p): (S₀ − X_p) + net (as a loss) BREAKEVEN: S₀ + net
Sign of "net": net = p₀ − c₀. If the put costs more than the call you collect (net > 0) it's a debit — it lowers max profit and raises max loss. A zero-cost collar picks strikes so c₀ ≈ p₀ → net ≈ 0, and the formulas collapse to (X_c − S₀) and (S₀ − X_p).
The reconstruction habit (use this when you blank)
1. Write the stock leg: S_T − S₀. Never skip it. 2. Write each option leg: payoff ± its premium (− if you bought, + if you sold). 3. For max profit, push S_T to the helpful extreme and add the legs. For max loss, push it the other way. 4. For breakeven, set total profit = 0 and solve for S_T.
Do this once on scratch paper and you'll never confuse "c₀" with "(X − S₀) + c₀" again — the stock leg is right there in front of you.

Universal identities worth memorising
▪ Profit line = value line shifted by net premium (down if paid, up if received); same shape as value. ▪ Put–call parity: c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − PV(X)  ⇔  S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). ▪ Synthetic long forward = long call + short put (same X, same expiry); value = S_T − X. ▪ Long & short of the same option share a breakeven; max profit/loss swap (zero-sum).

Payer vs Receiver swap — leg by leg
▪ Payer swap = pay fixed, receive floating (MRR), on a notional principal.   ↳ floating leg gains when realized floating rates > rates expected at initiation → payer swap value ↑   ↳ floating rates below expectations → payer swap value ↓ ▪ Receiver swap = the counterparty: receive fixed, pay floating. Mirror image. ▪ Netting: payments are netted at each settlement — the party owing the larger amount pays the difference (reduces credit risk). ▪ First settlement: the floating payment for the first settlement date is known at initiation; later ones are not (set by the MRR at each reset).
Capital-market replication: payer swap = issue a fixed-rate bond + buy an FRN. Receiver swap = issue an FRN + buy a fixed-rate note. This replication is what drives swap duration (next tab).

Trap: the locked-in cost is swap fixed rate + FRN margin — NOT the fixed rate alone. ABC pays 2% + 0.25% = 2.25% regardless of the realized MRR. Dropping the margin is the classic dropped-leg error.
Why a payer swap has NEGATIVE duration — two-leg decomposition
▪ Payer swap = issue fixed-rate note + buy FRN   ↳ leg 1: SHORT fixed-rate note → short a long-duration instrument → contributes negative duration   ↳ leg 2: LONG FRN → duration ≈ time to next reset (small) → contributes ≈ 0   ↳ net: MDₛ < 0 → payer swap gains value when rates rise ▪ Receiver swap = mirror → MDₛ > 0 → gains when rates fall (like a long bond) ▪ Portfolio effect: add payer swap → portfolio duration ↓  |  add receiver swap → portfolio duration ↑
Professorʼs note: all of this uses modified duration, which implicitly assumes a flat yield curve and parallel shifts.
Notional principal for a target duration
NPₛ = [ (MDₜ − MDₚ) / MDₛ ] × MVₚ NPₛ = notional swap principal MDₜ = target modified duration MDₚ = current portfolio MD MDₛ = modified duration of swap MVₚ = market value of portfolio
Target duration MDₜ

Direction first, formula second: MDₜ > MDₚ → need duration ↑ → receiver swap (MDₛ = +). MDₜ < MDₚ → payer swap (MDₛ = −). Textbook: increase 4.5 → 6 on £120m with MDₛ = 2 → receiver swap, NPₛ = £90m.
FRA mechanics — who takes which side
▪ Future BORROWER (fears rates ↑) → LONG FRA   ↳ if realized MRR > forward rate → receives payment → offsets higher borrowing cost   ↳ if realized MRR < forward rate → pays → offsets cheaper borrowing → cost still locked ▪ Future LENDER (fears rates ↓) → SHORT FRA ▪ Key rule: long FRA value ↑ when rates rise; short FRA value ↑ when rates fall.
2×6 FRA timeline (Fig 17.3)
Trap: the FRA settlement is the present value of the rate difference, discounted from the end of the loan period back to FRA expiry — it is exchanged at expiry (T60), not at T180.

STIR / Eurodollar futures — IMM pricing decomposed
▪ Price convention: futures price = 100 − annualized forward rate (IMM Index)   ↳ forward rates fall → price rises → LONG futures gains ▪ Contract size: $1 million deposit, 90-day rate, quarterly maturities ▪ Tick value: 1 bp = $1m × 0.0001 × 90/360 = $25 per contract ▪ Contracts needed: amount to hedge / $1 million
TRAP — direction flip vs FRA: a LONG Eurodollar futures gains when rates FALL (price = 100 − rate), while a LONG FRA gains when rates RISE. Future depositor/lender → long futures. Future borrower → short futures (or long FRA). The exam loves this inversion.
Futures vs FRA: futures are standardized, exchange-traded, marked to market with margin; FRAs are dealer-customized (not liquid) and carry counterparty risk. Both price off the same forward rate (no-arbitrage).

Fixed-income futures — mechanics decomposed
▪ Notional bond: Treasury futures are priced off a notional government bond with a 6% coupon. ▪ Conversion factor (CF): clean price of $1 face of the eligible bond discounted at YTM 6%   ↳ coupon = 6% → CF = 1  |  coupon > 6% → CF > 1  |  coupon < 6% → CF < 1 ▪ Delivery option: the SHORT chooses which eligible bond to deliver (e.g. any UST 15–25y).
principal invoice price = (futures settlement / 100) × $100,000 × CF total invoice amount = principal invoice price + accrued interest profit/(loss) on delivery = [(settlement × CF) + AIₜ] − (CTD clean + AIₜ)
▪ CTD identification — two equivalent methods:   ↳ 1. highest implied repo rate on a cash-and-carry trade   ↳ 2. lowest basis (basis = spot price − futures price); lowest basis ↔ highest implied repo
CF bias trap: CFs assume a flat 6% term structure. Yields below 6% → bias to short-duration (high coupon, low maturity) bonds as CTD. Yields above 6% → bias to long-duration bonds.
Professorʼs note: with mark-to-market, the short does not receive the initial futures price at expiry — daily P/L (FPₜ − FPₜ₋₁) settles via margin; at maturity the short receives final settlement × CF (+ AI).

Hedging with Treasury futures — the logic chain
▪ rates ↑ → bond prices ↓ → futures price ↓ → SHORT futures gains → short futures hedge a long bond portfolio ▪ short futures → portfolio duration ↓  |  long futures → portfolio duration ↑ ▪ futures price tracks the CTD: Δfutures price = ΔCTD / CF (CTD and futures share the same duration)
ΔP = HR × Δfutures price HR = (ΔP / ΔCTD) × CF BPVHR (full hedge) = [ −BPVₚₒₙₜ / BPV⁋ₜ₃ ] × CF BPVHR (target) = [ (BPVₜₐₙₒₜ − BPVₚₒₙₜ) / BPV⁋ₜ₃ ] × CF BPVₚₒₙₜ = MDₚ × 0.0001 × MVₚ BPVₜₐₙₒₜ = MDₜ × 0.0001 × MVₚ BPV⁋ₜ₃ = MD⁋ₜ₃ × 0.0001 × MV⁋ₜ₃ MV⁋ₜ₃ = (CTD price / 100) × $100,000
Two classic dropped details: (1) MV⁋ₜ₃ uses the CTD price scaled to $100,000 face, not the raw quote. (2) The result is × CF at the END — multiply, never divide. Negative BPVHR = SELL that many contracts.

Why the hedge is imperfect — 3 factors
▪ 1. CTD switch: the hedge is built on the CTD; if the level or slope of the term structure changes significantly, the CTD bond — and hence the futures duration — may change. ▪ 2. Convexity ignored: duration is a linear approximation of price/yield; it ignores the convexity of the bonds. ▪ 3. Shaping risk: modified duration only captures parallel shifts; nonparallel changes (steepening, flattening, curvature) are unhedged. ▪ Plus basis / spread risk: portfolio bonds and the CTD are not perfect substitutes — mismatch between Δportfolio and Δhedge value.
Currency swap — mechanics decomposed
▪ Structure: each party pays periodic interest on a notional in ONE currency; the two notionals are equivalent at the inception FX rate. ▪ Purpose — synthetic borrowing: a firm without good access to foreign capital markets borrows domestically and swaps → effectively borrows in the foreign currency, hedging the FX risk of foreign cash flows. ▪ Cross-currency basis swap: the variant where notionals are exchanged at the beginning AND re-exchanged at the end. ▪ Typical legs: fixed or floating, but the standard market swap is floating-for-floating. ▪ Interest direction: each counterparty pays variable interest on the currency it initially received.
Terminology trap: in the euro-company example, the European company is the dollar payer and the dealer the euro payer — the label refers to the interest flows and final principal payment, NOT to the swap of initial principal.
No FX risk on principals: at expiration the notionals re-exchanged are the SAME amounts as at initiation — changes in the exchange rate over the life of the swap do not affect the principal flows.
Cross-currency basis swap — 3 phases (€ company, €50m @ 1.1236)
Cross-currency basis — what it is, why it exists
▪ CIRP: under covered interest rate parity, borrowing USD directly = borrowing foreign currency + hedging with a currency swap. Held well for 3 decades pre-2008. ▪ Definition: basis = the additional cost of borrowing dollars synthetically (via swap) relative to direct USD cash-market borrowing. ▪ Convention: basis is quoted from the foreign-currency perspective, not the USD perspective. ▪ Negative basis = synthetic USD cost > direct USD cost. Most currencies have shown a negative basis vs USD since the crisis.   ↳ implication: the USD borrower must accept a lower rate on the foreign-currency interest it receives. ▪ Why CIRP fails since 2008 — three drivers:   ↳ 1. stricter capital adequacy rules → covered interest arbitrage became much more costly for banks   ↳ 2. high demand for USD loans   ↳ 3. USD lending via swaps has attracted a premium since the crisis
USD investor angle: when a foreign currency shows a negative basis, a USD investor can swap USD → foreign currency, buy foreign-currency bonds, and use the swap to convert returns back — earning MORE than direct USD bonds (the basis is harvested as extra yield).

All-in synthetic rate decomposed: pays €ref + spread on the loan; receives €ref + basis on the swap → net € outflow = spread − basis; pays $ref on the swap → all-in = $ref + (spread − basis). Currency forwards vs futures
▪ Forwards: customized — tailored to the exact quantity AND the exact date of the expected foreign-currency flow. ▪ Futures: standardized quantity and delivery dates; limited currency-pair range; greater liquidity attracts investors and dealers. ▪ Direction: expecting to RECEIVE foreign currency → SELL futures on it (promise to deliver). Having to PAY foreign currency → BUY.
HR = amount of currency to be exchanged / futures contract size
Settlement-date mismatch — risk decomposed:
▪ futures settle BEFORE the currency arrives → exchange-rate risk from settlement until receipt
▪ futures settle AFTER → position closed early at the then-futures price ≠ spot → basis risk (more or less USD than delivery would have given)

Equity swaps — structure decomposed
▪ Purpose: synthetic exposure to stocks — the economic benefits of ownership without the cost and expense of ownership. ▪ 3 main types:   ↳ 1. pay fixed, receive equity return   ↳ 2. pay floating, receive equity return   ↳ 3. pay another equity return, receive equity return (e.g. pay Nasdaq, receive S&P 500) ▪ Equity return basis: single stock | basket of equities | equity index ▪ Return type: price return (typical) or total return (price + dividends) ▪ To REDUCE exposure: pay equity return, receive floating/fixed = synthetic sell equity + invest in money markets

Equity futures & forwards — uses and mechanics
▪ Futures: exchange-traded, standardized, margin, low transaction costs; on indexes and single stocks. ▪ Uses: tactical allocation (SELL → reduce / BUY → increase equity exposure), diversification, international exposure, directional bets. ▪ Forwards: same advantages but illiquid, no mark-to-market, counterparty credit risk (no clearinghouse); major advantage = customization. ▪ Multiplier: actual futures value = quoted points × multiplier (S&P 500: $250 | FTSE 100: £10).
number of contracts (hedge) = monetary value to hedge / (futures price × multiplier) number of futures required = [ (βₜ − βₚ) / βₒ ] × [ MVₚ / F ] F = futures price × multiplier full hedge: βₜ = 0
Trap: negative result = SELL contracts. And a hedged-but-rounded HR leaves a small residual (FTSE example: net −£300 from rounding 821.9 → 822).

Effectiveness check, leg by leg: realized beta = % change in portfolio / % change in index. Textbook: −1.2% / −1.5% = 0.8 — the target beta is achieved. A portfolio with β > 1 falls MORE than the market.
Cash equitization — concept decomposed
▪ Problem: cash yields less than equity/FI → cash drag → risk of underperforming the benchmark. ▪ Solution: BUY index futures to replicate the index return on the cash balance. ▪ Why futures: liquidity + low transaction costs vs direct equity investment. ▪ Aliases: cash securitization, cash overlay. ▪ Alternative: buy calls + sell puts, same strike & expiry = synthetic forward position. ▪ Setup in the beta formula: βₚ = 0 (cash), βₜ = 1 (match the index), MVₚ = cash position.

VIX — what it actually measures
▪ Definition: implied volatility of the S&P 500 over a forward period of 30 days — a weighted average inferred from traded S&P 500 calls AND puts with avg expiration of 30 days.   ↳ NOT actual/realized volatility — it is the expected volatility priced into options ("fear index / fear gauge"). ▪ Interpretation: annualized SD of expected ±% moves over the next 30 days, at 68% confidence. ▪ Rules of thumb: < 20 = low-risk environment | > 30 = high-risk. Very low → excessively bullish market; very high → excessively bearish. ▪ Two empirical properties: (1) mean reversion — spikes do not last; (2) negative correlation with stock returns, even more pronounced in downturns → VIX derivatives can offset equity losses. ▪ Other indexes: VSTOXX (EURO STOXX 50), VFTSE (FTSE 100), VDAX-NEW (DAX 30); US: S&P 100, DJIA, Nasdaq, Russell 2000.

VIX futures — how they differ from every other future
▪ No cost-of-carry pricing: impossible to invest directly in spot VIX → the cost-of-carry model cannot determine fair value. ▪ Price meaning: expected S&P 500 volatility in the 30-day period AFTER the futures expiration date. ▪ LONG VIX futures = tail-risk protection: vol ↑ in a crash → equity portfolio ↓ but VIX futures ↑. ▪ SHORT VIX futures = short volatility: captures the volatility risk premium embedded in S&P 500 options — but large losses if expected volatility spikes. ▪ History: CBOE futures 2004, options 2006 → volatility became a separate, tradeable asset class (pure-play bets).
VIX options
▪ Cash-settled, European-style — exercisable only at contract maturity. ▪ Value driven by expectations of VIX at contract expiry (not spot VIX today): calls gain when expected volatility at maturity ↑; puts gain when it ↓.
Contango vs backwardation — decomposed
▪ Basis = spot − futures price. Negative basis defines contango (longer-dated > short-dated): market expects 30-day vol to RISE. Typical when VIX is low (textbook: 18 Jul 2011, spot 20.95, upward curve). ▪ Backwardation: downward curve — market expects vol to FALL back. Typical after a spike (textbook: 9 Aug 2011, spot 35.06 after the S&P US-debt downgrade of 5 Aug 2011). ▪ Convergence: VIX futures settle against spot VIX → futures price converges to spot at expiration; the basis moves toward zero over the life of the contract.   ↳ contango: futures price declines toward spot → long loses on the roll   ↳ backwardation: futures price rises toward spot → long gains on the roll ▪ Roll yield = the P/L generated as basis → 0. Steeper short end of the curve → roll yield magnified.

Variance swap — structure decomposed
▪ Payoff basis: variance (σ²), not volatility (SD). ▪ Fixed leg: implied variance over the period = variance strike — known at initiation. ▪ Variable leg: realized variance of the underlying over the swap life — known only at maturity. ▪ Long (purchaser): RECEIVES realized variance, PAYS the strike. Gains when realized > implied. Pure play on realized vs expected variance. ▪ Mechanics: NO notional exchange at initiation, NO interim settlements — one single payment at expiration. Value = 0 at initiation (implied vol = best ex ante estimate of realized). ▪ Any underlying works as long as it is traded with a record of daily prices.
settlementₜ = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike) N₍ₐₙ = vega notional / (2 × K) profit/(loss) = N₍ₐₙ × (σ² − K²) = N₌ₒ₏ₐ × (σ² − K²) / (2K) realized: Rᵢ = ln(Pₜ / Pₜ₋₁) daily variance = Σ Rᵢ² / (N − 1) annualized = daily × 252
Two squaring traps: (1) both σ and K are quoted as volatilities (SD) — square them before any payoff computation (strike 20 → K² = 400). (2) Market quotes vega notional, not variance notional — divide by 2K first.
Professorʼs notes: (1) realized variance does NOT deduct the mean — movement is measured regardless of direction, which makes variances perfectly additive (one-year variance = two equal six-month pieces). That additivity is what powers the MTM valuation. (2) Vega = Δpremium/Δvolatility — why vega notional is the natural market quote.
Convexity — why hedgers love variance swaps
▪ Payoff is in variance, strike in volatility → payoff is convex in volatility (like bond price vs yield).   ↳ realized vol BELOW strike → losses smaller than a linear volatility derivative   ↳ realized vol ABOVE strike → gains greater than the linear derivative ▪ Tail-risk appeal: when equities crash and vol explodes, the swap profit increases at an accelerating rate.
Valuing a variance swap during its life — 3 steps
Step 1: expected variance at maturity (time-weighted, thanks to additivity) E[var] = σₜ² × (t/T) + K²₍ₜ₋ₜ₎ × ((T−t)/T) σₜ² = realized vol (initiation → valuation date), squared K₍ₜ₋ₜ₎ = implied vol quoted NOW for the REMAINING period, squared Step 2: expected payoff at maturity payoff = N₍ₐₙ × (E[var] − original strike²) Step 3: discount back to the valuation date value = payoff / (1 + r × remaining/12)
Dropped-detail watch: Step 2 uses the ORIGINAL strike (squared), not the currently quoted strike — the current quote only feeds the remaining-period leg of Step 1. And the discount rate is unannualized over the remaining months only.

Inferring market expectations — which derivative for what
ApplicationDerivative
Inferring expectations of FOMC movesFed funds futures
Inferring expectations of inflationCPI swaps
Inferring expectations of future volatilityVIX futures and options
Market expectations are derived from market prices — and can change rapidly after a market shock.
Fed funds — the two rates, decomposed
▪ Federal funds rate: rate deposit institutions charge each other on overnight interbank loans. The FFE (Fed funds effective) = weighted average of rates actually charged. ▪ Federal funds target rate: set by FOMC governors (8 meetings/year), as a range (e.g. 2.25%–2.50%), driven mainly by inflation and GDP growth. ▪ Control mechanism: the Fed does NOT directly set the FFE — it steers it into the range via open-market operations and interest paid on bank reserves. ▪ Fed funds futures: trade on the CME; price = 100 − expected average FFE at contract maturity; monthly maturities out to 36 months.
Probability of a target-rate change
% probability of rate change = (FFE implied by futures − current target rate) / (target rate assuming the change − current target rate) = (implied FFE − current target) / expected size of change current target = MIDPOINT of the target range
Trap: "current Fed funds target rate" in the formula = the midpoint of the range (1.50–1.75 → 1.625), not the bottom or top of the range.

📌 Read the Command Word
Global essay method · applies to every reading
Before writing an essay answer, read the command verb — it tells you the SHAPE a full-credit answer must take. After writing, count your slots against that shape. This replaces "do I feel done?" (which only tracks whether you said something TRUE) with a structural check (did I fill every slot?).
The 20-second check, every answer
1. Circle the command verb in the prompt
2. Name the shape it demands (concede+challenge? chain? list of N? delta?)
3. Count your slots against the shape — short means incomplete
4. Scan for trigger words you read past
Trigger words = slots the grader put there on purpose: all / every · only / never · over and above / in addition to · two / main / persistent / relative to. Each one is a deliberate instruction. Reading past them is how essay points get silently lost.
Why this works: you're not summoning missing content from nowhere — you're using the PROMPT'S structure to flag an empty slot, which then cues the retrieval. "Describe wants a cause — what's the cause here?" is a far better memory prompt than staring at a blank feeling like you forgot something.
The 17 CFA command words
Official definitions · grouped by the answer shape each one demands
STATE / RECALL — short, precise, no argument needed
DefineTo state exactly the meaning of
IdentifyTo recognize, to correctly pick out or name
CalculateTo compute, to determine by mathematical processes
DemonstrateTo show practical mastery of
FormulateTo express in a precise form; to devise
LAY OUT FEATURES — the describe-shape: a chain or a list of characteristics
DescribeTo state characteristic features of something, to portray it in words
ExplainTo make clear and intelligible, provide insight into
AnalyzeTo examine the constituent parts of something and how the parts relate to each other and to the whole
InterpretTo explain the meaning or implications of something, to reach a conclusion about something by application of knowledge
COMPARE / CONTRAST — two-sided: watch whether they want similarities too
CompareTo state the similarities and differences between
ContrastTo state the differences between
JUDGE / CONCLUDE — the highest bar: reach a position and back it
DiscussTo examine critically from various points of view, considering pros and cons and relevant details
EvaluateTo reach a conclusion about something by application of knowledge and judgment
JustifyTo provide good reasons for, to show to be valid or appropriate
DetermineTo decide on through analysis of alternatives, to find or ascertain definitely
RecommendTo advise as suitable or fit for purpose
EstimateTo determine an approximate value for something; to reach an informed but possibly imprecise evaluation of something
Definitions are the official CFA Institute command-word glossary, verbatim. The grouping maps each verb to the answer shape from the decoder above.
